# External Binding

The volume is bound in dark reddish-brown leather, showing the dignified wear of age at the corners and along the spine. The cover is elaborately decorated with <term>gold tooling</term> <note>A decorative technique where gold leaf is pressed into the leather using heated metal stamps or rollers.</note>.

->At the center of the cover is a large, ornate <term>mandorla</term> <note>An almond-shaped or diamond-shaped frame, often used in religious art to surround sacred figures.</note> composed of scrolling leaf and floral motifs.<-

Inside this central frame is a depiction of the **Crucifixion**: 

*   **Jesus Christ** is shown on the cross.
*   He is flanked by two standing figures, likely the **Virgin Mary** and **Saint John the Evangelist**, the traditional witnesses to the scene. 
*   Above Christ's head is a small rectangular plaque representing the <term>titulus crucis</term> <note>The sign placed above Jesus on the cross, traditionally inscribed with the Latin 'I.N.R.I.' (Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum).</note>.

Outside the central frame, in each of the four corners, is a stamped **fleur-de-lis** <note>A stylized lily symbol often associated with royalty or the purity of the Virgin Mary.</note>. The entire composition is surrounded by a border consisting of three thin, concentric gold lines. 

Several small circular indentations or dark spots are visible on the leather, likely indicating the locations where metal studs or protective bosses were originally fixed to the volume to prevent the leather from touching the surface of a desk.

<summary>This page describes the ornate leather binding of the manuscript, which features a gold-tooled scene of the Crucifixion and symbolic fleur-de-lis motifs.</summary>
<keywords>binding, leather, gold tooling, gilt, Crucifixion, fleur-de-lis, foliate scrolls, mandorla</keywords>

# Frontispiece: Hermetic Philosophy

The page is dominated by a central symbolic emblem, surrounded by faint, largely illegible handwritten annotations.

<insert>
M <note>Likely an initial or abbreviation, perhaps for "Magister" (Master) or a personal name.</note>

->HERMETIC PHILOSOPHY<-
<note>original Latin: "PHILOSOPHIA HERMETICA". This title refers to the esoteric tradition based on the writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, focusing on the hidden laws of nature and the spirit.</note>

The central vignette illustrates several layers of <term>Hermetic symbolism</term>:
*   **The Pelican in its Piety:** A bird is shown piercing its own breast to feed its young with its blood. In this context, it represents both the sacrifice of Christ and the alchemical stage of "multiplication," where the spiritual "essence" is nourished and increased.
*   **The Nest:** The pelican’s nest is shaped like a crescent moon, a symbol often associated with the feminine principle or the "silver" stage of alchemical work.
*   **The Pedestal:** The nest rests on a square stone base, symbolizing the material world or the four elements. 
*   **The Rose Cross:** The pedestal is inscribed with a cross and four roses, the signature emblem of the **Rosicrucians**, a secret philosophical society that emerged in the early 17th century.
*   **Divine Light:** Golden rays shine down from above, suggesting divine inspiration or the "Sun of Philosophy."
</insert>

# Dialogue of the Seraphic

holy virgin Saint Catherine of Siena: which most profoundly treats of Divine Providence; of nearly all mortal sins & of many other stupendous & marvelous things: as clearly appears in its table of contents <note>The original term "repertorio" refers to an analytical index or a detailed list of chapters designed to help the reader navigate the saint's complex theological arguments.</note>. Together with her life & canonization <note>Catherine was canonized in 1461 by Pope Pius II, and this inclusion suggests the book was intended as a comprehensive resource for her devotees.</note> & some notable chapters composed in her glory & praise. Newly revised & with the highest diligence corrected <note>original: "castigato." In early printing, this term indicated that the text had been carefully proofread and purged of errors found in earlier manuscript or printed versions.</note>.

<note>Saint Catherine of Siena (1347–1380) was a mystic and diplomat who remains one of the most influential figures in the history of the Catholic Church. The "Dialogue" is her masterpiece, dictated while she was in a state of ecstasy.</note>

In her right hand, she holds a flowering lily branch <note>The lily is a traditional symbol of purity and Catherine’s status as a "bride of Christ."</note> that supports a crucifix with the figure of Christ. In her left hand, she holds a book, upon which rests a flaming heart inscribed with the "IHS" Christogram <note>The "IHS" represents the first three letters of the name of Jesus in Greek; the flaming heart symbolizes her intense divine love.</note>. The background features a landscape with a fortified city or monastery on the left and a cluster of trees on the right.</image-desc>

# Index of the Dialogues
<meta>catchword: Love</meta>

¶ This is a table of all the things contained in this book.

->Abstinence<-
Abstinence in and of itself is worth nothing: and how it ought to be practiced. <note>Saint Catherine often emphasized that physical penance like fasting is merely a tool, and without internal desire for God, it lacks spiritual value.</note> Chapters 7, 11, 12, 104.

->Adam<-
Of the sin of Adam & Eve. Chapter 121, page 135.

->Ambition<-
Against the sin of ambition. Chapter 34.

->Love<-
Self-love <note>original: "amor proprio." For Catherine, "amor proprio" or disordered self-centeredness is the root of all evil and the primary obstacle to the soul's union with God.</note> deprives one of every virtue. Chapter 7.
Likewise, against self-love. Chapter 7.
Self-love is the cause of all sins. Chapters 38, 128.
There are many defects that arise from self-love. Chapter 127.
Self-love is pride and the cause of disobedience. Chapter 156.
Self-love is the deception of the disobedient: and many evils follow from it. Chapter 161.
The love of God and of one's neighbor is all one. Chapter 7.
Love and contrition satisfy for the fault <note>original: "satiffa a la colpa." This refers to the theological concept of "satisfaction," where the depth of one's love and sorrow for sin can make amends for the guilt of that sin.</note>. Chapter 4.
All labors performed without love are considered words and not deeds: and these do not enter into eternal life. Chapter 11.
On the order of the love of neighbor <note>In medieval theology, the "order of love" (ordo caritatis) dictated how one should love God first, then oneself properly, then one's neighbor.</note>. Chapter 11.
How one should love God and neighbor. Chapter 64.
By what signs one may know if love is perfect or imperfect. Chapter 64.
Against those who love God for temporal consolation <note>Referring to "mercenary" love—loving God only for the sake of the spiritual "sweetness" or earthly rewards He provides.</note>. Chapters 60, 67, 68.
On the third degree of love: which is perfect. Chapter 72.
In what manner one arrives at this love. Chapter 73.
On the signs to know that the soul has reached perfect love. Chapter 64.
On the riches that God gives to his lovers who ask him. Chapter 141.

When the powers of the soul are united, one walks with desire. Chapter 54.

Against those who do not correct themselves through the rebuke of the apostles. Chapter 36.

On the instability of temporal riches. Chapter 150.

More regarding this avarice. <meta>catchword: Poverty</meta>

[Concerning Saint Catherine] <note>original Latin: "De sancta Catharina." This serves as a general header for the index of her works.</note>
[Index ✠ iii] <note>original: "Repertorio." A finding aid or table of contents arranged by topic.</note>

## Counsel
**Whoever** does not observe the counsels at least mentally:
cannot observe the commandments. Chapter 47. <note>The "counsels" (evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience) are paths to perfection, while "precepts" or commandments are the minimum requirements for all believers.</note>
**The** perfect observe the counsels in practice. Chapter 47.

## Consolation
**On** the deception of those who love God only for consolation: which they feel in that love. Chapters 60, 67, 68, 99. <note>original: "consolatione." In Catherine’s writing, this refers to "spiritual sweetness" or the emotional joy felt during prayer, which can becomes a distraction if sought for its own sake.</note>
**God** sometimes deprives the soul of consolation for its own benefit. Chapter 64.
**On** the deception of those: who do not help their neighbor in necessity so as not to lose their spiritual consolation and devotion. Chapter 70, Chapter 59.
**On** the deception of those: who have placed their affection in consolation and mental visions. Chapter 71, 106.
**Repetition** of the aforementioned consolations. Chapter 72.
**The** servants of God do not care for consolation in this world. Chapter 143.

## Contemplation.
**Everything** must be left behind when God sends some contemplation into the mind. Chapter 66. <note>Catherine teaches that even good works or planned prayers should be set aside if God grants a direct moment of contemplative union.</note>

## Contrition.
**Contrition** and love satisfy for the punishment: and for the guilt. Chapter 4. <note>In medieval theology, "guilt" (colpa) refers to the offense against God, while "punishment" (pena) refers to the debt of justice that must be paid through penance or Purgatory.</note>
**How** one must have contrition especially at one's death. Chapter 37.
**Everything** must be left behind to attend to the contrition that God gives. Chapter 76.
**When** contrition is valid without confession and when not. Chapter 75.

## Body.
**How** the body hinders the soul. Chapters 83, 84.

## Bodily (Exercises).
**Bodily** exercise satisfies neither for the punishment: nor for the guilt. Chapters 9, 11, 12. <note>original: "Exercitio corporal." Catherine emphasizes that external penance (like fasting) is a tool, but only the internal "affection" of the heart can truly satisfy for sin.</note>

<summary>This page of the index organizes Catherine of Siena's teachings on spiritual discipline, warning against the "deception" of seeking emotional joy in prayer and emphasizing that internal contrition is more valuable than external bodily penance.</summary>
<keywords>evangelical counsels, spiritual consolation, spiritual deception, contemplation, contrition, penance, body and soul, bodily exercises</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical index (Repertory) of Catherine of Siena’s *Dialogues*. Following the entries for Counsel, Consolation, and Contemplation, this page organizes topics under "Correction," "Side," "Cruelty," "Damnation," and "Desires."</meta>

# Repertory of Dialogues
## Correction
**Against** prelates <note>In the Catholic Church, a prelate is a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot, who has authority over others.</note> who do not correct their subjects. Chapter 118.
**Faulty** prelates cannot correct their subjects; and subjects do wrong by not accepting correction even if the prelates are wicked. Chapter 125.
**Prelates** who do not correct their subjects are the cause of all evils. Chapter 125.
**On** the correction by holy prelates toward their subjects. Chapter 119.
**How** one ought to correct their neighbor without false judgment. Chapter 102.

## Side
**For** many reasons, Christ opened his side on the cross. Chapter 75. <note>This refers to the wound in Jesus's side, which Catherine frequently describes as a refuge for the soul and a symbol of God's open heart.</note>

## Cruelty
**On** cruelty against one's neighbor. Chapter 6.

## Damnation
**The** damned cannot desire any good. Chapter 40.
**Their** punishment will increase on the day of judgment upon seeing the glory of the blessed. Chapter 42. <note>In medieval theology, the "pain of loss" was intensified for the damned by witnessing the joy they rejected.</note>

## Desires
**What** the desires of the righteous are. Chapter 2.
**Desires** of the perfect, and especially in suffering pain for Christ. Chapters 78, 79.
**How** much the desire to suffer pain pleases God. Chapter 5.
**How** it is necessary to walk through the virtues with desire. Chapter 54.
**One** walks with desires when the powers of the soul are united. Chapter 54. <note>The "powers of the soul" traditionally refer to the memory, the intellect, and the will.</note>
**According** to the soul's desire, God manifests Himself to it. Chapter 61.
**On** the desire for tears <note>original: "lachryme." In mystical tradition, the "gift of tears" is a physical manifestation of deep spiritual contrition or love.</note> and how much it pleases God. Chapter 91.
**On** the infinite desire of tears. Chapter 92.
**God** fulfills the holy desires of those who persevere in knocking at the door. Chapter 107. <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 7:7: "Knock and the door will be opened to you."</note>
**God** delays His gifts to make our desires grow. Chapter 42.

<keywords>prelates, correction of subjects, Side of Christ, cruelty, damnation, holy desires, gift of tears, powers of the soul</keywords>

# On Saint Catherine
## Repertory ✠ 4

### Concerning the will.
->Disobedience<-
On disobedience concerning obedience.
->Despair<-
On despair: and on hope, especially at the point of death. Chapter 131.
->The Devil<-
On the deception of the devil regarding our souls. Chapter 44.
The devil transforms himself into an angel or into another saint. Chapter 71.
In what way one recognizes the aforementioned transformations, when they are from the devil or not. Chapters 71, 106. <note>In mystical theology, "discernment of spirits" was the practice of determining whether a vision came from God or a demonic deception.</note>
How the devil is overcome and confounded by the perfect. Chapter 70. <note>In Catherine’s writing, "the perfect" refers to those who have reached the highest stage of spiritual union with God.</note>
->Dignity<-
On human dignity and how one must suffer to conform to Christ. Chapter 12.
Also on human dignity: and how much love God has shown it. Chapter 13.
->Discretion<-
On discretion and how it is planted in humility. Chapter 9. <note>Discretion (or discernment) is a central virtue for Catherine; she famously calls it a "child" born from the union of the soul with God through humility.</note>
Discretion renders first to God what is due. Chapter 7.
Discretion is joined with charity and humility. Chapter 10.
How much love God has shown to man. Chapters 13, 14.
God laments over his people and principally over the clergy. Chapter 18.
God constrains himself to mercy through the prayer of the just. Chapter 15.
No one can go out from the hands of God. Chapter 18. <note>Catherine often emphasizes that everything—even justice—is a manifestation of God's hand, and no one can escape His reach, whether through mercy or through the law.</note>
God draws man to himself through love if man does not resist. Chapter 26.
God manifests himself to the soul in many ways. Chapter 61.
God does not depart from the perfect through grace nor through feeling: but rather through union. Chapter 78.
The goodness of God extends over sinners. Chapter 80.
God induces his servants to pray and labor for the Church. <note>The text here cuts off at "chie<unclear>sa</unclear>" (Church).</note>

# Of Saint Catherine

How grave sinners are converted by good example. Chapter 47.

->Fortitude<-

Fortitude, patience, and perseverance conquer all things. Chapter 77.

->Glory<-

Sinners and worldly people give glory to God against their will. Chapter 180.

The truly humble person considers themselves the cause of all the evils in the world. Chapter 2.
Through self-knowledge and the blood of Christ, one comes to contrition. Chapter 4.
Humility cannot exist without charity and discretion. Chapter 10. <note><term>Discretion</term> in Catherine’s work refers to a "spiritual sobriety" or the ability to choose the middle path of virtue without falling into extremes.</note>
Concerning self-knowledge, which is attained through knowledge of divine goodness; and through knowledge of divine goodness, one comes to the knowledge of oneself. Chapters 13, 72, 73. <note>This "Cell of Self-Knowledge" is a central pillar of Catherine's spirituality: knowing one's own nothingness helps one recognize God's infinite love.</note>
The humble, God-fearing person is more capable of advising and understanding...

# Of Saint Catherine <note>original: "De sancta Catharina"</note>

How, having known the sins of the world by divine revelation, she considered herself the cause of them all: wherefore she desired to sweat blood. <note>original: "sudori di sangue"</note> Chapter 19.

How she marvels at the divine goodness and gives thanks. Chapters 25, 30, 108.

How she fell into great bitterness because of the ignorance of those who are damned. Chapter 50.

How the state of souls was shown to her. Chapters 57, 58.

In what manner she responded to the temptations of the devil. Chapter 66.

How it was shown to her why Christ willed to open his side. <note>Referring to the wound in Christ's side during the Crucifixion, often interpreted in mysticism as an opening to his heart.</note> Chapter 75.

How God moves her to tears for the whole Church. Chapter 86.

How she makes three petitions to God. Chapter 97.

How much she was beloved by God. Chapter 98.

How, filled with anxiety and intoxicated with love, she asks for an explanation of the fruits of tears. <note>term: intoxicated (ebria) — in mystical literature, this refers to a soul being "drunk" on divine grace or love, losing concern for worldly things.</note> Chapter 97.

How she makes a prayer for the Church and especially for her spiritual children and for two spiritual fathers. Chapter 108.

How she had a wondrous vision concerning the Sacrament of the Altar. <note>term: Sacrament of the Altar — the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note> Chapter 111.

How she offers a long thanksgiving to the divine goodness. Chapter 134.

How she offers a prayer with great affection and humility for all the people. Chapter 134.

How she was in awe of divine providence and thanked God. Chapter 153.

How she makes a most beautiful thanksgiving, act of humility, and prayer for the Church. Chapter 162.

The passing <note>original: "trāsito" — traditionally used to describe the death of a saint as a "passing over" to heaven.</note> of Saint Catherine is at the end of the book.

Tears: Saint Catherine asks God about the fruit of tears. Chapter 97.

<meta>catchword: for</meta>

Desires and actions of the perfect. <note>original: "Desiderii & opatiõe d' pfecti" — "Opatiõe" is an abbreviation for "operazione," meaning actions or spiritual workings.</note> Chapters 78, 79, 84

Also concerning their tears. Chapter 96
On the light of the perfect who consider themselves worthy of every tribulation and every evil. Chapter [not listed]

->Bridge<-

Since the way was broken by the first sin, Christ is made a bridge. <note>This is a central image in Catherine’s *Dialogues*: Christ's body serves as a bridge connecting humanity to God after the "road" was destroyed by Adam's fall.</note> Chapter 21
How that bridge extends from heaven to earth. Chapter 22
The said bridge has three stairs, namely the feet, the side, and the mouth. <note>These represent the three stages of the soul's journey: from the feet (stripping away of vice), to the side (the heart/love), to the mouth (peace and union).</note> Chapter 26
Those three stairs are figured by the three powers of the soul. <note>term: three powers of the soul — memory, intellect, and will.</note> Chapters 51, 54
Those stairs signify three states of man: namely the imperfect, the perfect, and the most perfect. Chapters 56, 57
The said bridge is raised on high without departing from the earth.

# Repertory of the Dialogue

To help one's neighbor, one should rather lose their own temporal and spiritual consolations: Chapter 69. <note>In Catherine’s theology, true charity involves being willing to sacrifice even one's own spiritual "comforts" or private prayer time to serve the needs of others.</note>
For one who must love God, love of neighbor is necessary: Chapter 99.
How one should correct their neighbor: Chapter 105.

->Purgatory<-

God provides even in purgatory: Chapter 148.

->Quiet<-

Of the evil that follows the just when in a state of quiet without tribulation: Chapter 145. <note>Catherine warns that a life without challenges or "tribulations" can lead to spiritual stagnation or false security.</note>

->Redemption<-

Of the benefit of redemption: Chapters 13, 14, 15, 135.
Sin committed after redemption is punished more severely than before: Chapter 15. <note>The argument here is that having received the grace of Christ’s sacrifice, the soul is more accountable for turning away from God.</note>

Against religious who do not live in community: Chapter 158.
Of the excellence of obedient religious: Chapter 159.
Of the bitterness of disobedient religious, who taste the earnest-money of hell in this life: Chapter 161. <note>original: "lara" (l'arra) — A legal or commercial term for a down payment or pledge. Catherine uses it to mean a "foretaste" of eternal suffering.</note>
The disobedient have more toil in religious life than the obedient: Chapter 161.
Of negligent religious who nevertheless do not wish to sin mortally: Chapter 163.
Of the great danger of the aforementioned: Chapter 162.

# Life of Saint Catherine

## Proemial epistle in the most profound and sublime book of the Dialogue of the seraphic <note>The term "seraphic" refers to the Seraphim, the highest order of angels, characterized by their burning love for God. Catherine was often called the "Seraphic Virgin."</note> and most beloved spouse of our sweetest Savior Jesus Christ: Sister of the Third Order <note>A branch of the Dominican Order for laypeople or those living in the world rather than in a cloistered monastery.</note> of Saint Dominic: Saint Catherine of Siena: in which is contained her life and doctrine very briefly:

To the most illustrious and most excellent ladies and duchesses, Lady Isabella, consort of the most illustrious Lord Gian Galeazzo Sforza, most powerful Duke of Milan; and Lady Beatrice, consort of the most illustrious Lord Ludovico Sforza, most worthy Duke of Bari; most singular protectors and benefactresses of the Order of Friars Preachers <note>The official name of the Dominican Order.</note> of Saint Dominic: Brother N. <note>The letter "N." is likely a placeholder for "Nomen" (Name) or refers to a specific friar whose identity was known to the recipients but is abbreviated here.</note> of the aforementioned Order of the Observance <note>A movement within the Dominicans that sought to strictly observe the original, more rigorous rules of the order.</note>, and a professed member of the convent of **Santa Maria delle Grazie** in Milan, with humble recommendation, sends greetings in the sweetest Savior, our true salvation, Jesus Christ:

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring a portrait of a man in a cap and robes, possibly a scholar or cleric, set against a shaded background within a square frame.</image-desc>

How great the divine goodness and clemency toward the human race has been, and is at present, most illustrious and most excellent ladies—I do not say my own tongue, nor indeed any human one, but even the angelic tongue would not be sufficient to narrate. Therefore: for He, having created humanity as a most noble creature, both in regard to the soul and also the body—distinguished and adorned with many most illustrious gifts, graces, and privileges—even after the lapse into sin, committed by humanity's own will, He never ceased to lead it back to Himself, giving it, according to the times and current needs, the remedy of salvation. Primarily teaching humanity through the holy patriarchs and prophets, through diverse signs and miracles, through most horrible and terrifying judgments, and in infinite other ways: so that humanity—which through many sins and especially that of idolatry had departed and separated itself from that true fountain of goodness, and had drawn near to the foul, rotten, and abominable cesspool <note>original: "sentina," literally the bilge water of a ship, used here to describe the filth of sin.</note> of sin...

sin and of every malice: through so many terrors [humanity] might be led back to divine worship and to good works. But seeing that divine goodness—noticing that through fear nothing or very little was gained—decided to draw humanity to Himself through love. Wherefore, moved by inexhaustible <note>original: "iextiabile" (likely *inestinguibile*), meaning unending or unquenchable.</note> love toward His so-beloved creature, He sent His only-begotten Son to it, who is the living and true God: who would take on human flesh, and with many hardships, labors, pains, torments, and finally with the shameful death of the cross, would free it from sin. This was done so that seeing such love toward himself, man might return to Him and be ashamed not to show some sign of love and reciprocity of charity toward God, who for his love suffered so much for him. 

O blind and darkened human mind, how ungrateful you are toward your Lord, you who do not deign to serve Him who has suffered so much for you! If it does not please you to love Him, at least do not find it burdensome to love Him in return. 

This sweetest and loving Lord also gave the doctrine of life to human nature, teaching it through the holy apostles, who as most victorious captains carried the banner <note>original: "confalone," a processional standard or heraldic banner.</note> of this sacred doctrine, traveling throughout the entire world, destroying idolatries and planting the true faith of the Creator, which was entirely missing from the world. 

But the enemy of human nature <note>The Devil.</note> stirring up pagan princes against this truth, God kindled the spirit of the most holy martyrs, who with their endurance overcame the aforementioned tyrants. Peace being then restored to the holy Church, the aforementioned enemy sowed the weeds <note>original: "zinzania," referring to the tares or darnel from the Parable of the Weeds in Matthew 13.</note> of infinite errors within the holy Church. Against these, Eternal Goodness sent the most sacred Doctors of the Church: Athanasius, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, John Chrysostom, Hilary, Jerome, Ambrose—the most excellent and unshakeable protector of your Milanese people—Augustine, and Pope Gregory.

She wished to perform the duties of the maidservants in her father's house, and she helped the poor of Christ with the greatest generosity. She served the sick with the greatest charity, and she overcame the continuous battles and temptations of the demons with the shield of patience and the helmet of holy faith. She consoled the imprisoned and the oppressed as much as was possible for her; never did an idle or irreligious word come from her mouth, but she always spoke of God, of the salvation of souls, and of holy things.

All her speech was of good morals, the study of a holy life, the practice of piety, the contempt for the world, the love of God and neighbor, and the heavenly homeland. No one went to her who did not return better and more learned. -># Saint Catherine #<-
->Life of St. Catha. +++ iiii<-

she had never learned to read or write, except through a miracle so that she would know how to recite the **canonical hours of the office** <note>original: "hore canonice del officio"; the set of daily prayers, consisting of psalms and readings, recited by clergy and members of religious orders.</note>, which she often recited together with her sweet spouse Jesus Christ, walking or pacing through her room together with him. So great was the grace of God in that holy tongue, that there was no heart so hard or obstinate that it would not be converted to penance. When she exhorted people to do good works, her face seemed like that of a **cherub** <note>An angelic being often depicted in art with a radiant or beautiful face; here suggesting a divine glow during her speech.</note>, and she would never have ceased speaking as long as she had listeners. Because of this teaching, her fame grew so much that hundreds and thousands of people came—not only from Siena and its countryside, but also from various other parts of Italy, representing different ranks and conditions of people. Prelates, notable priests, religious men and women of every order, gentlemen, citizens, craftsmen, and women of every dignity and status flocked to the sacred teaching of Catherine. And those who could not have personal access to her wrote to her according to their needs; she, responding to them through many **epistles** <note>Letters, often containing formal teaching or spiritual guidance.</note>, gave instructions for the salvation of their souls. So great was the number of letters that she wrote—and had written by four **secretaries** <note>original: "scriptori"; Catherine famously dictated her letters, often to multiple scribes at once while she was in a state of spiritual ecstasy.</note>—that after her holy death, some of her devotees gathered them into two volumes (though not all of them, only some). ...recently [supporting] the convent of **Saint Mary of the Angels** in Ferrara, giving and most liberally providing for every need of those venerable fathers who reside in that convent and pray to God for the preservation of your most illustrious Ladyship. 

But what shall I say of our most illustrious Lord, **Gian Galeazzo Sforza** <note>Gian Galeazzo Sforza (1469–1494) was the Duke of Milan, though his uncle Ludovico held the actual power.</note>, the most invincible Duke of Milan? I have been moved to offer, attribute, and dedicate this present most worthy book to your most excellent and illustrious Ladyships; both for your consolation and also for the honor of this holy book itself. Being full of sanctity and virtue, it should not be dedicated to anyone but virtuous persons, such as your Excellencies, who—though in the youthful age of your years—are aged in virtue and manners. You are worthily deserving of having such a **mirror** placed before your eyes, so that by reflecting upon the life of this saint, as well as her sacred doctrine, you may always fulfill the will of God. 

May it please your most illustrious Ladyships to receive this gift from this humble servant of yours, and to take as your advocate, teacher, and **seraphic** <term>seraphic: A title often given to Saint Catherine of Siena (and Saint Francis) to describe a soul "on fire" with divine love, like the Seraphim angels.</term> **Saint Catherine of Siena**, the bride of blessed Jesus Christ.

# OF POPE PIUS II
### The letter regarding the life and canonization of the blessed Catherine of Siena happily begins; in which many things drawn from the most profound moral and natural philosophy, as well as sacred theology, are contained.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'P' containing a portrait of a bearded man in profile, likely representing Pope Pius II, wearing a papal tiara or cap.</image-desc>Pius, bishop, servant of the servants of God <note>original: "servus servorum dei" — a traditional title for the Pope expressing humility</note>, to all the faithful of Christ, greetings and apostolic blessing. The mercies of the Lord, which we experience more abundantly day by day, no mortal tongue can sufficiently explain. Divine favors surpass human eloquence, nor is it given to man to praise his Creator enough—not even if all his limbs were turned into tongues. For we were created from nothing; from non-existence, we were brought into being. Nor were we made as stones, or plants <note>OCR "plate" is a likely error for "plantae" (plants)</note>, or brute animals, but we were made partakers of reason and capable of divine things. We were crowned with glory and honor, made not only like the angels, but in a certain way similar to the invisible and high God himself, having gained mastery over all His works. 

Yet, if we compare ourselves to all other things, no creature is found more ungrateful than man. If we set aside the pride of Lucifer and his companions, man alone among all others is rebellious toward God and most ungrateful. All other things praise the divine mercy in their very being, and they never oppose His commands; they obey the laws of nature and carry out those things for which they were produced. The earth endures the plow, and receiving the seeds as if they were its own, returns them multiplied with interest. Obeying the command of God, it provides for the human race through both cultivated and uncultivated lands. Stones are ready at hand when used for buildings; they do not resist being split or fired <note>original: "excocta" — referring to the processing of stone or clay into building materials like lime or bricks</note>. Trees flourish in the field, and after they have withered, they either feed the fire or stand as houses and roofs. How great is the virtue of herbs, whether in their leaves or in their roots...

# OF SAINT CATHERINE
### iii

Whether in flowers, in seeds, or in juices, there is usefulness; how great is the convenience found in rivers, how much in lakes and in the seas, which, while ships travel upon them, provide commerce among the most distant peoples. What of other animals, whether they live in water or on land? In all of them, God is praised as they follow the commands of nature. The elements and the stars perform what is commanded: the sun completes its course and does not exceed the prescribed boundaries of the <term>zodiac<note>The imaginary belt in the heavens through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move; here used to signify the divinely ordained path of the stars.</note></term>; nor, shining with its own light, is the moon <note>original: "luna"</note> lacking in its duty; nor do the "wandering stars" <note>original: "errantes stelle" — a common term for planets in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> stray, as they always move on a fixed and established path. All things in heaven and on earth praise God, and remaining in their duty, they bless Him; nor do they resist the laws imposed upon them. Heavy things fall downward; light things are carried upward; all things show gratitude to the Divinity; they obey God and nature. 

Man alone is found to be ungrateful, disobedient, and rebellious among so many created things; he imitates the ruin of the perverse angel <note>A reference to the fall of Lucifer.</note>. That one, becoming proud in heaven and desiring to be like his Creator, was cast headlong into the abyss and paid the penalty for his calculated crime. Man, made from the mud <note>original: "limo" — the earth or clay from which Adam was formed in Genesis.</note> and placed on the earth, unmindful of his own weakness, also began to desire high things; by eating from the forbidden tree, he wished for equality with the gods through the knowledge of good and evil. Because of this, he was cast out from the paradise of delights and given over to many hardships; and with the gate of the kingdom of heaven closed, death entered into the world, sparing no man. 

How much the sons of Adam wandered before the <term>Deluge<note>The Great Flood described in the Bible.</note></term>, and how far they withdrew from the divine will, the vengeance that followed made clear, which wiped out all flesh in a flood of waters—except for those who were saved with the pious Noah in the ark. Furthermore, wickedness and sloth were not lacking even among his sons; they themselves became malicious and fell into every kind of sin. The Tower of Babel was begun as an insult to the Lord, and there the universal language of the earth was divided. From these people, wars were introduced; robberies...

# CANONIZATION
### iii

<meta>catchword: blasphemies</meta>

...riots, fires, and slaughters: only a very few lovers of the divine law were found up until the time of Abraham. He, truly a unique and certain example of piety, so submitted himself to the will of God that he did not hesitate to sacrifice his own son; because of this, all nations were blessed in his seed <note>original: "in semine eius" — a biblical reference to the covenant with Abraham in Genesis, promising that his descendants would bless the world.</note>. From his children arose not only the prophets, the preachers of the divine law, but also the Savior Christ himself deigned to be born according to the flesh. He, for the salvation of the human race—though he was in the form of God and equal to the Father—emptied himself, taking the form of a servant <note>original: "exinanuit seipsum formam serui accipiens" — a direct quotation of Philippians 2:7, describing the "Kenosis" or Christ's voluntary humility.</note>. 

Having become man, he underwent the weariness of the flesh, bore torments and tortures, and sustained even the final death upon the wood of the cross. This death was not according to nature, but was ignominious, violent, most bitter, and scarcely tolerable for a man. Dying in this way, he destroyed our death and restored life. He despoiled the underworld <note>original: "Spoliauit inferos" — a reference to the Harrowing of Hell, a popular medieval belief that Christ descended into the afterlife to rescue the righteous souls of the Old Testament.</note>, led away the holy fathers, and as the victor over death and the triumphant conqueror of the devil, opening heaven which had been closed for so long, he ascended to the Father. 

He showed us the way by which we might follow him, having handed down the law of the Gospel, and having opened <term>baptism<note>A ritual of purification and admission into the Christian Church.</note></term> and the other <term>sacraments<note>Sacred rites, such as the Eucharist or Confirmation, considered to be outward signs of inward grace.</note></term>, through which those who have fallen might be restored and saved. Yet our arrogance and wickedness have not rested, though drawn by so many and such great benefits. Man has neither shown a grateful soul nor abandoned his vices; rather, the greater the gift of grace we have received, the more ungrateful we are found to be, and the more inclined toward forbidden things. 

For in what way do we love or honor the sublime God? How do we keep His commandments? Who obeys the most holy Gospel? What subjection is there toward superiors, what charity toward inferiors? What devotion is there to equity or <term>justice<note>original: "iustitie"</note></term>? What religion? What are the morals of men? There are those who say in their hearts, "There is no God" <note>original: "non est deus" — a reference to the opening of Psalm 14.</note>; others bring forth impious dogmas and blasphemies.

# THE CANONIZATION OF SAINT CATHERINE
### iiii

...they cast blasphemies against God. Others, slaves to pleasure, think of nothing else except how they might satisfy their lusts. Some gape at the wealth of others; others thirst for human blood. Innocence is rare, and it is hardly safe. Neither the rights of kinship nor written laws or those laws made holy by custom are of any use; all things obey force and fraud. Thus, it is not without reason that the devil is called the "prince of this world" <note>original: "princeps mundi huius" — a title for Satan used in the Gospel of John.</note>, since the greater part of the globe is led by his will. 

For how great a portion is possessed by the insanity of the false prophet Muhammad: the chief part of the East, and the greatest kingdoms of Africa; and in Spain, the people of Granada <note>The "Granatenses" refers to the Emirate of Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, which fell to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492. This suggests the text was written before that date.</note>; and in Greece, many provinces under Muhammad blaspheme Christ. Nor is the nation of the Jews small, widely dispersed throughout the circle of the earth, an enemy to the holy Gospel and the Christian law; nor are idol worshippers lacking in the North and the East. 

Christianity has been reduced to Europe. For although not a few Christians are said to be dispersed through Asia and Libya <note>In the medieval period, "Libya" often referred to the continent of Africa generally.</note>, nevertheless their faith is not sincere; because they live far from the Apostolic See <note>The "Apostolic See" refers to the authority of the Pope in Rome.</note> among infidels and communicate with heretics, they hold to certain wicked views and teem with many errors. 

Nor do the Christians who are in Europe exist as Christians in reality as much as in name; the religion of many is shadowed and feigned, just as their works themselves manifest. For he is a Christian who does works worthy of a Christian; "by their fruits you shall know them," says the Lord in the Gospel <note>original: "a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos" — quoting Matthew 7:16.</note>. If we live as Christ commands, we will be Christians. John the Apostle asserts that men are the children of him whose commands they do. If we keep the commands of God, we are undoubtedly children of God. But if we keep those of the devil, we belong to him, as the Lord says: "You are of your father the devil" <note>original: "Vos ex patre diabolo estis" — quoting John 8:44.</note>. 

This is a harsh judgment, and yet true: for he is surely the son of, and belongs to him, whose commands he follows. However, how far ungrateful Christians have strayed from divine precepts, and how much they have adhered to diabolical suggestions, anyone can understand for themselves; let each person question their own conscience and place their past life before the eyes of their mind...

# THE CANONIZATION
### iiii

...and how far one has retreated from the duty of a true Christian, he shall plainly recognize. Since these things are so, the kindness of the most high God is greatest, and His mercy is incredible; He tolerates us and allows us to live, waiting for us to eventually be converted and return to the right path. 

But in every age, there have been found several holy men pleasing to God who, living in the flesh, conquered the desires of the flesh and led a heavenly life on earth. By their merits and intercession, the fabric of the world <note>original: "mundi machina" — a classical term for the structure of the universe.</note> has been sustained, the fires of judgment have been held back and diminished, and the wrath and vengeance of God has been suspended. Nor do we doubt that today, also, there are others accepted by God, whose prayers might render the heavenly King appeased and kind toward us. 

Among others who have pleased God and appeased divine mercy for us, the city of Siena—noble among the Etruscans <note>The "Etruscans" refers to the people of Tuscany.</note>—nourished in our own time Bernardino <note>Saint Bernardino of Siena (1380–1444), a famous Franciscan preacher known for his devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus.</note>. Born of a noble house, he renounced the world in the flower of his youth. Having entered the religious order of Blessed Francis, he found that the brothers of his order had strayed far from the original institutions and the Rule of the Fathers, and he corrected them sharply. Since he could not lead them all back to the way, he set apart the many who were pleased to keep the Rule; with these he frequented monasteries, many of which he built anew and reformed with the holiest of institutes <note>This refers to the "Observant" movement within the Franciscan Order, which sought a stricter adherence to St. Francis's original vision of poverty.</note>. 

He traveled throughout Italy preaching; he thundered against vices and raised up virtues. Wondrous was his abstinence, wondrous his integrity, his moderation, his gravity, the great sweetness of his eloquence, and his vast learning. Because he was a true devotee of poverty, a foe to money, and an enemy of all luxuries, a great cheerfulness always shone in his face and a supreme peace dwelt in his mind. As one who rejoiced in innocence alone, conscious of no crime, he confronted many scandals in Italy and performed many miracles. Because of these, even while he was still living, he was considered a saint and was honored by the common people with wondrous devotion. He was never seen without a crowd of people and a singular...

...was received with reverence. When he <note>Referring to Saint Bernardino of Siena, mentioned on the previous page.</note> had finished the course of this life at L'Aquila, a city of the Marsi <note>The Marsi were an ancient people of Italy; here it refers to the region around L'Aquila in Abruzzo.</note>, he was enrolled among the holy confessors of Christ by Nicholas V <note>Pope Nicholas V (reigned 1447–1455).</note>, our predecessor, in the very year of the Jubilee <note>The Jubilee of 1450.</note>, when the Christian world was visiting the city in great numbers to purge the filth of their vices. There was also in an earlier age, within the memory of our parents, in that same city [Siena], and of the female sex, the virgin Catherine. She was of no less merit, nor was she less accepted by God; we do not doubt that her prayers in the sight of the most high Divinity have been in the past, are now, and will be in the future, very beneficial to the human race. For just as the sins and blasphemies of evil men provoke the wrath of God upon us, so also do the works and prayers of the saints turn it away. 

But Catherine, although she led an angelic life on earth and, departing eighty years ago <note>Catherine died in 1380; this speech takes place in 1461.</note>, migrated to heaven, and was renowned for many signs and glorious miracles, had not yet been received among the holy virgins of Christ by the Church Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the Christian church on earth, as opposed to the "Church Triumphant" in heaven.</note>. For the Roman pontiffs who were before us had not decreed it. Urban VI had wished to bestow this honor upon her, and after him Innocent VII, and then Gregory XII, all of whom had special knowledge of this virgin and her holy conversation <note>original: "sancte cōuersationis" — in this context, "conversation" refers to her way of life and conduct.</note>. 

But they were vexed by the disturbance of the Schism <note>The Great Western Schism (1378–1417), a period when there were rival claimants to the papacy.</note> which flourished in their time. Agitated by many whirlwinds of wars and troubles, they omitted this act by divine counsel (as we believe), lest while the storm of division raged, what one obedience <note>In the Schism, the factions following different popes were called "obediences."</note> decreed as sacred, the other would deem profane. The matter was delayed until our times, and the canonization of this most holy virgin was reserved for us, as if for our fellow-countrywoman and fellow-citizen; so that the holiness of the Sienese virgin might come into the light by the decree of a Sienese man sitting on the Roman see. In this matter, I do not deny that we have been drawn by a certain holy and pious affection. For who is there who [does not seek] the praises of his own city, of his own fatherland...

### Canonization

...praises: [the Church] does not willingly seek to publicize the virtues of its own kind <note>original: "sui generis"</note> even when it is able to do so both rightfully and honorably. There is no one who does not eagerly look upon excellent deeds and men illustrious in virtue of every kind and in every part of the world; yet one does so more willingly and with greater joy in one’s own fatherland and among one's own people. And indeed, if we had seen the sublime gifts, noble intellect, divine mind, and most sacred will of the blessed Catherine in any nation, however distant, we would nevertheless be more joyful [to see them] in the city of Siena, which gave us birth. Indeed, we trust that we are far more specifically sharers in her merits than if this virgin had been born in Africa, or in Scythia <note>A region in central Eurasia, used here to represent a remote, "barbaric" frontier.</note>, or in India. For while it cannot be denied that proximity to the saints provides a prerogative to others, nevertheless, nothing may be said for this reason more or less than what is true; nor because of kinship or love of country <note>original: "patrie charitate"</note> should anyone be numbered among the saints without merits, without the customary examination, or without the usual solemnities. 

Therefore, although we heard with joy that the blessed Catherine, whose canonization was requested, was from Siena, we have omitted nothing in her canonization from those things required in so great a solemnity. Many petitions were present, not only from the people of Siena, but also from others; likewise, our most dear son in Christ, Frederick, the august Emperor of the Romans <note>Frederick III (1415–1493), who was crowned by Pius II.</note>, together with our beloved son, the noble man Pasquale, Doge of the Venetians <note>Pasquale Malipiero (reigned 1457–1462).</note>, entreated us not to allow this virgin to be further deprived of her honor on earth, toward whom the devotion of many peoples had been kindled, and many miracles concerning her were being made known. 

While we were heading toward Mantua <note>Pius II traveled to the Council of Mantua in 1459 to organize a crusade against the Ottoman Empire.</note> and had stayed for some time among the Sienese, and her immense merits and miraculous signs had been set before us in a public consistory <note>A formal meeting of the college of cardinals presided over by the Pope.</note>, and petitions had been offered most abundantly that we should decree for her the honors of the saints of Christ, we by no means assented immediately. But, according to ancient custom, [we entrusted the matter] to three of our brothers of the Holy Roman [Church...] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next word is "Church."</note>

->**Saint Catherine**<-

...to the cardinals of the church: one a bishop, another a priest, and the third a deacon. We commissioned them by oral decree <note>original: "vive vocis oraculo"</note> to diligently inquire—following the necessary legal procedures—into the life and character of the blessed Catherine herself, as well as her miracles, whether performed during her life or after her death, and into all other matters necessary for canonization. We commanded these commissioners to provide a faithful report to us in a secret consistory <term>Consistory: A formal meeting of the Pope and the College of Cardinals to discuss church business.</term>, as is the custom. They worked for a year and more, until I returned to Rome from Mantua <note>Pius II presided over the Council of Mantua in 1459 to organize a crusade against the Ottoman Empire.</note>. 

During this time, they discussed the matter by examining ancient records found among the Venetians and others, questioning new witnesses, and weighing every detail with the utmost diligence. After they had provided a true report to us privately among the cardinals alone regarding all they had discovered, they then arranged for those findings they had presented to us to be recited again by an advocate in a public consistory. Finally, having summoned all the prelates of the churches then present in the Roman Curia to our hall in Rome, with the cardinals assisting us, the aforementioned commissioners spoke again through the voice <note>original: "per organum," literally "through the organ"</note> of our venerable brother William, Bishop of Porto <note>Guillaume d'Estouteville (c. 1412–1483), a powerful French cardinal and diplomat.</note>, who was the leader among them. He once more explained in our presence everything they had found and which appeared to be duly proven.

From their report, which was most extensive, we have received these summaries, which have been discovered, recognized, and explored as true:

The virgin Catherine, hailing from the city of Siena and born to parents of modest means, dedicated herself to God before she was even of an age to know Him. At six years old, desiring to serve the Lord, she longed for the wilderness; leaving the city, she hid in a cave in a solitary place, although she returned home after a short stay at the command of the Spirit. Having been taught the Angelic Salutation <note>The "Hail Mary" (Ave Maria) prayer, based on the Archangel Gabriel's greeting to Mary.</note>, whenever she climbed the stairs of her father's house, she knelt on every single step to [honor] the most blessed Virgin Mother...

# Canonization

...greeted the Lord. And as she grew older, she consecrated her virginity to Christ, whom she beheld in a wondrous vision sitting in His majesty; she heard the secrets of the heavenly court, which a mortal tongue cannot utter. She renounced all worldly delights and gave herself entirely to prayer; she afflicted her small body <note>original: "corpusculum," a diminutive often used in hagiography to emphasize a saint's physical frailty or humility</note> with fastings and scourgings, and she taught and persuaded girls of her own age to do the same. Having reached puberty, she cut her hair and refused mortal marriage; she despised the insults and curses of men. 

She extorted rather than simply obtained the habit of Blessed Dominic, which women wear who are called "of Penitence" <note>The "Brothers and Sisters of Penance" was the name for the Dominican Third Order; Catherine's group was known as the *Mantellate* because of their black cloaks.</note>. She performed the duties of a servant in her father's house, desiring nothing more than to appear lowly and abject among men. She helped the poor of Christ with a generous hand—for her father had allowed her this—and ministered to the sick with the greatest diligence. She overcame diabolical temptations and the constant battles of malignant spirits with the shield of patience and the helmet of faith; she consoled the imprisoned and the oppressed in whatever ways she could. 

No word that was not religious or sacred ever escaped her lips. All her speech was about morals, religion, piety, the contempt of the world, the love of God and neighbor, and the heavenly homeland. No one approached her who did not leave more learned and better; her teaching was infused <note>original: "infusa," meaning it was granted by divine grace rather than through formal study or "acquired" knowledge</note>, not acquired. She appeared as a teacher before she was seen as a disciple; indeed, when professors of sacred letters and even bishops of great churches proposed very difficult questions about divinity to her, she responded most prudently. She satisfied them to such an extent that she sent back as tamed lambs those whom she had received as ferocious wolves and lions. Some of these men, marveling at the divine wisdom in the virgin, soon distributed their possessions to the poor and, taking up the cross of the Lord, bound themselves to an evangelical life. The abstinence of this virgin was of the highest degree—

### Saint Catherine

...abstinence was: and a wonderful austerity of life. She was found at one time to have extended her fast from Ash Wednesday even unto Pentecost, content with the communion of the Eucharist alone. For about eight years she was sustained by a very small amount of herb juice—and that little was barely retained—and by holy communion. 

She approached food as if it were a punishment; but she set out for the communion of the altar, which for her was nearly a daily occurrence, with the greatest alacrity, as if she had been invited to a heavenly wedding. She assisted the miserable enduring unworthy things; she rebuked sinners; she recalled them to repentance with the sweetest words; she joyfully gave the precepts of salvation to everyone. 

With a cheerful countenance, she showed what ought to be followed and what ought to be avoided; with the greatest zeal she settled those who were in disagreement; she extinguished many hatreds and calmed mortal enmities. ### Saint Catherine

[Absti]nence was hers, and a wonderful austerity of life. For since she had entirely cast aside the use of wine and meat, and did not even use common pottages, she was eventually brought to such a point that she ate neither legumes nor bread—except for the heavenly bread which a true Christian receives in the Sacrament of the Altar <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>. It was found that she sometimes extended her fast from Ash Wednesday until Pentecost, content with the communion of the Eucharist alone. For about eight years, she was sustained by the juice of a few herbs—which she rarely kept down—and by Holy Communion. She approached food as if it were a punishment; yet she went to the communion of the altar, which for her was almost daily, with the greatest eagerness, as if she had been invited to a heavenly wedding. 

She wore a hairshirt <note>original: *cilicio*, a garment of rough animal hair worn against the skin to cause discomfort as a form of penance</note> under her clothing, with which she wore down her flesh; she had no feathers or pillows. She constructed a bed for herself out of wooden boards, and lying upon it, she took only the shortest sleep. Indeed, she rarely slept more than two hours during the day and night; all the rest of her time she spent in waking, praying, preaching, and performing works of mercy. 

She wore down her flesh with thorny cords; she was tortured by a nearly constant pain in her head; she burned with fevers, and was never free from their torment. She struggled very frequently with demons and was vexed by many of their harassments, but she said with the Apostle: *when I am weak, then I am strong* <note>original: *cum infirmor, tunc fortior sum*; a reference to 2 Corinthians 12:10</note>. 

For she did not fail in such great labors, nor did she neglect the works of charity. She assisted the wretched who were suffering indignities; she rebuked sinners; she called them back to penance with the gentlest words; she joyfully gave the precepts of salvation to everyone. She showed with a cheerful face what should be pursued and what should be avoided; she settled disputes with the greatest zeal; she extinguished much hatred and calmed mortal enmities. For the sake of the peace of the Florentines <note>original: *florentiorum*</note>, who were in discord with the Church and had been placed under an ecclesiastical interdict <note>A "spiritual strike" where the Church withholds certain sacraments and public worship from a city or region as a punishment</note>, she [crossed] the Apennines and the Alps...

# Canonization

...to the end; and she did not hesitate to travel all the way to Avignon to see Pope Gregory XI <note>Gregory XI (r. 1370–1378) was the last of the Avignon popes; Catherine is famously credited with persuading him to return the Papacy to Rome.</note>, our predecessor. To him, she showed that she had divinely recognized his own vow to return to the city of Rome—a vow made in secret, known only to himself and God. For in her was the spirit of prophecy: she predicted many things before they happened and revealed the most hidden secrets. 

She was often seized by the Spirit; suspended in the air, she fed upon divine contemplations, so far outside of herself that she felt nothing at all, even when she was pricked or struck. This happened to her frequently when the most divine Eucharist <note>The Sacrament of Holy Communion</note> was being offered. The name of Catherine was great and holy among the common people; the sick and those harassed by evil spirits were brought to her from all sides, and many were cured. 

She commanded illnesses in the name of Christ and forced demons to depart from the bodies of the possessed. Because of these things, she was most highly regarded by two Roman Popes—Gregory, whom we mentioned shortly before, and Urban VI—to such an extent that she performed diplomatic missions <note>original: *legationibus*, referring to her role as a papal legate or envoy</note> for them and was bestowed by them with many great spiritual graces. 

When she had finished her life's struggle, around her thirty-third year of age, she closed her days in the city of Rome. Regarding the assumption of her soul into heaven and its glorious reception, wondrous and admirable revelations are found among those persons who loved the Virgin. 

Especially, however, they are found with her confessor, Raymond of Capua <note>A prominent Dominican friar and Catherine's spiritual director who wrote her primary biography, the *Legenda Major*.</note>, a Master of Sacred Theology, who later became the father, master, and rector general of the entire Order of Preachers <note>The Dominican Order</note>. He recounts that while he was in Genoa on the night the Virgin passed away <note>original: *migrauit*, literally "migrated" or "departed"</note>, in the morning hour within the dormitory, near an image of the Mother of the Lord, he beheld her shining with a miraculous splendor and speaking words of consolation to him.

### Saint Catherine

...ended with the greatest devotion and reverence of the people. At her touch, many who were sick attained health; indeed, it brought healing to some just to touch the things that had touched the sacred limbs of the virgin. 

Afterward, the virgin herself, having been received into heaven, kindly heard the prayers of those pleading, and she saw to it that they were granted by her spouse and Lord, Christ the Savior. For many were cured of various illnesses who, having heard of the most glorious fame of Blessed Catherine, immediately sought her patronage. For this reason, in Venice—where the virgin herself had never been—and in many other places, her name is found with veneration, and many vows are made to her. 

When the same venerable Bishop of Porto <note>Porto is a "suburbicarian" diocese near Rome; its bishop traditionally holds a high rank in the Papal Curia and played a key role in investigating candidates for sainthood.</note> had set forth these and many other matters in the assembly of cardinals and prelates, and affirmed they were clearly proven, all the cardinals and prelates—of whom many were present—were asked individually to give their opinion. By the votes of everyone, the Blessed virgin was seen as worthy to be declared among the heavens and the stars, nor was there anyone who did not greatly approve of performing her canonization. 

Having heard these things at length, we ordered a decorated platform to be prepared in the Basilica of Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles, upon which today—with the people and clergy standing by—after a sermon on the life and miracles of this virgin was delivered by us, and the solemnity of the Mass celebrated, and the customary ceremonies performed in due order, we have decided to proceed to the canonization of this virgin with these words: 

"To the honor of the Almighty and eternal God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit; for the exaltation of the Catholic faith and the growth of the Christian religion; by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ and of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul: we declare this our Catherine of Siena, a virgin of illustrious and indelible memory—whose body lies here in Rome, in the church of the <term>Preachers</term> <note>The Order of Preachers, commonly known as the Dominicans, to which Catherine belonged as a member of the Third Order.</note> called 'of Minerva' <note>The Church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, which still houses the majority of Catherine's relics.</note>—to be [numbered] in the heavenly Jer[usalem]..."

### Canonization of Saint Catherine

...[into the heavenly] Jerusalem among the choirs of blessed virgins. Since her virtue, with the aid of divine grace, deserved long ago to have been received there, we declare—by the counsel of our brothers <note>The "brothers" refers to the College of Cardinals, whom the Pope consulted for the decision.</note>—that she has been granted the crown of eternal glory. We decree and define that she is to be honored as a saint both publicly and privately, and we command that she be entered and enrolled in the catalog of holy virgins whom the Roman Church venerates. 

We establish that her feast day is to be celebrated by the universal Church every year on the first Sunday of the month of May, and that she be granted all the honors known to befit other holy virgins. Furthermore, to those visiting her tomb on that feast day, we mercifully grant in perpetuity a remission of seven years and seven <term>quarantines</term> <note>A "quarantine" refers to a 40-day period of fasting or penance; this refers to the partial indulgence granted to pilgrims.</note> of the penances enjoined upon them, according to the custom of the Church. 

Given at Rome at Saint Peter’s, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1461, on the twenty-ninth of June <note>original: "tertio kalendas iulias" (the third day before the Kalends of July).</note>, in the third year of our pontificate.

Here ends the letter of canonization of Blessed Catherine of Siena by the Lord Pope Pius II, together with the entire sequence of her most holy life described very briefly, and many other matters worthy of knowledge, as can be easily read by everyone.

# In the name of Jesus Christ crucified: and of sweet Mary: and of the glorious patriarch Dominic.

The Book of Divine Providence, composed in the vernacular <note>original: "vulgare"—this refers to the common Italian language rather than the formal Latin used for official Church business.</note> by the seraphic virgin Saint Catherine of Siena, a sister of the Third Order of Saint Dominic <note>The "Third Order" consisted of laypeople who lived according to a religious rule while remaining in their homes, rather than in a cloistered monastery.</note>. While she dictated this to her scribe, she was caught up in a singular ecstasy and abstraction of mind. In this book, there occurs a conversation between God the Father and the virgin Catherine by way of a dialogue—that is, in a manner of speaking that takes place between two persons—and within it are contained high and most sweet divine secrets.

How a soul, uplifted by the desire for the honor of God and for the salvation of her neighbor, exercising herself in humble prayer, after she had seen the union of the soul with God—which is achieved in charity—asked of the same God four petitions. Chapter I.

**W**hen a soul, anxious with the greatest desire for the honor of God and the salvation of souls, came to exercise herself for some space of time in habitual virtue, she remained dwelling in the cell of self-knowledge <note>The "cell of self-knowledge" is Catherine's famous metaphor for internal reflection; she taught that one should always carry an "inner cell" of prayer regardless of their physical location.</note> in order to better know the goodness of God within her. For love follows knowledge; and by loving, she seeks to follow and clothe herself in the truth. But in no way does a creature taste so much of that truth, or become so illuminated by it, as through the means of humble and continuous prayer, founded on the knowledge of oneself and of God. For prayer, exercised in the manner described, joins the soul to God, following the footsteps of Christ <note>original: "xpō," a Greek-derived abbreviation for Christ.</note> crucified; and thus, through desire and affection and the union of love, it makes her another "self" with Him. This seems to be what Christ meant when He said: "He who loves me and keeps my word, I will manifest myself to him, and he will be one thing with me, and I with him." ### Providence III

<margin>22.32.</margin>
This desire was great and continuous, but it grew much greater when the First Truth <note>original: "prima uerita." Catherine frequently uses this title for God the Father.</note> showed her the needs of the world, and in what a tempest and offense against God it remained. She had also understood a letter which she had received from the father of her soul <note>Referring to her confessor and biographer, Raymond of Capua.</note>, in which he showed unbearable pain and sorrow for the offense against God, the loss of souls, and the persecution of the Holy Church. All of this set the fire of her holy desire ablaze with grief for the offense and with the joy of a hope through which she expected God to provide for such great evils. 

And because in Communion the soul seems to bind itself more sweetly between itself and God, and better knows His truth—since the soul is then in God and God is in the soul, just as the fish is in the sea and the sea is in the fish—for this reason, the desire came upon her for the arrival of the morning so she could have Mass, which was the day of Mary the Virgin <note>Likely referring to a Marian feast day, such as the Annunciation or Assumption.</note>. When the morning and the hour of the Mass had come, she took her place with anxious desire and with great self-knowledge, being ashamed of her own imperfection. It seemed to her that she was the cause of the evil being done throughout the whole world, conceiving a hatred and a displeasure for herself with a holy justice. In this self-knowledge, hatred, and justice, she purified the stains of guilt that appeared to be (and were) in her soul, saying: "O Eternal Father, I appeal from myself to You, that You may punish me for my offenses in this finite time. And because I, through my sins, am the cause of the pains that my neighbor must bear, <margin>32: is-</margin> <margin>an: ij</margin> I therefore pray You benignly that You punish them upon me."

Her desire [grew] stronger: acting as was done in the **Old Testament**: for when they made a sacrifice to God, a fire would come and pull the sacrifice to Himself, as it was acceptable to Him. The Sweet Truth <note>A title Catherine frequently uses for God the Father.</note> did the same to that soul: He sent the fire of the clemency of the **Holy Spirit** and snatched up the sacrifice of desire which she made of herself, saying: "Do you not know, daughter, that all the pains that the soul sustains, or can sustain, in this life are not sufficient to punish even the smallest fault? And therefore, I want you to know that not all the pains given in this life are given for punishment, but for correction, and to chastise the child when he offends. But this is true: that through the soul's desire, satisfaction is made; that is, with true contrition <note>original: "contritione." Sincere, heart-felt remorse for sin.</note> she makes satisfaction for the fault and for the penalty. This is not because of any finite pain she might endure, but because of her **infinite desire**. 

For I, who am infinite, require infinite love and infinite sorrow. I require infinite sorrow from the creature in two ways. One is for her own offense, which she has committed against Me, her Creator; the other is for the offense she sees her neighbor commit against Me. Regarding such people: because they have infinite desire—that is, they are joined to Me by the affection of love, and therefore they grieve when they offend Me or see Me being offended—every pain they endure, whether spiritual or physical, from whatever side it comes, receives **infinite merit**. It makes satisfaction for the fault that deserved infinite punishment, even though these were finite actions performed in a finite time. But because the virtue of desire was employed, and the pain was sustained with desire,
<margin>20:ns-</margin>
and with contrition and an infinite displeasure <note>original: "despiafimẽto" (dispiacimento).</note> for the fault, it therefore had such value. 

This was demonstrated by **Paul** when he said: *If I had the tongues of angels, if I knew future things, if I gave my possessions to the poor, and gave my body to be burned, and did not have charity...* <note>original: "charitade." Referring to the famous passage on love in 1 Corinthians 13.</note>

<summary>God explains to Catherine that human suffering in this life is intended for correction rather than full punishment, and that finite acts of penance only gain "infinite merit" when they are fueled by a deep, loving desire for God.</summary>

<margin>25. 5-30: 25-</margin>

# Providence IV

if he delays: once time has passed: there is no remedy at all because he has not brought the **dowry** <note>original: "dota." In this mystical context, the "dowry" refers to the natural faculties of the soul given by God at creation.</note> that was given to him by me: that is, giving him **memory**: so that he might retain my benefits; and the **intellect**: so that he might see and know the truth; and the **affection** <note>original: "laffecto." This is the **dowry** that I have given to you, which ought to return to me, the Father; but having sold and bartered it to the **devil** <note>original: "demōio"</note>: the devil, along with him, must carry away that which he acquired in this life. And filling the memory with delights and the remembrance of dishonest pride, avarice, and self-love, and hatred and displeasure toward one’s neighbor: being also a persecutor of my servants: and in these miseries he has clouded the intellect through his disordered will: therefore they receive eternal punishment with their stenches: because they did not satisfy their **guilt** <note>original: "colpa"</note> with **contrition** <note>Sincere sorrow for sin motivated by love for God.</note> and displeasure for the sin.

And they do not only satisfy the guilt, but also the punishment that follows the guilt for those who have this perfection: and in general, as I have said: and if the guilt is satisfied: that is, those who are deprived of **mortal sin** <note>A grave sin that separates the soul from God's grace.</note> receive **grace** <note>original: "grā" (grazia)</note>: and not having sufficient contrition and love to satisfy the punishment, they go to the pains of **purgatory** <note>A state of final purification for those who die in God’s friendship but still need to "pay the debt" of temporal punishment for their sins.</note> having passed by the second and final means. So you see: that satisfaction is made through the desire of the soul united in me, who am infinite good: more or less according to the measure of the perfect love of the one who offers the **prayer** <note>original: "oratiōe"</note> and the desire of the one who receives it. Wherefore, with that same measure that he gives to me, he receives into himself: and with that same measure, it is measured out by my goodness. Therefore, increase the fire of your desire: and do not let a single moment of time pass that you do not cry out with a humble voice and with continuous prayers before me for them. Thus I say to you and to the **father of [your] soul** <note>original: "padre d lanima." Likely referring to Catherine of Siena’s spiritual director and confessor, Raymond of Capua.</note>.

### How the desire to want to bear or suffer for Him is very pleasing to God. Chapter V

It is very pleasing to me, dearest daughter, the desire to want to bear every pain and labor even until death for the **salvation of souls**. Therefore, the more a soul sustains, the more she demonstrates that she loves me; loving me more, she knows more of my **truth**; and the more she knows, <margin>19:16-</margin> the more she feels intolerable pain and sorrow for the offenses committed against me. 

You asked to sustain and to punish the defects of others upon yourself: and you did not realize that you were asking for love, light, and knowledge of the **truth**; for I already told you that as love was greater, so grew the sorrow and the pain; therefore, as love increases in a person, sorrow also increases. Therefore I say to you: ask and it shall be given to you; for I will not deny anyone who asks of me in truth. For the love of <term>divine charity|The highest form of love; a selfless, spiritual love for God and others.</term> which is in the soul is so closely joined with perfect <term>patience|In this context, patience refers to "long-suffering" or the ability to endure hardship for a higher purpose.</term> that one cannot leave the soul without the other leaving as well. 

And therefore the soul, just as she chooses to love me, so she must choose to bear for me pains in whatever way and from whatever source I grant them to her. **Patience** is not proven except in times of pain, and **patience** is united with **charity**, as has been said. Therefore, bear your burdens manfully; otherwise you would not be, nor would you demonstrate yourselves to be, spouses of my **truth** and faithful children; nor would you be among those who taste my honor or the **salvation of souls**.

# On the Divine Chapter

...companion: counseling him sincerely: as if he were himself: and without the passion of his own self-love: and he does not do this: because he is already deprived of affection <note>original: "dilectiõe"</note> toward him: so you see: that by not doing so: he does him specific harm. And not only does he do him harm: by not doing the good that he can: but he does him harm: and evil continually. In this way, sin becomes an actual and mental harm. Mental harm is already done: since he has conceived pleasure in sin: and hatred of virtue: that is, pleasure in his own sensual love: which has deprived him of the affection of **charity** <term>charity|In this theological sense, charity (caritas) is not merely giving to the poor, but the supernatural love for God and neighbor.</term>: which he ought to have for me: and for his neighbor <note>original: "pximo"</note> as has been said. And after he has conceived it: he gives birth to one after another against his neighbor: according as it pleases his perverse sensual will in diverse ways. 

Wherefore we sometimes see: that he gives birth to a cruelty: both in general: and in particular. Generally, it is to see himself and other creatures in damnation: and in a state of death through the deprivation of grace <note>original: "grã" (grazia)</note>: and he is so cruel: that he does not remember for himself: nor for others the love of virtue: and the hatred of vice. But as a cruel man he actually extends his cruelty further: that is, not only does he not give an example of virtue: but he, like a wicked person, takes on the office of the demons: drawing the creature away from virtue according to his own view: and leading it into vice. This is cruelty toward the soul: which has been made an instrument to take away its life: and give it death. 

He uses bodily cruelty out of greed: so that not only does he not help his neighbor: but he takes from others by robbing the poor. And sometimes he does this by an act of authority: and sometimes with deceit: and with fraud, forcing his neighbor to buy back his own things: and often his own person. O miserable cruelty: which will be deprived of my mercy <note>original: "misericordia"</note>: if he does not return to pity: and benevolence toward him. And sometimes he gives birth to injurious words: after which words homicide <note>original: "lhomicidio"</note> often follows. And some...
