gentleness and kindness toward the angry person. All virtues are proven and are brought to birth through the neighbor <note>In this context, "neighbor" refers to any other person. Faith and hope do not diminish in the one who has conceived them within themselves through love for me; instead, they are strengthened and proven in the affection of the love of the neighbor.

For even though he sees that the other is unfaithful and without hope in me or in my servant—since he who does not love me is even less able to have faith or hope in me, but rather places it in his own sensuality, which he loves—my faithful servant does not cease to love faithfully, nor does he stop seeking his salvation with hope in me. Thus, you see that in the other's unfaithfulness and lack of hope, the virtue of faith is proven. In these and other things where it is necessary to test them, he proves it within himself and in his neighbor.

In the same way, justice is not diminished by the injustices of others; rather, it demonstrates and proves its justice. That is, one shows that they are just through the virtue of patience, just as kindness and gentleness are made manifest in times of anger through sweet patience. And envy, or displeasure, and hatred are met with the affection of charity <note>original: "charita"</note>, and with a hunger and desire for the salvation of souls.

These are the holy and sweet works that I seek from my servants: that is, these are the internal virtues of the soul, proven as I have told you. These virtues demonstrate that the will is dead, and that it continually kills the sensual self <note>The "sensual self" refers to the part of human nature driven by physical urges and ego rather than spiritual love.</note> through the affection of the love of virtue. This was to show you that he who only calls to me with the sound of the word, saying "Lord, Lord, I would like to do something for you," or he who desires for my sake and wants to mortify the body with many penances without <note>The text here implies that performing penance while still "loving one's own will" (senza [cessare di] amare la propria uolunta) is ineffective.</note> giving up his own self-will, was not very pleasing to me. 

Rather, I wanted the many deeds of enduring virilely <note>original: "uirilmente" — meaning with courage, strength, or "manly" fortitude, a common medieval descriptor for spiritual vigor.</note> and with patience, and with the other internal virtues of the soul which I have spoken of to you; all of which are active and produce fruits of grace. Every other operation based on any other principle than this, I consider to be only a calling with the word: because these are finite works. And I, who am infinite, seek infinite works: that is, an infinite affection of love. I wish, then, that the works of penance and other exercises—which are bodily—be used as an instrument <note>original: "instrumento" — a tool or means to an end, rather than the end itself.</note> and not as the principal affection. For if the principal affection were placed there, I would be given a finite thing. It would be like a word: which, as soon as it has come out of the mouth, exists no more—unless that word came out with the affection of the soul, which conceives and brings forth virtue in truth. That is to say, that the finite operation—which I have called the "word"—must be joined with the affection of <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charita" — the highest form of love; selfless, divine love.</note>; then it would be pleasing and acceptable to me. ...and because <note>The sentence continues from the previous page, explaining why the soul's action must be properly oriented.</note> it would not be alone, but accompanied by true discretion <term>discretion: in this context, the medieval virtue of *discretio*, meaning spiritual discernment or the ability to moderate one's actions according to reason and God's will.</term>: using bodily operation as an instrument, and not as the principal goal. For it would not be fitting that the principle and head should be placed only in penance, or in any other external bodily act; because I already told you that those were finite deeds <note>original: "opatiōe finite" — actions that are limited in time and scope, as opposed to the infinite nature of love.</note>, and finite they are, because they are performed in a finite time. It also happens that sometimes the creature leaves them behind, or is made to leave them behind by circumstances. 

Wherefore, when one leaves them out of necessity—being unable to perform the act they started due to various accidents that befall them, or sometimes out of the obedience commanded by their prelate <note>prelate: a superior in a religious order, such as an abbot or bishop.</note>—if they were to continue the act [against that obedience], they would not be meriting grace, but rather offending me. So you see: these acts are finite. One must, therefore, take them up for use, and not as a primary principle; because if they were taken as the principle, and it became necessary to leave them at some time, the soul would then remain empty. 

My glorious Paul, my trumpet, showed this to you when he said in his epistle that you should mortify the body and kill your own self-will <note>original: "mortificasti el corpo: & amazasti la ppria uolunta" — a reference to St. Paul's exhortations in the New Testament to "put to death the deeds of the body."</note>. This means knowing how to keep the body in check by macerating the flesh when it wishes to fight against the spirit. But the will must be entirely dead, denied, and subjected to my will. Your self-will is killed with that "debt" which I told you the virtue of discretion pays to the soul: that is, a hatred and displeasure for offenses and for one’s own sensuality, which is acquired through the knowledge of oneself. 

This is the knife that kills and cuts away all self-love founded in one's own will. Now, these people are those who do not give me words alone, but many deeds; and in this I delight. And therefore I said: that I wanted few words and many deeds. In telling you "many," I do not assign a specific number: because the affection of the soul, founded in charity <note>charity: here meaning *caritas*, the highest form of Christian love.</note>—which gives life to all virtues and good works—must reach toward the infinite. And not for this [reason] do I shun... <note>original: "schiuo" — the text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

...the word; but I said that I wanted few words, showing you that every outward deed <note>original: "opatiõe actuale" — literally "actual operation," referring to visible, external acts of penance or service as opposed to internal states.</note> was finite; and therefore I called them "few." And therefore no one should judge or place greater perfection in the great penances of one who gives himself much to mortifying his body <note>original: "amazare el corpo" — literally "to kill the body," a common medieval expression for extreme physical asceticism or fasting.</note> than in one who does less; because, as I have told you, virtue and merit do not reside there. It would go poorly for those who, for legitimate reasons, cannot perform outward deeds and actual penances [if merit were found only there]; rather, merit resides only in the virtue of charity seasoned with the light of true discretion <term>discretion: the virtue of *discretio*, or spiritual discernment, which acts as a "moderator" to ensure all other virtues are practiced in the right measure.</term>, for otherwise it would be worth nothing.

And this love and discretion the soul gives without end and without measure <note>original: "senza modo" — in medieval theology, God is to be loved "without measure" because He is infinite, whereas love for created things must be measured.</note> toward me, because I am God, the highest and eternal Truth; whence the soul puts no law nor limit to the love with which it loves me. But the soul certainly does apply measure with ordered charity toward its neighbor. The light of discretion—which proceeds from charity, as I have told you—gives an ordered love to the neighbor; that is, with an ordered charity <note>original: "charita ordiãta" — referring to the *ordo caritatis*, the theological concept that there is a right hierarchy and method for loving others.</note> that does not cause the damage of sin to oneself in order to provide a benefit to the neighbor. 

For if one were to commit even a single sin to save the whole world from hell, or to perform some great virtue, it would not be charity ordered with discretion; rather, it would be indiscreet. This is because it is not lawful to perform a great virtue or a benefit for the neighbor by the fault of sin. But holy discretion is ordered in this way: that the soul directs all its powers to serve me courageously with all diligence; and it loves the neighbor with an affection of love, offering up the life of the body for the salvation of souls—if it were possible, a thousand times—enduring pains and torments so that the neighbor may have the life of grace. And the soul puts its temporal substance to the use and relief of the body of its neighbor. This performs the highest office of discretion, which proceeds from charity. So you see that the soul discreetly renders, and ought to render, every...

# Providence XI

...the soul wants grace: that is, it gives me infinite love and love without measure <note>original: "senza modo" — a reference to the theological principle that the measure of loving God is to love Him without measure.</note>. And the neighbor must be loved with measure and with ordered charity <note>original: "charita ordiata" — *caritas ordinata* is the principle that one's love must follow a specific hierarchy, beginning with God, then one's own soul, then the neighbor.</note>: as I have said, not rendering the evil of sin to oneself for the sake of being useful to another. St. Paul advised you of this when he said: that charity must first move and begin with oneself; otherwise it would not perform a work of perfect utility for others. For when perfection is not in the soul, everything is imperfect; and whatever it performs in itself and in others is imperfect.

Wherefore it would not be a fitting thing that, in order to save creatures—who are finite and created by me—I, who am the infinite Good, should be offended. That sin would be more grave and great than any fruit that could come from that sin; thus, in no way should you commit the fault of sin. And true charity knows this well, since it carries with it the light of holy discretion <term>discretion: *discretio*, the spiritual gift of discernment that allows a person to balance virtues and avoid extremes.</term>. It is that light which dissolves every darkness and takes away ignorance; it seasons every virtue, and every instrument of actual virtue is seasoned by it.

It is a prudence that cannot be deceived. It is a fortitude that cannot be conquered. It is a great perseverance even unto the end, reaching from heaven to earth: that is, from the knowledge of me to the knowledge of oneself, and from my charity to the charity of the neighbor. With true humility it escapes and passes through all the snares of the world and of creatures with its prudence. With unarmed hands <note>original: "mane desarmate" — a metaphor for achieving victory not through physical force, but through patient endurance and suffering.</note>—that is, with much suffering—it defeats the devil and the flesh with this sweet and glorious light; because with this light, the soul knows its own fragility, and knowing it, renders it the "debt of hatred" <note>This refers to a "holy hatred" of one's own selfish sensuality or ego, which Catherine of Siena frequently cites as a path to purification.</note>.

Wherefore it has trampled the world and placed it under the feet of its affection, despising it and holding it as vile; and thus the soul has become its lord, mocking the world. And therefore the men of the world cannot take away the virtues of the soul; rather, all their persecutions lead to their increase, and

# Providence XIII

Knowing the great goodness of God, and seeing the breadth of His charity—who with such sweetness had deigned to respond to her request and satisfy it, giving hope to the bitterness which had seized her on account of the offense against God, the damage to the Holy Church, and her own misery, which she saw through <term>self-knowledge</term><note>A central theme in Catherinian spirituality: knowing one's own nothingness to better know God's everything</note>—it mitigated the bitterness, and yet the bitterness also grew. For because the supreme and eternal Father had manifested to her the way of perfection, and was showing her anew His offense and the damage to souls, as I have stated more extensively below. And because in the knowledge that the soul has of itself, it knows God better; and knowing the goodness of God in itself, and in the **sweet mirror of God**, it knows its own dignity and its own utility <note>In this context, 'utility' refers to the soul's purpose or beneficial state</note>—that is, the dignity of creation, seeing itself to be the **image of God**, and this being given by grace and not by debt <note>original: "nō p debito"; meaning it is a free gift, not something God owed to humanity</note>. And also in that mirror of the goodness of God, I say that the soul knows its own condition, into which it has fallen through its own fault. 

For just as the stain on a man's face is better seen by looking into a mirror, so the soul, which with true self-knowledge rises through desire with the eye of the intellect to look at itself in the **sweet mirror of God** through the purity that it sees in Him, better recognizes the stain on its own face. Therefore, because the light and the knowledge were greater in that soul in the manner described, I say that a **sweet bitterness** had grown within her; and yet the bitterness was diminished. It was diminished, I say, by the hope given to her by the <term>First Truth</term><note>A primary name for God in Catherine's theology, emphasizing God as the ultimate source of reality and honesty</note>. And just as fire grows when wood is given to it as fuel, so the fire grew in that soul in such a way that it was not possible for the human body to endure it without the soul departing from the body. I am speaking of my ministers, who are those who feed and stay at her breasts; and not only do they feed themselves, but they must feed and hold to these breasts the universal body of the Christian people, and anyone else who wishes to rise from the darkness of infidelity and bind themselves as a member in my church. See then with what ignorance, and with what darkness, and with what ingratitude this glorious milk and blood of this bride is administered, and handled with filthy hands; and with what presumption and without reverence it is received. And therefore, that thing which gives life often gives them death through their own defect: that is, the precious blood of my only-begotten Son, who took away death and darkness and gave light and life, and confounded falsehood. <note>original: "bosia," an archaic form of *bugia* (lie or falsehood).</note> He also gave this blood for everything, and it works toward salvation and to fulfill perfection in the person who disposes themselves to receive it. For just as it gives life and endows the soul with every grace—some more and some less, according to the disposition and affection of the one who receives it—so it gives death to him who lives iniquitously. Thus, on the part of the one who receives it unworthily with the darkness of <term>mortal sin</term> <note>A grave sin committed with full knowledge and consent that separates the soul from God's sanctifying grace.</note>, it brings him death and not life. This is not through a defect in the blood, nor through a defect in the minister (even if he were in that same evil or worse), for his evil does not spoil or stain the blood, nor diminish its grace and power; and furthermore, it does not harm the one to whom he gives it, but only himself

<summary>God the Father laments the corruption of the Church and its ministers, explaining that while the Eucharist (the "Blood") is inherently pure and life-giving, it brings spiritual death to those who receive or administer it in a state of mortal sin.</summary>

### Providence XIII
->Dialogue of St. Catherine C<-

...he does harm to himself by the guilt, which is followed by punishment if he does not correct himself with true contrition and displeasure for his guilt. I say, then, that it does harm to him who receives <note>Referring to the unworthy reception of the Eucharist.</note> unworthily: not through any defect of the blood, nor of the minister, as has been said, but through his own bad disposition and through his own defect, because with such misery and uncleanness he has defiled his mind and his body, and has shown such cruelty to himself and to his neighbor. 

To himself he was cruel by taking away grace from himself, trampling under the feet of his affection the fruit of the blood which he drew from **holy baptism**, the stain of **original sin** already having been taken from him through the power of the blood—which stain he drew from a single source when he was conceived by his father and mother. And therefore I gave the **Word** of my only-begotten Son, because the mass <note>original: "massa," referring to the *massa damnata* or the "condemned mass," the theological concept that all humanity inherited Adam's fallen state and was thus "unfit" for heaven.</note> of human generation was corrupt through the sin of the first man, Adam; and therefore all of you, as vessels made from this mass, were corrupt and not disposed to have eternal life. <margin>39. 23.</margin> 

Wherefore I, through this height, joined myself with the lowliness of your human generation, in order to restore it to the grace which it lost through sin. Wherefore, as I could not suffer punishment <note>In traditional theology, God the Father is "impassible," meaning He cannot suffer. Thus, the Son had to take on human nature to endure the penalty of sin.</note>, and yet my divine justice required that punishment should come for the guilt. <margin>39. 7.</margin> And man not being sufficient to make satisfaction—and even if man had satisfied in some way, he would have satisfied only for himself and not for other creatures who possess reason—nevertheless, for this guilt, man could satisfy neither for himself nor for others, because the guilt was committed against me, who am infinite goodness. 

Wishing nonetheless to restore man, who was weakened and could not make satisfaction for the reason stated—and because he was weakened—I sent the **Word** of my Son, clothed in this same nature <margin>42: 16.</margin> of yours, the corrupt mass of Adam, so that he might suffer punishment in that same nature which had offended; suffering, I say, upon his body even unto the shameful death of... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the next page likely completes this as "death of the cross."</note>

<summary>God explains that because humanity's "mass" was corrupted by Adam, and because a finite human could not satisfy a debt against an infinite God, the Word (Christ) had to take on human nature to suffer the punishment required by divine justice.</summary>
<keywords>Atonement, Original Sin, Incarnation, Divine Justice, Holy Baptism, The Word, Adam, Corruption of Humanity</keywords>

# Chapter of the Divine
<meta>catchword: life</meta>

...the cross. And thus he satisfied my **justice** and satiated **divine mercy**; which mercy wished to satisfy for the guilt of man and dispose him to that good for which he had created him. So that the human nature joined with the divine nature was sufficient to satisfy for all the human race, not only for the punishment he sustained in the finite nature—that is, from the mass of Adam—but by the power of the said eternal, infinite divine nature. 

Thus, with one nature joined to the other, I received and accepted the **sacrifice** of the **blood** of my only-begotten Son, mixed and kneaded with the divine nature by the fire of **divine charity**; which was that bond that held him fastened and nailed to the cross. Now, in this way, human nature was sufficient to satisfy for the guilt, only through the power of the divine nature. And in this way, the rot <note>original: "marza," referring to the putrefaction or corruption of sin.</note> of **Adam’s sin** was removed; but there remained only the sign, that is, the inclination to sin and toward every physical defect, just like the scar <note>original: "margie," meaning the mark or scab left behind.</note> that remains when a man is healed of a wound. 

Thus, the guilt of Adam no longer brings mortal rot. Then, when the great physician of my only-begotten Son came, he cured this sick person by drinking the bitter medicine that man could not drink because he was too weakened. And he acted as the nurse <note>original: "baila," referring to a wet nurse or caregiver who takes care of an infant's needs.</note> does, who takes the medicine on behalf of the small child because she is large and strong, and the child is not strong enough to bear the bitterness. So he was a nurse to them, carrying with the greatness and strength of the said union with your nature the bitter medicine of the painful death of the cross, to heal and give life to you children weakened by guilt. 

Only the sign, then, I say, remained of **original sin**—which sin you contract from your father and your mother when you are conceived by them. Which sign is removed from the soul, though not entirely <note>A reference to the "fomes peccati" or the lingering inclination to sin (concupiscence) that remains after baptism.</note>, and this is done in **holy baptism**, which baptism has power and gives...

<summary>God the Father explains how Christ’s dual nature allowed him to satisfy divine justice by acting as a strong nurse who endures the "bitter medicine" of the cross for humanity's sake. He describes how baptism removes the "rot" of original sin, leaving only a "scar" or inclination toward defect.</summary>

->Providence 14<-

...life of grace through the virtue of that glorious and precious **blood**. Wherefore, as soon as the soul has received **holy baptism**, original sin is taken away and grace is infused into it. And that inclination to sin—which is the scar <note>original: "margine," referring to the mark or scab left over after a wound has healed, mentioned on the preceding page.</note> that remains from **original sin**, as has been said—weakens, and the soul can restrain it if it wishes. 

Then the vessel of the soul is disposed to receive and to grow grace within itself, much or little, according to how it pleases the soul to dispose itself with affection and the desire to love and serve me. And thus it can dispose itself toward evil as well as toward good, notwithstanding that it has received grace in **holy baptism**. Whence, once the time of discretion <note>The "age of discretion" or "age of reason" (historically around seven years old), when a person is considered capable of distinguishing right from wrong.</note> has come, through their **free will**, they can use good or evil according to what pleases their own will. 

And so great is the liberty that man has, and he is made so strong by the virtue of this glorious blood, that neither the devil nor any creature can compel him to the slightest fault of sin unless he himself wills it. Servitude <note>The slavery to sin and the devil.</note> was taken from him and he was made free, so that he might master his own sensuality <note>original: "sensualita," referring to the lower physical appetites and instincts that lead one away from reason.</note> and reach the end for which he had been created. O miserable man, who delights in the mud like an animal and does not recognize such a great benefit as he has received from me! For the miserable creature, full of such ignorance, could not have received more.

# Providence XV
## C iii

[...with]out consuming by divine justice: that is, it afflicts more: and by afflicting, it feels itself consumed by the worm of conscience. <note>The "worm of conscience" is a common medieval metaphor for the internal gnawing of guilt that haunts the sinner, a reference to Mark 9:48.</note> Nevertheless, it does not consume: because the damned do not lose their being through any torment that they receive. Wherefore I tell you: that these damned ones ask for death: and cannot have it: because they cannot lose their being; they lose indeed the being of grace through their own fault: but the natural being they do not. So it is that the fault is more punished after the redemption of the blood than it was before: because they have received more: and it does not seem that they are aware of it: nor that they feel their own evils: and they have made themselves my enemies, even though I have reconciled them through the means of the blood of my son. But there is a remedy: with which I will appease my wrath: that is, through the means of my servants: if they will be diligent in constraining me with tears: and binding me with the bonds of desire. You see: that with this bond you have bound me: which bond I have given you: because I wished to show mercy to the world. And therefore I give hunger: and desire in my servants toward my honor: and toward the salvation of souls: so that, constrained by their tears, I may come to mitigate the fury of my divine justice. Take then the tears: and your sweat: and draw them from the fountain of my divine charity, you and my other servants: and with them wash the face of my bride. <note>In Catherine’s theology, "the bride" refers to the Church, which she often described as having a face "befouled" by the sins of the clergy and the faithful.</note> I promise you: that by this means her beauty shall be restored to her: not with the knife: nor with cruelty will she regain her beauty: but with peace: and with humble: and continual prayer: sweats: and tears shed with anxious desire by my servants. And thus I will fulfill your desire with much suffering, casting the light of your patience into the darkness of the perverse men of the world. And do not fear: because the world persecutes you: for I will act for you: and in nothing will my providence fail you.

->How, the road to heaven being broken by the disobedience of Adam, God made of his Son a bridge by which one could pass<-

Thus the flesh immediately waged war against the spirit, and losing the state of **innocence**, it became...

# Providence XXVI

D ii

<meta>Catchword: Dialogue of St. Catherine.</meta>

Therefore, he could show you no greater love than to give his life for you. By force, then, he is drawn by love, provided that man, in his ignorance, does not resist being drawn. He said, therefore, that being lifted up on high, he would draw all things to himself; and so it is the truth. This is understood in two ways: first, that the heart of man is drawn by <term>desire: original "affecto," referring to the soul’s emotional and volitional drive toward God</term> of love, as I have told you. It is drawn along with all the powers of the soul: namely memory, intellect, and will. When these three powers are in harmony and gathered in my name, all the other operations he performs, both in action and in thought, are drawn in a pleasing way and joined to me through the desire of love, because he was lifted on high following his bitter suffering on the cross. <note>original: "amaro cruciato," referring to the agony of the crucifixion which "elevated" Christ.</note> Thus, my Truth spoke truly when he said: "If I am lifted up on high, I will draw all things to myself"; for when the heart and the powers of the soul are drawn, all his deeds will be drawn as well.

The second way is this: that everything is created for the use of man. Therefore, created things were made to serve and provide for the needs of rational creatures; and the creature who possesses reason was not made for them, but for me, so that he might serve me with all his heart and all his desire. Thus you see that when man is drawn, everything is drawn, because everything was made for him. Therefore, it was necessary for the bridge to be lifted on high and to have steps, so that one might climb with greater ease.

How this bridge is built of stones that signify the virtues; and upon the bridge is a shop where food is given to the wayfarers; and whoever keeps to the bridge goes to life, and whoever stays below goes to perdition and death.

# Of the Divine Chapter

<meta>catchword: to see again</meta>

And therefore they were hindered: so that no one could reach their goal, even though they walked the way of the virtues; for heaven was not yet unlocked with the key of the blood, and thus the rain of justice <note>original: "iustitia"; here depicted as a torrential storm of divine judgment that barred humanity from heaven until the atonement.</note> did not let them pass. But after the stones were made and fashioned upon the body of the Word, my sweet Son—of whom I have told you that he is the Bridge—he himself built the walls and mixed the mortar to set the stones with his blood. That is, the blood is mixed with the mortar of the Deity, and with the strength and fire of <term>charity: original "charita," meaning the selfless, sacrificial love of God</term>. By my power, these stones of virtue are walled upon him himself; for there is no virtue that has not been tested in him, and from him all virtues receive life. 

And therefore, no one can possess virtue that gives the life of grace except from him—that is, by following in his footsteps and his teaching. He has walled the virtues and planted them like living stones, setting them with his blood so that every faithful person can walk swiftly and without any servile fear of the rain of divine justice, because the path is covered with mercy. This mercy descended from heaven in the <term>Incarnation: the doctrine of God becoming human in the person of Jesus</term> of this my Son. With what did he open it? With the key of his blood. So you see: the Bridge is built and covered with mercy. 

And the shop of the garden of the Holy Church is his; it holds and administers the Bread of Life and gives the Blood to drink, so that my creatures, traveling as pilgrims, do not grow weary and faint on the way. <note>The "shop" (botega) is a metaphor for the Church acting as a provider of spiritual nourishment and medicine through the sacraments.</note> And for this reason, my charity has ordained that the blood and the body of my only-begotten Son—wholly God and wholly man—be administered to you. 

And having crossed the Bridge, one reaches the gate; this gate is the Bridge itself, through which you must all enter. And therefore he says: **"I am the way, and the truth, and the life; whoever walks through me does not walk in darkness, but in light."** <note>original: "Io son uia: & uerita: & uita"; a translation of John 14:6.</note> And in another place my Truth says that no one could come to me except through him; and so it is. And if you remember well, this is what I told you and showed you, wanting to make you see

### Providence XXVII
->D iii<-
<meta>catchword: Dialog.de.S.catha.</meta>

...to see the way again. Wherefore if he says that he is the Way, this is the Truth; and I have already shown you that he is the Way in the form of a Bridge. And he says that he is the Truth; and so he is, because he is one with me, who am the Truth. And whoever follows him goes by way of the Truth and the Life; for whoever follows this Truth receives the life of grace and cannot perish from hunger, because the Truth has made itself food for you. Nor can such a person fall into darkness, because he is light, devoid of any lie <note>original: "busia"; an archaic Italian form of "bugia," meaning a lie or deceit.</note>. Moreover, with the Truth, he confounded and destroyed that very lie of the devil which was spoken to Eve—the lie that broke the road to heaven. But Life <note>Referring to Christ as the personification of Life.</note> has repaired it and walled it with his blood. 

Therefore, those who follow this way are children of the Truth, because they follow the Truth and pass through the gate of Truth. They find themselves united in me through the gate and way of my Son: eternal Truth and a peaceful sea <note>The "peaceful sea" is a signature metaphor in Catherine’s mysticism, representing the soul’s immersion in the calm and infinite depths of God's grace.</note>.

But he who does not hold to this way walks below through the river. This way is not paved with stones, but consists of water. And because water has no solid footing, no one can walk there without drowning. Such are the delights and the states of the world. Therefore, because their affection is not set upon the stone <note>Refers to Christ as the firm foundation of the Bridge.</note>, but is placed with <term>disordered love: original "disordinato amore"; a love that is out of balance because it prizes temporary, worldly things over eternal, spiritual ones</term> upon creatures and created things—loving them and holding them apart from me—they drown. These things are like the water that continually flows. 

And so man flows like a river, even though it seems to him that it is the created things he loves that are flowing away; yet it is he himself who is continually running toward the boundary of death. He would wish to hold onto himself—that is, his life—and the things he loves so that they would not slip away. But they fail him, either through death, which leaves them behind, or by my providence <note>original: "dispēsatione"; God's sovereign arrangement of circumstances.</note>, when created things are taken away from my creatures. These people follow the lie, walking the path of falsehood, and are children of the devil, who is the father of lies. And because they pass through the gate of the lie, they receive eternal damnation. So you see, I have shown you...

### How each of these two roads is traveled with labor: that is, by the bridge and by the river; and of the delight that the soul feels in going by the bridge. Chapter XXVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a floral/leaf motif inside a square frame.</image-desc>

**Q**ueste—these are two roads, and each is traveled with labor. Look, then, how great is the ignorance and blindness of man who, having had the way made for him, wishes instead to walk through the water. This way <note>The "way" refers to the Bridge, symbolizing Christ and the life of virtue.</note> is of such delight to those who travel by it that every bitterness becomes sweet to them, and every great burden becomes light. 

These people, while still in the darkness of the mortal body, find the light; and being mortal, they find immortal life, tasting through the affection of love with the light of eternal truth—which promises to give refreshment <note>original: "refrigerio"; in a theological context, this implies the cooling relief of divine grace or the rest of paradise.</note> to whoever labors for me. For I am grateful and mindful, and I am just: I render to everyone according to what they deserve, wherefore every good is rewarded and every fault is punished. 

The delight that he has who goes by this way, your tongue would not be sufficient to tell, nor the ear to hear, nor the eye to see. For in this life he tastes and participates in that good which is prepared for him in the lasting life. Truly, then, he is a fool <note>original: "mato," a variant of "matto" meaning mad or foolish.</note> who avoids such great good and chooses instead to taste the air of hell <note>original: "lara de l'iferno," referring to the "aura" or atmosphere of suffering.</note> in this life, walking by the way below. There, he travels with many labors, and without any refreshment, and without any good. For through their sin, such people are deprived of me, who am the supreme and eternal Good. 

You have good reason, then, to grieve; and I want you and my other servants to remain in continual bitterness for the offense against me, and in compassion for their ignorance and the loss they suffer, for with that ignorance they offend me. Now you have seen and heard of the Bridge, and how it stands; and I have said this to clarify what I spoke of before: that my only-begotten Son was the Bridge. And so you see that he is the Truth, created in the manner

...the manner that I have told you: that is, the height united with the lowliness.

### How this bridge, having ascended to heaven on the day of the Ascension, did not however depart from the earth. Chapter XXIX.

After my only-begotten Son returned to me forty days after the resurrection, this bridge was raised from the earth—that is, from the conversation <note>original: "conuersatione"; here meaning the physical presence and social interaction of Christ among humanity.</note> of men—and ascended into heaven by the power of my divine nature, and sits at the right hand of me, the Eternal Father <note>The OCR "et no" is likely a truncated or misread "eterno" (eternal).</note>. Just as the angel said to the disciples on the day of the Ascension while they stood almost as if dead—for their hearts were raised on high and had ascended into heaven with the wisdom of my Son—"Do not stay here any longer," said the angel, "because he sits at the right hand of the Father." 

Having been raised on high, then, and returned to me, the Father, I sent the Master: that is, the Holy Spirit. He came with my power and with the wisdom of my Son, and with his own clemency: that is, the Holy Spirit himself. He is one thing with me, the Father, and with my Son; wherefore he strengthened the way of the doctrine which my Truth <note>In Catherine’s writing, "my Truth" is a frequent title for Jesus Christ.</note> left in the world. And so, although his presence departed, the doctrine did not depart, nor the virtue of the stones founded upon this doctrine, which is the way that this sweet and glorious bridge has made for you. 

First he acted, and with his deeds he made the way, giving the doctrine to you by example more than by words. He first did, and then he taught <note>original: "pma fece: che dicesse"; a reference to the biblical description of Jesus beginning "to do and to teach" (Acts 1:1).</note>. This doctrine was confirmed by the clemency of the Holy Spirit, strengthening the minds of the disciples to testify to the life and announce this way: that is, the doctrine of Christ crucified <note>original: "xpō crucifixo"</note>. Through them, he rebuked the world for its injustices and false judgments; of which injustices and judgments I will tell you more extensively below. I have told you this so that in the minds of those who hear, no darkness could fall to cloud the mind—that is, so they might not say that from this body of Christ a bridge was made through the union of the nature...

<summary>This page explains that while Christ physically ascended to heaven, He remains present on earth through His doctrine and the Holy Spirit, which serves as the "Master" and strengthener of the Way. It emphasizes that Christ taught by example before words, establishing a firm foundation for the disciples.</summary>

-> Of the Divine Bridge: Chapter XXIX <-

...divine nature with human nature: and this sees: that He is the truth. But this bridge departed from you, ascending into heaven: and He was a way that taught the truth, seeing His example and His manners <note>original: "costumi"; refers to Christ's way of living and his moral character.</note>. Now, what has remained? And where does one find the way? I tell you: that is, I will say to those into whose minds this ignorance might fall: I say that the way is the way of His doctrine, which I have told you: confirmed by the apostles, and declared in the blood of martyrs, illuminated with the light of doctors <note>the "Doctors of the Church," revered for their theological wisdom.</note>, and confessed by the confessors, and set down on paper by the evangelists—who all stand as witnesses to confess the life in the mystical body of the holy church.

And they are like a lamp placed on the lampstand to show the way of truth, which leads to life with perfect light, as I have told you. And as they tell it to you by experience <note>original: "per pua" / "per prova"; meaning they have tested and confirmed the truth through their own lives.</note>, since they have proven it in themselves, so that every person is illuminated in knowing the truth if they wish—that is, provided they do not wish to take away the light of reason through their own self-centered and disordered love.

So it is the truth: that His doctrine is true, and it remains like a little ship <note>original: "nauicella"; a common metaphor for the Church or divine doctrine navigating the world.</note> to draw the soul out of the tempestuous sea and lead it to the port of salvation. So, at first, I made for you the bridge of my Son in person <note>original: "actuale"; referring to the physical incarnation of Christ.</note>, as I have told you, conversing with men; and when the physical bridge was taken away, there remained the bridge and the way of the doctrine, as was said: the doctrine being joined with my power <note>original: "patiētia" / "potentia"; though the OCR reads patience, Catherine consistently attributes "Power" (Potenzia) to the Father in her Trinitarian theology.</note>, and with the wisdom of the Son, and with the clemency of the Holy Spirit.

This power gives the virtue of fortitude to whoever follows this way; wisdom gives them light, because in this way they know the truth; and the Holy Spirit gives them love, which consumes and takes away every sensory love of the soul, and only the love of virtue remains. So in every way—whether in person or through doctrine—He is the Way, the Truth, and the Life <note>A reference to John 14:6: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life."</note>; which way is the bridge that leads you to the height of heaven. This is what He meant when He said: "I came from the Father, and I return to the Father, and I will return to you." <note>A synthesis of John 16:28 and 14:18.</note>

### Providence XXIX

That is to say: My Father sent me to you and made me your bridge, so that you might be out of the river and be able to reach [eternal] life. Then He says: "And I will return to you; I will not leave you orphans, but I will send you the Paraclete <note>From the Greek 'parakletos,' meaning advocate or helper; referring here to the Holy Spirit.</note>," as if My Truth were saying: "I will go to the Father and I will return." This means that when the Holy Spirit comes—who is called the Paraclete—He will show you more clearly and confirm Me as the Way of Truth; that is, the way and the doctrine which I have given you.

He said He would return, and He did return; because the Holy Spirit did not come alone, but came with the power of Me, the Father, and with the wisdom of the Son, and with the mercy <note>original: "clemencia"; here implying the loving-kindness or grace associated with the Holy Spirit.</note> of the Holy Spirit Himself. See, then, that He returns not in His physical person <note>original: "actuale"; referring to a literal, bodily presence.</note>, but with power, as I have told you, strengthening the path of doctrine. 

This path and road cannot fail, nor can it be taken away from whoever wishes to follow it; for it is firm and stable, and proceeds from Me, who do not move. Therefore, you must courageously <note>original: "uirilmente"; literally 'manfully,' implying strength of spirit and fortitude.</note> follow this way, without any cloud [of doubt], but with the light of faith, which is given to you as your primary garment in holy baptism. 

Now I have fully shown and declared to you the actual bridge and the doctrine, which is one and the same thing with the bridge. And I have shown to those who were ignorant that this way is manifest to them, that it is truth, and where those who teach it stand. And I said they were the apostles, the evangelists, the martyrs, the confessors, and the holy doctors, placed in the position of the Holy Church like a lamp. 

And I have shown and said how, by coming to Me, He returned to you—not in physical presence, but with power, as I have told you—that is, through the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples. For He will not return in person until the last day of Judgment, when He will come with My majesty and divine power to judge the world, and to return good to the good and reward them for their labors—soul and body together—and to return the evil of eternal punishment to those who have lived wickedly.

### Providence XXX

...death of sin took the physical life of the immaculate lamb <note>original: "immaculato agnello"—referring to Jesus Christ</note>. Who remained conquered? Death. What was the cause? Mercy. Your mercy gives life and light, through which your clemency is recognized in every creature: in the righteous and in sinners. In the height of heaven your mercy shines—that is, in your saints. If I turn to the earth, it abounds with your mercy. In the darkness of hell your mercy shines, by not giving as much punishment to the damned as they deserve. With your mercy you mitigate justice. By mercy you washed us in blood; and by mercy you wished to live among your creatures. O madman of love! It was not enough for you to become incarnate, for you also wished to die. Death was not enough, for you also descended to hell, drawing out the holy fathers <term>holy fathers: the patriarchs and prophets of the Old Testament</term> to fulfill your truth and your mercy in them. Because your goodness promises good to those who serve you in truth, you then descended into limbo <term>limbo: the "Limbo of the Patriarchs," where the souls of the just waited for the Resurrection</term> to pull out from pain those who had served you and to give them the fruit of their labors. Your mercy constrains you to give even more to man: that is, leaving yourself as food, so that we who are weak might have comfort, and the ignorant and forgetful might not lose the memory of your benefits. And so you give yourself every day to man, representing yourself in the sacrament of the altar <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>, in the body of the holy church. Who has done this? Your mercy. O mercy, the heart suffocates <note>original: "sasoga"—an archaic expression meaning to be overwhelmed or "choked" with emotion</note> to think of you; for in every corner where I turn to think, I find nothing but mercy. O eternal Father, forgive my ignorance, that I should presume to speak before you; but let the love of your mercy excuse me before your kindness.

# Providence XXXI

...all their works, both in action and in thought, are dead as far as grace is concerned. Wherefore they cannot defend themselves from their enemies, nor help themselves, except insofar as they are helped by me. 

It is indeed true that whenever this dead person—in whom only free will <term>free will: the human capacity to choose, which remains even when grace is lost</term> remains—while still in the mortal body, asks for my help, they can have it; but by their own power they can never achieve it. They have become unbearable to themselves; and wishing to rule the world, they are instead ruled by that which is not—that is, by sin. Sin is nothingness, and they have become servants and slaves of sin. I made them trees of love with the life of grace, which they received in holy baptism; but they have become trees of death because they are dead, as I have told you. 

Do you know where the root of this tree comes from? It is found in the height of pride, which is nourished by their own sensual love of themselves. Its branch is impatience, and its child is indiscretion <term>indiscretion: here meaning a lack of spiritual discernment or the inability to judge what is right and moderate</term>. These are four principal vices which completely kill the soul of him who, as I said, was a tree of death; for he has not drawn the life of grace. Inside the tree, a worm of conscience <note>original: "uermo di ɔfciētia"</note> is nourished; while a person lives in mortal sin, they are blinded by self-love and feel it but little. 

The fruits of this tree are mortal, because they have drawn the sap from the root of pride; and the wretched soul <note>original: "topinella ania" (tapinella anima)</note> is full of ingratitude, from which all evil proceeds. But if the soul were grateful for the benefits received, she would know Me; and knowing Me, she would know herself; and thus she would remain in My love. But like a blind person, she goes along clinging only to the river <note>The "river" is a common metaphor in this work for the flowing, transient world that leads to destruction</note>, and does not see that the water does not wait for her.

The philosophers recognized this, not through the light of grace—for they did not have it—but because nature offered them that light: namely, that this dishonest sin darkened the intellect; and therefore they maintained chastity and continence in order to study better. And they also threw riches away from themselves, so that the thought of wealth would not occupy their hearts. Not so does the ignorant and false Christian, who has lost grace through his fault.

### How it is for some others who hold a state of lordship: their fruits are injustice. Chapter 33.

There are others who hold their heads high due to their **lordship** <note>original: *signoria*; here referring to those in positions of political, social, or legal authority</note>, in which lordship they bear the banner of injustice. They practice injustice toward me, God, toward their neighbor, and toward their own selves. Toward themselves, they do not render the debt of virtue; toward me, they do not render the debt of honor, which is to give glory and praise to my name—a debt they are bound to pay. But like thieves, they steal what is mine and give it to the service of their own **sensuality** <note>original: *sensualità*; the part of the human soul driven by physical instincts and ego rather than reason</note>. Thus, they commit injustice toward me and toward themselves, like one blinded and ignorant, not recognizing me within themselves; and all this is because of **self-love**. 

This is just as the Jews and the ministers of the Law did, who acted out of envy and self-love; and therefore they did not recognize the truth of my only-begotten Son. Thus they did not pay the debt of acknowledging the eternal life that was among them, as my Truth <note>referring to Christ</note> said: "The kingdom of God is among you" <note>original: *El regno di dio e tra uoi*; a reference to Luke 17:21</note>. But they did not recognize it because, in the manner described, they had lost the light of **reason**. Because of this, they did not pay the debt of rendering honor and glory to me and to Him, who was one thing with me. Wherefore, like blind men, they committed injustice by persecuting Him with many insults, even to death on the cross. So, in the same way, these people render injustice to themselves and to me, and also to their neighbor, unjustly "selling the flesh" of their subjects and of any other person who comes into their hands.

### How through these and other defects one falls into false judgment: and concerning the indignity into which one falls. Chapter 35.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'P' containing a portrait of a bearded man in profile, possibly a saint or scholar, wearing a hood or cowl.</image-desc>

Through these and through other defects, these people fall into false judgment, as I shall explain to you further below. Therefore, they are always scandalized by my works, all of which are just and all, in truth, performed for love and for mercy. With this false judgment—and the venom of envy and pride—the works of my Son were slandered and judged unjustly; and with false lies they said: "He does this by the power of Beelzebub." <note>original: *belzebub*; a biblical name for a prince of demons. Catherine refers here to Matthew 12:24, where critics attribute Christ's miracles to evil spirits.</note>

Just so, these wicked ones, situated in self-love, impurity, pride, and avarice—founded upon envy and perverse **indiscretion** <note>original: *indiscretione*; here meaning a lack of spiritual discernment or the inability to distinguish between good and evil</note>, with an impatience and many other evils they commit—are always taking offense at me and at my servants, judging that they only practice virtue hypocritically. Because their heart is rotten <note>original: *marzo* (marcio); meaning decayed or corrupted</note> and their taste is spoiled, good things seem bad to them; that is, a disordered life seems good to them.

O human blindness! You do not regard your own dignity: how from being great you have been made small; from being a lord you have been made a slave—of the vilest lordship you could have—because you have been made a servant and slave of sin. For while you were servants of the devil, he drew you out of his servitude. He made himself a servant to take away your servitude, and he took upon himself obedience to consume the **disobedience of Adam**. # Of the Divine Providence. Chapter
## Chapter 36.
<meta>catchword: cto</meta>

...had made an anvil of himself. <note>original: *haueua facto āchuzine*; a metaphor for a heart hardened against grace, where God’s mercy is struck but the heart remains unyielding.</note> All remedies are provided to save them from eternal death, yet they despise the blood and have trampled it under the feet of their disordered affection. This is the injustice and the false judgment for which the world is rebuked, and for which it will be answered on the last day of judgment. And this is what my Truth <note>original: *la mia uita*; literally "my life," but Catherine frequently uses this as a title for Christ, "my Truth"</note> meant when he said: **"I will send the Paraclete, who will rebuke the world for its justice and for its false judgment."** <note>original: *Io mādero el paclito: ch repndera il mōdo...*; referring to the Gospel of John 16:8.</note> This rebuke was first given when I sent the Holy Spirit upon the apostles.

¶ **Here He speaks regarding the word that Christ said: "I will send the Holy Spirit, who will convict the world of injustice and judgment," and one of these rebukes is continuous.**

There are three rebukes. The first was given when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, as was said, who were fortified by my power and illuminated by the wisdom of my beloved Son; they all received the fullness of the Holy Spirit. At that time, the Holy Spirit—who is one thing with me and with my Son—rebuked the world through the mouths of the apostles by the doctrine of my Truth. They, and all the others who have followed them by living the life they learned through them, continue to rebuke the world. This is that continuous rebuke that I give to the world by means of the Holy Scripture and through my servants, as the Holy Spirit places himself upon their tongues to announce my Truth—just as the demon places himself upon the tongues of his own, that is, those who pass wickedly through the river. <note>The "river" is a central metaphor in Catherine’s *Dialogue*, representing the turbulent world and its vices, contrasted with the "Bridge" of Christ.</note> This is that sweet rebuke that I have placed continually throughout the world in the manner described, out of the very great affection of love that I have for the salvation of souls. And they cannot say, "I had no one to rebuke me," because the truth has already been shown to them, showing them both vice and virtue. And I have made them see the fruit of virtue and the harm of vice in order to give them holy love and holy fear.

Then a person wishes to be helped by me when they exit the river <note>The "river" represents the world's chaotic passions and the path to damnation.</note> and go by the bridge <note>The "Bridge" is Catherine's primary metaphor for Christ, connecting Earth to Heaven.</note>, following the doctrine of my Life. ### ¶ Of the second rebuke: in which the soul is rebuked for injustice and judgment. Chapter 37.

This second rebuke, my dearest daughter, is based on the soul's actual deeds: because it has reached the very end, where there can be no remedy. The soul has been brought to the extremity of death, where there dwells the "worm of conscience" <note>original: *uerme de la cōscientia*; a traditional medieval metaphor for the gnawing remorse and self-reproach that torments a guilty soul.</note>. I told you before that this worm was blinded by the self-love the person had for themselves; but now, at the point of death, because the soul sees that it cannot escape my hands, this worm begins to see. It then gnaws at the person with self-rebuke, as they see that through their own fault they have been led into such great evil.

Yet, if this soul possessed the light to recognize and grieve for its fault—not simply because of the pain of hell that follows it, but because of Me, whom it has offended (for I am the Supreme and Eternal Goodness)—it would still find mercy. But if the soul passes the threshold of death without that light, and only with the gnawing worm of conscience, without the hope of the Blood <note>original: *sangue*; Catherine frequently references the Blood of Christ as the ultimate source of mercy and salvation.</note>, and trapped in its own passions—grieving more for its own personal loss than for the offense against Me—then it arrives at eternal damnation.

And then it is cruelly rebuked by my Justice. It is rebuked for its injustice and for its false judgment. This is not just for the general injustice and judgment it practiced throughout its life in all its actions, but even more so it will be rebuked for the particular injustice and judgment it exercised at the very end: that is, judging its own misery to be greater than my Mercy. This is the sin that is forgiven neither in this life nor in the next <note>A reference to the "unpardonable sin" against the Holy Spirit, which Catherine interprets here as final despair or the rejection of God's mercy.</note>, because the soul has refused to hope, despising my mercy; for more...

They are also rebuked for their injustice, and this occurs when they grieve more for their own loss <note>original: *dãno*; refers to the "pain of loss," the theological term for being deprived of the sight of God.</note> than for the offense against me. In this, they commit injustice because they do not render to me what is mine, and to themselves what is theirs. For to me they ought to render love, and to themselves bitterness with contrition of heart, offering it before me for the offense they have committed against me. Instead, they do the opposite: they give themselves a compassionate love of their own selves, and feel sorrow only for the penalty which they expect for their fault. So you see, they commit injustice, and therefore they are punished for both one and the other together. Since they have despised my mercy, I justly send them together with their own cruel sensuality—which was their servant—and with the cruel tyrant, the devil, to whom they made themselves subjects by means of that very servant of their own sensuality. Thus, they are punished and tormented together, just as they offended me together. They are tormented by my ministers—I mean the demons—whom my justice has appointed to render torment to those who have done evil.

### Of the third reproach: which is made on the day of judgment. Chapter 29.

Now it remains for me to speak of the third reproach: that is, of the last day of judgment. I have already told you of the first two, but now, so that you may see clearly how much man deceives himself, I will tell you of the third: that is, the general judgment. In this judgment, the pain of the wretched soul is refreshed; and the pain having been refreshed and increased through the union that the soul will make with its body, it will face an intolerable reproach which will generate confusion and shame. Wherefore know that on the last day of judgment, when my Word <term>Word</term> <note>original: *uerbo*; a theological title for Jesus Christ, the second person of the Trinity.</note>, my Son, shall come with my divine majesty to reproach the world with divine power, he will not come as a poor man, as when he was born—coming into the womb of the Virgin and being born in the stable among the animals—and then dying in the middle between two thieves. For at that time, I hid my power in him, letting him endure pain and torments as a man—not that my divine nature <term>divine nature</term> was therefore separated from the human nature <term>human nature</term> <note>A reference to the "Hypostatic Union," the Christian belief that Jesus is both fully God and fully man.</note>—but letting him suffer as a man to satisfy <note>original: *satisfare*; to pay the spiritual debt owed for human sin through his suffering.</note> for your faults. Wherefore he will not come in that way at that final moment; but he will come with power to reproach them in his own person, and he will render to everyone what is due...

...to His own, and there will be no creature that does not feel fear. To the just, He will bring a fear of reverence <note>This refers to "filial fear," a respectful awe rather than a terrifying dread.</note> with great joy; not because He changes His face—for He is immutable, being one with Me according to the divine nature—and according to the human nature, His face is also immutable, since He took on the glory of the resurrection. 

But to the eye of the damned, He will appear as such because they will see Him with that terrible and dark eye that they have within themselves. Just as the diseased eye sees nothing but darkness when looking at the sun, which is so bright, while the healthy eye sees the light—and this is not through a defect of the light, which does not change for the blind man any more than for the sighted one, but through a defect of the eye that is diseased—so the damned will see Him in darkness, in confusion, and in hatred. This is not through a defect of My divine majesty, with which I will come to judge the world, but through their own defect.

### How the damned cannot desire any good. Chapter 40.

And so great is the hatred they have that they cannot will or desire any good, but they blaspheme Me continually. And do you know why they cannot desire good? Because when a man's life is finished, his **free will** <term>libero arbitrio: the capacity to choose between good and evil</term> is bound; therefore they cannot earn **merit** <note>In medieval theology, "merit" refers to the ability to perform actions that are pleasing to God and deserve a spiritual reward. After death, this capacity is lost.</note>, since they have lost their time. 

Thus, if they end their lives dying in hatred with the guilt of **mortal sin**, by divine justice the soul remains forever bound with the bond of hatred, and remains forever obstinate in that evil which it possesses, gnawing at itself. Therefore, their pains are always increasing, and especially for certain individuals for whom the soul may have been the cause of their damnation. This is as I showed you with that rich damned man <note>A reference to the biblical parable of Dives (the rich man) and Lazarus found in Luke 16:19–31.</note>, when he asked for the grace that **Lazarus** should go to his brothers who remained in the world...

He did it because he had been the elder and had nourished them in the miseries in which he had lived. Thus he was the cause of their **damnation** <term>dannatione: the state of eternal separation from God</term>, for which reason he saw his own punishment increase by their arrival at the agonizing torment together with him, where they always gnaw at each other in hatred, because his life ended in hatred.

### Of the glory of the blessed. Chapter 41.

Thus the just soul, which finishes its life in the affection of charity and is bound in love, cannot grow in virtue once time has run out. But it can always love with that love with which it comes to me, and with that measure it is measured to it. Hence it always desires me and always loves me; and yet its desire is not empty: for having hunger it is satisfied, and being satisfied it has hunger; but it is far from the boredom of satiety and the pain of hunger.

In my love they rejoice in the eternal vision of me, participating in that good which I have in myself and give to each according to their measure; that is, with that measure of love with which they have come to me, it is measured to them. For they have lived in my **charity** <term>charità: the highest form of love, directed toward God and neighbor</term> and in that of their neighbor, and they are united together with common charity and with particular love, both of which proceed from one and the same charity. And they rejoice and exult, participating in the good of one another with the affection of love, besides the universal good that they all have together. And they rejoice and exult with the **angelic nature** <note>The medieval belief that the saints occupy the ranks in heaven left vacant by the fallen angels.</note>, with which the saints are placed according to the diverse and various virtues which they principally practiced in the

Hence, when the soul reaches eternal life, everyone participates in the good of that soul, and that soul in the good of others.

# Providence XLI

my will: so that they cannot will anything except what I will. For their **free will** <note>original: "arbitrio"</note> is bound in the bond of charity in such a way that, when time ends for the creature who possesses reason, and they die in a state of **grace**, they can no longer sin. And their will is so united with mine that if a father or mother were to see their child in hell, or a child their father and mother, they would not be troubled; indeed, they are content to see them punished as my enemies. Thus, in nothing are they in disagreement with me, and all their desires are fully satisfied. 

The desire of the blessed is to see my honor in you **wayfarers** <note>The "viandanti" or "pilgrims" are those still living on earth, traveling through life toward the afterlife.</note>, who are pilgrims always running toward the end that is death. Thus, in their desire for my honor, they desire your salvation, and therefore they are always praying to me for you. This desire is fulfilled by me on my part there, even when you, in your ignorance, kick against my **mercy**. 

They also have a desire to receive again the **dowry of their body** <note>In medieval theology, the "dowry of the body" refers to the "four gifts" granted to the body at the Resurrection: impassibility (no pain), brightness, agility, and subtlety.</note>. This desire does not afflict them, even though they do not possess it at this moment; rather, they enjoy it by anticipation through the certainty that they shall have their desire filled. Thus, it does not cause them suffering, for not having it does not diminish their **bliss** <note>original: "beatitudine"</note>, and therefore it gives them no pain. 

And do not think that the bliss of the body after the **resurrection** will give more bliss to the soul. If this were so, it would follow that until they received the body, they possessed an imperfect bliss—which cannot be, because no perfection is lacking in them. So, it is not the body that gives bliss to the soul, but the soul that will give bliss to the body; for the soul will give from its own abundance and will clothe itself on the last day of **judgment** in the garment of its own flesh, which it left behind in the world. And just as the soul is made **immortal**, fixed and established in me, so the body in that union becomes immortal; it loses its heaviness and is made subtle and light.

...of wisdom: that the **glorified body** <note>original: "corpo glorificato"</note> would pass through the middle of a wall, and neither fire nor water would harm it. But the eye of your body, as I told you, will delight in the glorified humanity of the Word, my only-begotten son. Why is this? Because their life ended in the love of my charity, and therefore it lasts for them eternally. Not that they can perform any [new] good, but they rejoice and enjoy that which they have brought with them. That is to say, they can no longer perform any **meritorious act** <note>In Catholic theology, "merit" refers to a good deed done in a state of grace that God rewards; the Church teaches that one can only earn such merit while alive on earth.</note> by which they might deserve anything further, because only in this life does one merit or sin, according as it pleases one's own will with **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note>. These souls, therefore, do not wait for the divine judgment with fear, but with joy. And the face of the Son will not appear to them...

### ¶ How after the general judgment the pain of the damned will increase. Chapter XLII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial H featuring floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>**I** have told you of the dignity of the just, so that they may recognize the misery of the damned; and this is their other pain: to see the **bliss** <note>original: "beatitudie" / "beatitudine"</note> of the just. This vision is an increase of pain for them, just as the damnation of the damned is an increase of exultation in my goodness for the just; because light is better known through darkness, and darkness through light. So the vision of the blessed will be a pain to them, and with pain they await the last day of judgment, because they see an increase of suffering following from it. And so it shall be; for at that terrible voice, when it shall be said to them: **"Rise, you dead, come to judgment"** <note>original: "Surgite mortui: uenite ad iudiciū"</note>, the soul will return with the body; and in the just it shall be glorified, and in the damned it shall be eternally tortured. And they shall receive great shame and reproach in the sight of my **Truth** <note>referring to Christ as the Eternal Truth</note> and of all the blessed. The **worm of conscience** <term>worm of conscience: a traditional medieval metaphor for the gnawing, eternal remorse that torments the soul of the sinner</term> will then gnaw the pith of the tree—that is, the soul—and it will also gnaw the outer bark—that is, the body. They will be reproached for the blood that was shed for them, and for the works of my **mercy** <note>original: "miſericordia"</note> which I performed for them through the spiritual and temporal Son; and for what they ought to have done for their neighbor, as is contained in the **Holy Gospel** <note>original: "ſctō euāgelio"</note>. They shall also be rebuked for the cruelty they have held toward their neighbor, seeing the mercy they have received from me. They shall be rebuked for the pride of their self-love, for their foulness and their **avarice** <note>original: "auaritia"</note>, and in everything...

# From the Divine Chapter

...these things will harshly renew their rebuke. At the time of death, only the soul <note>original: "laia" (l'anima)</note> receives judgment; but at the general judgment <term>general judgment: the final trial of all humanity at the end of time</term> both the soul and the body shall receive it together. This is because the body has been the companion and instrument of the soul in doing both good and evil, according to what pleased its own will. Every action, good or bad, is performed through the means of the body. 

And then, my daughter, glory and infinite good is justly rendered to my elect <term>elect: those chosen by God for salvation</term> along with their glorified bodies, rewarding them for the labors they bore for me together with the soul. And to the perverse <note>original: "puerſi" (perversi)</note>, eternal pain and evil shall be rendered through their bodies, because the body was the instrument of evil. Their pain will thus be renewed and will increase as they behold their bodies in the presence of my Son. 

Their wretched sensuality with all its impurity will then receive rebuke upon seeing their own nature—that is, the humanity of Christ <note>original: "hũanita di xp̃o"</note>—united with the purity of my deity. They will see this mass of Adam’s nature <note>original: "maſſa de adaz," referring to the human nature inherited from Adam</note>, your own nature, raised above all the choirs of angels, while they, through their own fault, see themselves plunged into the depths of hell. 

They will see the abundance and mercy shining in the blessed, as they receive the fruit of the blood of the Lamb <term>Lamb: a title for Jesus Christ, representing his sacrifice</term>. They will also see the sufferings the blessed once endured, all of which remain as an adornment upon their bodies, like a dye upon cloth. This is not through the power of the body itself, but solely through the fullness of the soul, which reflects to the body the fruit of its labor, because the body was a companion to the soul in practicing virtue. 

So it appears on the outside: just as a mirror reflects the face of a man, so in the body is reflected the fruit of its labors in the manner I have described to you. Therefore, when those in darkness see such dignity of which they are deprived, their pain and confusion will increase; for in their own bodies will appear the signs of the iniquities they committed, bringing pain and excruciating torment. Thus, they shall hear that terrible word: **"Depart, you accursed"** <note>original: "andate maledecti"</note>

### To their own place, that is, either to pain or to glory. Chapter 43.

Dearest daughter, the devil has been made my executioner <term>executioner: original "iustisiero," referring to one who carries out a sentence of justice or punishment</term> of my justice to torment the souls who have wretchedly offended me. And in this life, I have set him to tempt and harass my creatures—not so that my creatures might be defeated, but so that they might conquer and receive from me the grace of victory, proving the virtues within them. And in this, no one should fear any battle or temptation from the devil that comes to them, because I have made them strong and given them the strength of a will fortified in the blood of my Son. Neither the devil nor any creature can move this will, because it is yours, given by me with free will <term>free will: original "libero arbitrio," the power to choose between good and evil</term>. You, therefore, with free will, can hold it or let it go as you please.

This will is the weapon that you place in the hands of the devil; and truly it is a knife with which he strikes you and kills you. But if a person does not put this knife of their own will into the hands of the devil—that is, if they do not consent to his temptations and harassments—they will never be harmed by the guilt of sin through any temptation. Instead, it <note>The temptation</note> will strengthen them there, where they open the eye of the intellect to see my charity <term>charity: original "charita," meaning God's selfless and providential love</term>, which allows you to be tempted only to bring you to virtue and to prove that virtue. 

And one does not come to virtue except through the knowledge of oneself <note>original: "cognoscimento di se medesimo"</note> and the knowledge of me. This knowledge is most perfectly acquired in the time of temptation, for then one knows that they are nothing <note>original: "altro cognoscese non essere," a realization of human powerlessness without God</note>, being unable to remove the pains and harassments they wish to flee; and they know me in my will. Therefore, they do not consent to these thoughts, and they have seen that my charity grants this to them; for the devil is weak <note>original: "ifersmo" (infermo)</note> and by himself can do nothing except what I allow him. And I let him tempt you out of love and not out of hatred, so that you may conquer and not be defeated, and so that you may come to a perfect knowledge...

they received my mercy, valuing my mercy more than their own sins. But the wicked sinners do the opposite: wherefore, seeing their place with despair, they embrace it with hatred, as I have told you. So it is that they do not wait to be judged, neither the one nor the other; but departing from this life, each one receives their own place, as I have told you. And tasting it and possessing it before they depart from the body: at the extremity of death, the damned arrive with hatred and with despair; and the perfect with love and with the light of faith and with the hope of the blood; and the imperfect <note>original: "impfecti"; referring to those who have started the path of virtue but are not yet fully purified</note> with mercy and with that same faith reach the place of purgatory.

### ¶ How the devil catches souls under the appearance of some good; and those who stay by the river and not by the aforementioned bridge are deceived, because wishing to flee pains they fall into them; placing here the vision of the tree which this soul had once. Chapter 44

I have told you that the demons invite men to the dead water: that is, to that which they have; and blinding them with the delights and states of the world, with the hook of pleasure they catch them under the appearance of good. For in no other way could they catch them, since souls would not allow themselves to be caught if they did not find some personal good or pleasure there. But it is true that the soul, blinded by self-love <term>self-love: original "amore proprio," a central theme in Catherine's work referring to selfish desire that prioritizes the self over God</term>, does not know nor discern what is truly good and what provides utility to the soul and to the body. And therefore the devil, being wicked, seeing that the soul is blinded by its own sensory love, places before it diverse and varied pleasures, which are colored with the appearance of some utility or some good. And to everyone he gives according to their state and according to those principal vices in which he sees them most disposed to receive. Wherefore he gives one thing to the secular person <term>secular: original "seculare," meaning a layperson living in the world rather than in a religious order</term>, another to the religious <term>religious: original "religioso," referring to those under monastic vows</term>, another to prelates <note>high-ranking church officials</note>, another to lords, and to each according to the different states they hold.

<summary>This page describes the transition of souls at death—damned, perfect, and imperfect—and explains how the devil uses specialized temptations tailored to a person's social and spiritual standing to lead them astray.</summary>

# Providence XLVI
-> Of holy faith <-
