...of holy faith, gazing upon me: who am supreme goodness and who can will nothing but good. For their own good, I grant these things out of love and not out of hatred. And once they have recognized the love within me, they look at themselves and, recognizing their own defects, they see by the light of faith that good must be rewarded and guilt punished. They see that every sin deserves infinite pain because it is committed against me, who am infinite goodness; hence they consider it a grace that I wish to punish them in this life and in this finite time.

And so, they cast out sin with **contrition** <term>contrition: sincere and complete remorse for one's sins, arising from a love for God</term> of the heart, and through perfect **patience** <term>patience: here, the spiritual endurance of suffering without losing one's peace or turning from God</term> they merit reward; thus their labors are remunerated with infinite good. Furthermore, they realize that every labor of this life is small because of the shortness of time. Time is only as long as the point of a needle and no more; and once time has passed, the labor is passed. Therefore, you see that it is small.

Hence, they bear actual thorns and pass through them with patience, and these do not touch the heart; for their heart has been drawn out of them, away from **sensory love** <note>original: "amōr ſenſitiuo"; love driven by physical feelings and worldly desires</note>, and it is placed and joined in me through the affection of love. It is truly the truth, then, that these people taste eternal life, receiving the **earnest money** <note>original: "lara" (from the Latin 'arrha'); a down payment or deposit that guarantees a future transaction—here, a "foretaste" of heaven</note> in this life. Even while standing in the water, they do not get wet; they pass through the thorns and are not pricked, as I have told you; because they have known me, the supreme good, and have sought me where I am found: that is, in the **Word** <term>Word: the Logos, the second person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ</term> of my only-begotten son.

...of faith: so is infidelity. **Of infidelity, I speak of those** who have received holy baptism, in which baptism the pupil of faith was placed within the eye of the intellect. Thus, when the time of discretion <term>discretion: the age of moral reason or accountability, traditionally considered to be around seven years old</term> arrived: if they exercised themselves in virtue, they preserved the light of faith and gave birth to living virtues, bearing fruit for their neighbor. Like a woman who gives birth to a living child and presents him alive to her spouse, so these people give living virtues to me, who am the spouse of the soul.

These wretched ones do the opposite; when the time of discretion arrives, when they ought to exercise the light of faith and give birth to virtues through the life of grace, they instead give birth to them in death. They are "death" because all their works are dead, being performed in mortal sin and deprived of the light of faith. They indeed possess the form of holy baptism, but not the light, for they are deprived of it by the cloud of guilt committed through self-love, which has covered the pupil through which they once saw. Therefore, it is said of these: those who have faith without works, their faith is dead. <note>A reference to the Epistle of James 2:26: "For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also."</note>

And just as a dead man does not see, so the eye of the intellect—with the pupil covered as I have told you—neither sees nor recognizes that it itself is nothing, nor does it recognize the defects it has committed. Nor does it recognize my goodness in faith, from which it received its being and every grace that is placed upon that being. Therefore, not knowing me nor itself, it does not hate its own sensuality <note>sensuality: in this context, the lower, selfish impulses of human nature that resist the spirit</note> within itself; rather, it loves it, seeking to satisfy its own appetite. Thus, it gives birth to dead children of many mortal sins; and it does not love me. Not loving me, it does not love what I love—that is, its neighbor—and it does not take delight in practicing what pleases me.

And these are the true and real virtues which I am pleased to see in you: not for my own benefit, for no benefit can be done for me, since I am the one without whom nothing was made—except for sin, which is nothing <note>sin as "nothing": a common medieval theological concept (from St. Augustine) that sin has no positive existence of its own; it is merely the absence or privation of good</note>, and which deprives the soul of me, who am...

Therefore, being reproved by me for their defects, and because my goodness still wishes to reward that action—that is, that little service they have performed—I reward them with temporal things. # IV. Regarding Divine [Providence]

...their delights and pleasures they have taken, acquired, and possessed without me, and with selfish and disordered love. They bear the exact likeness of scorpions, which I showed you at your beginning <note>referring to an earlier vision in the text</note>, after the figure of the tree. ### How those who do not observe the counsels can still observe the commandments; and how in every state of life a person chooses, if they have good will, they are pleasing to God. Chapter 47.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' containing a portrait of a tonsured monk or saint in profile, looking to the right.</image-desc> I told you about these people: that with the two-edged knife—that is, with the hatred of vice and the love of virtue for the love of me—they cut away the poison of their own sensuality. And those who possessed [wealth] are those who observe the commandments and the counsels in spirit, though not in actual practice. 

But because the counsels are bound to the commandments, no one can observe my commandments who does not also observe the counsels—if not in outward action, then at least in the mind. ### ¶ How worldly people cannot be satisfied, and of the suffering of the perverse will in this life. Chapter xlviii.

I told you above that only the will gave suffering to man; and because my servants are stripped of their own will and clothed in mine, they feel no afflictive pain. Instead, they are satisfied, feeling me by grace in their souls. But without me, people cannot be satisfied, even if they possessed all the wealth of the world. This is because created things are lesser than man, for they were made for man, and not man for them; and therefore he cannot be satisfied by them, but only I can satisfy him. And so these miserable ones, placed in such blindness, always toil and are never satisfied; they desire that which they cannot have, because they do not ask it of me, who can satisfy them. Being deprived of [worldly things], they suffer intolerable pain; and they lose them with as much grief as the disordered love with which they possessed them. Whereas, if they had held them as things lent—and not as their own—the loss would leave them without pain. They have pain, therefore, because they do not have that which they desire; for as I told you, the world cannot satisfy them, and not being satisfied, they endure pain <note>The OCR reads "n̄ hano la pena" (they do not have pain), but the context of "not being satisfied" suggests they suffer the pain of lack.</note>. 

How many are the pains of the sting of conscience! How many are the pains of him who hungers for revenge! He continually gnaws at himself, and has first killed himself—that is, his soul—before he has killed his enemy. How much pain the miser sustains, who through avarice stints his own necessity! How much torment the envious man has, who always gnaws at his own heart and does not let himself take delight in his neighbor! Wherefore, from all the things that they love sensually, they draw pain with many disordered fears. 

And thus they already carry the cross of the devil, tasting the foretaste <note>original: "lara," likely a contraction of "l'arra," meaning a down payment or earnest-money.</note> of hell; and in this life they live as if infirm in many different ways; and if they do not correct themselves, they will receive eternal death afterward. Oh, these are they who are struck by the stings <note>original: "spie," here referring to the sharp "points" or "thorns" of tribulation.</note> of many tribulations, torturing themselves with their own and disordered will. These have a cross of the heart and of the body; that is, the soul and the body pass through pain and torment without any merit, because they do not bear their labors with patience, but with impatience. 

And because they have possessed and acquired gold and the delights of the world with disordered love, being deprived of the life of grace and the affection of charity, they are made **trees of death** <note>A recurring image in Catherine's work where the soul rooted in selfish love produces only "dead" fruit.</note>. Therefore all their works are dead, and with pain they go through the river, drowning themselves; and they reach the dead water, passing with hatred through the gate of the devil, and they receive eternal damnation. Now you have seen how they deceive themselves, and with how much pain they go to hell, making themselves martyrs of the devil. And you have seen what that thing is which blinds them...

It contrasts their "dead works" with the life of grace, describing them as "martyrs of the devil" who suffer without merit.</summary>

# Of the Divine <note>original: "De la diuina"</note> Chapter
<meta>catchword: or from the demons</meta>

...love: and not only in fear: it is not sufficient to give eternal life. It is necessary, therefore, that one place both feet on the first step <note>original: "scalone"</note> of the bridge: that is, the affection and the desire; these are the feet that carry the soul into the affection of My Truth, of which I have made a bridge. This is the first step, of which I told you that it was necessary to climb, saying to you how He <note>Referring to Christ.</note> had made a ladder of His body. It is indeed true that this is almost a general lifting up, which the servants of the world commonly perform, rising first through fear of punishment. And because the tribulations of the world sometimes make them grow weary of themselves, the world begins to displease them; thus, if they exercise this fear with the light of faith, they will pass to the love of virtue. 

But there are some who walk with such lukewarmness that they often return back after they have reached the shore; when contrary winds arrive, they are struck by the waves of the tempestuous sea of this dark life. Hence, if the wind of prosperity arrives, and they have not climbed the first step through their negligence—that is, with their affection and with love of virtue—they turn their head back toward delights with disordered pleasure. And if the wind of adversity comes, they turn away through impatience, because they have not hated their own fault for the offense they committed against Me, but only for fear of the punishment which they see follows from it; by which fear they were lifted from their vomit <note>This is a common biblical metaphor (Proverbs 26:11) for a sinner returning to the sins they had previously repented of.</note>. 

Therefore, because every virtuous thing requires perseverance, and without persevering one does not achieve the effect of their desire—that is, to reach the end for which they began—one who does not persevere never arrives. Thus, perseverance is necessary to fulfill one's desire. Now you have seen how these people turn according to the various movements that come to them: either within themselves, as their own sensuality <term>sensuality: in Catherine's theology, the "sensualità" refers to the lower, selfish nature of humans that struggles against the spirit.</term> fights against the spirit; or through other creatures, turning toward them with disordered love apart from Me, or through impatience for the injury they receive from them, or from the demons...

# Providence XLIX

G

...or from the demons through many and diverse battles: that is, sometimes with contempt to bring the soul to confusion <note>In this context, "confusion" refers to a state of spiritual despair or paralyzing shame.</note>, saying: "This good that you have begun is of no value to you because of your sins and defects." And the demon does this to make them turn back and abandon that little bit of spiritual practice they have taken up. At other times, he uses delight: that is, the hope they place in My mercy, saying: "Why do you want to weary yourself? Enjoy this life, and at the end of your life you will acknowledge your sins and receive mercy." And in this way the devil makes them lose the fear with which they had begun. Because of all these and many other things, they turn their heads back and are not constant, nor persevering. 

And it all happens because the root of self-love <note>original: "amore proprio"</note> remains; there is no spark of virility <note>original: "uirilita" — here meaning spiritual strength, courage, or "manliness" of soul</note> in them, and therefore they are not persevering. Instead, they receive My mercy with great presumption, taking hope not as they should, but ignorantly; with presumption, they hope in My mercy even while I am continually offended by them. For I have not given, nor do I give, mercy so that they may offend with it, but so that with it they may defend themselves against the malice of the demon and the disordered confusion of the mind. 

But they do the exact opposite, because they use the arm of mercy to offend Me. And this happens to them because they have not practiced the first transformation they made—washing themselves with the fear of punishment and being spurred by the thorn of many tribulations arising from the misery of mortal sin. Thus, because they did not truly change, they do not reach the love of virtue, and therefore they have not persevered. The soul cannot help but be in motion; hence, if she does not go forward, she turns back. So these people, by not moving forward in virtue—leaving the perfection of fear but not yet reaching love—must necessarily turn back.

## On the Divine [Treatise] Chapter
### XLII

Then that soul <note>The "soul" refers to St. Catherine of Siena, the protagonist and author of the dialogue.</note>, distressed with desire and grieving for her own and others' imperfection, was pained to hear and see such blindness in creatures. She had seen that the goodness of God was so great that He had placed nothing in this life that could be an impediment to salvation, regardless of one's state of life; rather, all things were given for the exercise and the prompting of virtue. Nonetheless, despite all this, she saw that because of self-love and disordered affection, so many sinners went down through the river <note>The "river" is an allegory for the world and its disordered passions, which lead to spiritual death if one does not cross over them via the Bridge.</note>, and because they did not correct themselves, she saw them reach eternal damnation. 

And many of those who had climbed and begun the journey turned back because of the reasons she had heard from the sweet goodness of God, who had deigned to manifest Himself to her. For this reason, she remained in bitterness; and fixing the eye of the intellect on the Eternal Father, she said: "O inextinguishable Love! Great is the deception of Your creatures! I wish that, when it pleases Your goodness, You would explain more distinctly to me the three stairs figured in the body of Your only-begotten Son, and what way they must hold to emerge entirely from the abyss and walk by the way of Your Truth; and who are those who leap over the stairs?"

You ask Me to explain the figure of the three stairs, and to tell you what manner they must keep to be able to exit the river and climb the bridge. ### Of the Divine Chapter

Therefore, if you wish to reach life, it is necessary for you to persevere in virtue: and whoever wishes to reach eternal death perseveres in vice. ¶ Exposition upon the word that Christ spoke: Let him who thirsts come to me.

He did not say "let him go to the Father and drink," but He said "let him come to me," because in me, the Father, no suffering can fall, but certainly in my Son. And while you are pilgrims and travelers in this mortal life, you cannot go without suffering, because on account of sin the earth brought forth thorns, <note>A reference to the curse of Adam in Genesis 3:18, here representing the difficulties and pains of earthly life.</note> just as I have told you. 

And why did He say "come to me and drink"? Thus you are invited to the fountain of the living water of grace. It is necessary for you, then, to walk through Him, who is made a bridge for you, with perseverance; so that no thorn, nor contrary wind, nor prosperity, nor adversity, nor any other suffering you might endure should make you turn your head back; but you must persevere until the end, so that you find me, who give you

# Of the Divine Providence, Chapter 6

...if: or two: or three: or more. But why does he say: or two: or three? Because there are not two without three: nor three without two: nor two without more: one is excluded: so that I might be in the midst of him: because he has no companion: so that I could stand in the midst: and it is nothing: because he who remains in <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "amore pprio" — for Catherine, this "ordered" or "selfish" love is the root of all sin and the opposite of divine charity.</note> of himself is alone. Why is he alone? Because he is separated from my grace: and from the charity of his neighbor: and being deprived of me by his own fault: he returns to nothing: because I alone am <term>He who is</term> <note>original: "colui: che son" — the Divine Name from Exodus 3:14. Thus, he who is one: that is, who stands alone in his own self-love: is not adorned by my life nor accepted by me. He says then: "if two: or three or more are gathered in my name: I will be in the midst of them." <note>A reference to Matthew 18:20.</note> I told you that two were not without three: nor three without two. This is the beginning: middle: and end of the commandments of the law. ### Concerning the imperfection of those who love and serve God for their own utility and consolation. Chapter 61.

There are some who have become my faithful ones; that is, they serve me faithfully without **servile fear** <note>original: "tiore suile"; the fear of a servant who obeys only to avoid punishment.</note>, not serving solely out of fear of punishment, but serving with love. Therefore, this love is not enough, nor does it last; instead, it slackens, and often they go on slackening toward me when sometimes, to exercise them in **virtue** and to lift them from imperfection, I withdraw the consolation of their minds to myself. I allow them to face battle and troubles, and I do this so that they may come to perfection and the knowledge of themselves, and recognize that they are nothing and have no **grace** from themselves. 

In times of battle, they flee to me, seeking me and recognizing me as their benefactor, seeking me alone and with true humility; and for this reason, I give and promise to them, yet I withdraw consolation from them, but not grace. Such people, I say, then slacken, turning back with an impatient mind; whence sometimes they abandon their spiritual exercises in many ways, and often under the **color of virtue** <note>Under the pretense or outward appearance of doing something good.</note>, saying within themselves: "this is a natural operation," feeling themselves deprived...

And this happens to them because the love in them was not pure, but was marked by that same imperfection with which they loved me—that is, loving me for their own utility, they love others with that same self-interested love. And if they do not recognize their **imperfection** with a desire for perfection, it would be impossible for them not to turn back. 

It is therefore necessary, if they wish for eternal life, that they love without self-interest. For it is not enough to flee sin out of fear of punishment, nor to embrace **virtue** <note>original: "uirtu".</note> for the sake of one's own utility; neither is sufficient to grant eternal life. Instead, it is necessary to rise from sin because it displeases me, and to love virtue for love of me. # Providence 61

H

[...is not yet] perfect; but from imperfection one must arrive at perfection, either during this life—by living in virtue with a sincere and generous heart, that is, loving me without any **selfish regard** <note>original: "rispecto"; meaning self-interest or looking for what one can gain.</note>—or at the moment of death, recognizing one’s own imperfection with the resolve that, if one had more time, they would serve me without regard for themselves.

It was with this imperfect love that **Saint Peter** <note>original: "sctõ petro".</note> loved the sweet and good Jesus, my only-begotten Son, feeling very sweetly the sweetness of his companionship. But when the time of tribulation came, his love failed, and he fell into such a failing: not because he was enduring pain himself, but because he fell into the **fear of pain** <note>original: "tiore d̃ la pēa".</note> and denied him, saying that he had never known him.

The soul that has climbed this ladder only with **servile fear** <term>Servile fear: A state of faith motivated by the fear of hell or punishment rather than love.</term> and with **mercenary love** <term>Mercenary love: Loving God like a hired hand, only for the sake of reward or personal comfort.</term> falls into many such failings. Therefore, they must rise up and become children, serving me without regard for their own interests. I am the rewarder of every labor, and I render to each according to their state and their practice.

And if these people do not abandon the practice of prayer and other good works, but instead continue to grow in virtue with perseverance, they will arrive at the love of a child. And I will love them with **filial love** <note>original: "amore filiale"; the love of a father for a child.</note>; for with that same love with which I am loved, I respond to you. That is to say: while you love me as a servant loves a master, I, as a master, pay what is owed to you according to what you have merited; but I do not manifest myself to you. For **secret things** are manifested to a friend, who has become one with his friend, and not to a servant.

It is true that a servant can grow through their virtue and the love they bear for their master, until they become a most dear friend. And so it happens with these people: as long as they remain in mercenary love, I do not manifest myself to them. ### In what way God manifests himself to the soul that loves him. Chapter 62.

### Why Christ did not say: I will manifest my Father, but myself. ->Chapter 64.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral motifs and a central stem.</image-desc>

**A**ccordingly, you see that my Truth spoke the truth of himself, saying: "Whoever loves me will be one thing with me," because by following his doctrine through the affection of love, you are joined in him; and being joined in him, you are joined in me, because we are one and the same thing. The second [reason] was: because in manifesting himself to you, he did not offer anything else than what he had received from me, the Father. It was as if he wanted to say: "The Father has manifested [himself] to me because I am one thing with him; and I manifest myself, and he manifests through me; I will manifest [this] to you."

The third was: because I, the invisible, cannot be seen by you who are visible, except when you are separated from your bodies. Then you will see me, God, face to face <note>original: "a facia a facia"</note>, and the Word <term>Word: From the Latin 'Verbum,' referring to Christ as the eternal expression of God's wisdom and the second person of the Trinity.</term> of my Son intellectually from that time of the general resurrection <term>General resurrection: The Christian belief that at the end of time, all people will be raised from the dead in their bodies to face judgment.</term>, when your humanity will be conformed to and settled in the humanity of the Word, just as I told you above in the treatise on the resurrection. So you cannot see me as I am. 

And therefore I have veiled the divine nature with the veil of your humanity, so that you could see me. Thus I, the invisible, made myself almost visible, giving you the Word of my Son, veiled in the covering of your humanity, and through him I manifest myself to you. And so he did not say: "I will manifest the Father," but he said "I will manifest myself to you"—as if to say <note>original: "quasi dicat"</note>: "according to what my Father has given me, I will manifest myself to you." So you see that in this manifestation, by manifesting himself, he manifests me. And you have also heard why he did not say: "I will manifest the Father to you"—that is, because it is not possible for you in your mortal body to see me, the Father, as was said, and because he is one thing with me.

The first—that is, how he has come to be a friend—I tell you. This person was first imperfect, being in servile fear <term>Servile fear: Fearing God merely out of a dread of punishment, like a slave fearing a master, rather than out of love.</term>; but by practicing and persevering, he came to the love of delight and his own benefit, finding delight and benefit in me. This is the way, and through this passes he who desires to reach perfect love: that is, the love of a friendly son. I say that filial love is perfect, because in the love of a son he receives the inheritance from me, the Eternal Father. And because the love of a son is not without the love of a friend, I told you that the friend was made a son.

Every perfection and every virtue proceeds from charity, and charity is nourished by humility, and humility proceeds from the knowledge and holy hatred of oneself—that is, of one's own sensuality. He who loves with spiritual love <term>spiritual love</term> <note>original: "spirituale āore"; here referring to a love for others based on shared religious life or affection which may still be tainted by ego</note> feels an afflictive pain when it seems to him that the creature he loves does not satisfy his love, because it does not appear to him that he is loved as much as he thinks he loves. Watch, however, that she does not leave prayer except for obedience or for charity <note>The author emphasizes that one should only interrupt prayer to perform a duty or a necessary act of kindness</note>. The devil does this to make holy prayer feel tedious, often saying: "This prayer is worth nothing to you, for you should not be thinking of anything else, nor attending to anything other than what you are saying." The devil makes her see it this way so that she becomes weary and confused in mind, and abandons the exercise of prayer—which is a weapon with which the soul defends herself from every adversary, when held with the hand of love and the arm of **free will**, defending herself with this weapon by the light of most holy faith.

->Providence LXIX<-

I do this so that the ignorant soul may receive consolation: that is, so that she looks more at the present consolation given by me—who loves her—so that she looks more at the **affection** <note>original: "laffecto" (l'affecto)</note> of my **charity** <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charita"; referring to *caritas*, the highest form of selfless, divine love.</note> with which I give it, and her own unworthiness in receiving it, rather than at the delight of the consolation itself. One [deception] is this: she is deceived by her own consolation and takes delight in it; and more than once, feeling my consolation and my **visitation** <note>original: "uisitatiōe"; a moment of perceived divine presence or grace.</note> within her in some way, and then as it departs, she will go following the path she was on when she found it, in order to find that same one again. And if I [gave it] in only one way, it would seem as if I had nothing else to give; yet I give in various ways, according to what pleases my goodness and according to her necessity and need. 

But being ignorant, she will seek it only in that way, as if she wished to **lay down the law** <note>original: "pōere leze" (ponere legge); meaning to dictate terms or conditions to God.</note> to the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "spirito sācto"</note>. And there she should receive [grace] in 그hat way, in that place, and at that time that it pleases my goodness to give it. 

And if I do not give even that, I do it out of love and not out of hate; [I do it] so that she might seek me in truth and not love me solely for the delight, but rather receive with **humility** <note>original: "hūilita"</note> my charity more than the delight she finds. For if she does not do so, but seeks only the delight in her own way and not in mine, she will receive pain and intolerable confusion when she sees the object of delight taken away—the object she placed before the eye of her **intellect** <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "intellecto"; in this context, the faculty of the soul that perceives spiritual truth.</note>. And sometimes they are so ignorant that when I visit them in a way other than that [which they expect], they will offer resistance and will not receive it, but will want only that which they have imagined.

# Of the Divine Chapter
<meta>catchword: said that (hoti dicto)</meta>

This is a defect of one's own **passion** <term>passion</term> <note>original: "passione"; here meaning an intense emotional state or attachment rather than suffering.</note> and the spiritual delight that the soul finds in me. She is deceived, because it is impossible to remain continually in one state. Just as the soul cannot stand still, but must instead either move forward in **virtue** <note>original: "uirtu"</note> or turn backward, so the mind cannot remain fixed in me through only one delight that my goodness does not see beyond. And so, I grant many different delights: wherefore sometimes I give the delight of a mental joy. At other times, I give a **contrition** <term>contrition</term> <note>original: "contritione"; a state of sincere remorse for one's sins.</note> and a displeasure, such that it seems the mind is disturbed within itself. 

Sometimes I will act within the soul, and she will not feel me. At other times, I will shape my will—that is, Truth, the **Word Incarnate** <term>Word Incarnate</term> <note>original: "uerbo incarnato"; a theological reference to Jesus Christ as the Word of God made flesh.</note>—in various ways before the eye of her intellect. And nonetheless, it will not seem to her that she feels this in her soul’s sentiment with that heat and delight that, in that vision, it seems to her should follow. And at other times, she will feel a very great delight and yet see nothing. 

I do all of this out of love, and to preserve her and increase her in the virtue of **humility** and in **perseverance** <note>original: "pseuerantia" (perseverantia)</note>, and to teach her that she should not wish to set rules for me, nor place her ultimate goal in **consolation** <term>consolation</term> <note>original: "consolatione"; the emotional "reward" or warm feeling felt during prayer.</note>, but only in the virtue founded in me. And let her receive with humility both the one time and the other—the joy and the sorrow—and receive my affection with the affection of love, just as I give it. 

And let her believe with living faith that I give according to what is necessary: either for her salvation or for the necessity of making her arrive at great **perfection** <note>original: "pfectiõe" (perfectione)</note>. She must, therefore, remain humble, making the affection of my **charity** <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charita"; divine, selfless love.</note> her beginning and her end; and she will receive within that charity delight according to my will, and not according to her own. This is the way to avoid receiving deception: that is, to receive everything for the love of me, who am her end, founded in my sweet will.

I have told you of the deception that those receive who want to taste and receive me in their mind in their own way. Now I want to tell you of those whose whole delight is placed in receiving the consolation of their mind. This reaches such a point that they will often see their **neighbor** <term>neighbor</term> <note>original: "pxio" / "proximo"; in a theological sense, this refers to any person in need of help.</note> in necessity—either spiritual or temporal—and will not help them under the guise of **virtue** <note>original: "ūtu" / "virtu"</note>, saying: "I will lose my peace and the quiet of my mind." Therefore, because they do not have that consolation, it seems to them that they are offending me; but they are deceived by the proper spiritual delight of their own mind.

And they offend me more by not helping the necessity of their neighbor than by leaving all their consolations. For every exercise—both vocal and mental—is ordained by me so that the soul may perform it to arrive at perfect **charity** <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charita"; the highest form of love, directed toward God and one's fellow human beings.</note> for me and for the neighbor, and to preserve it within that charity. Thus, they offend me more by abandoning the charity of the neighbor for actual exercise and quiet of mind, than if they had left that exercise for the sake of the neighbor. This is because in the charity of the neighbor they find me; but in their own delight, where they seek me, they would be deprived of me. For by not helping the neighbor, they diminish the charity toward that neighbor, and my affection toward them diminishes accordingly.

When affection is diminished, **consolation** <term>consolation</term> <note>original: "cōsolatiōe"; the pleasant emotional or spiritual feelings that often accompany prayer.</note> is also diminished; so that by wanting to gain, they lose, and by being willing to lose, they gain. That is to say: by being willing to lose their own consolations for the salvation of the neighbor, they receive and gain me, as well as their neighbor, by helping and serving them charitably. In this way, they would taste the sweetness of my charity at all times.

By not doing so, they remain in pain; for it sometimes happens that they do help, whether by force, or for love, or because of a bodily or spiritual infirmity that the neighbor has. And helping him then, they help with pain, with weariness of mind, and a sting of conscience; and such a person becomes unbearable to themselves and to others. [having] lost peace and quiet of mind; and they say, "I have abandoned many of those things I used to do," and they believe they offend God. But it is not so. Rather, it is because their vision is focused on their own delight, and therefore they do not know how to discern or recognize in this life where their offense truly lies. ### Of the deception received by those who have placed all their affection in mental consolations and visions. Chapter 71.

And sometimes, because of this kind of love, they suffer even greater harm. As I told you before, I come and go within the soul, departing not in terms of grace, but in terms of feeling, so that the soul may reach **perfection** <term>perfection</term> <note>original: "pfectione"; the state of spiritual maturity where the soul is fully united with God's will.</note>. Thus you see that the soul falls into bitterness, and it seems to her that she is in hell, feeling herself stripped of delight and experiencing the distress of many temptations. Therefore, she should not be ignorant, nor allow herself to be so deceived by spiritual self-love that she fails to recognize the truth. She must recognize me within herself—I who am the only **Supreme Good**—and the one who preserves her good will during times of spiritual battle, so that she does not chase after temptations for the sake of delight. She ought, then, to humble herself, considering herself unworthy of peace and quiet of mind. And for this reason, I withdraw myself from her: namely, to make her humble and to lead her to recognize charity...

Thus, she remains in a vigil, watching with the eye of the intellect in the doctrine of my Truth, humbled because she has known herself, and in continuous prayer—that is, holy and true desire—because she recognized the affection of my **charity** <note>original: "charita"</note> within herself.

They did not fear pain but gloried in their sufferings. They did not care about appearing before the tyrants of the world to announce and tell them of the way of life, for the praise and glory of my name. So the soul who waits...

And in this, I shared the **Holy Spirit** <note>original: "spō sctō"</note> within her **will** <note>original: "uolunta"</note>, strengthening the will to desire to suffer pain and to go out from the house for my name’s sake, and to **give birth** <note>original: "pturire"; a common Catherinian metaphor for manifesting internal virtues as outward acts of service.</note> to the virtues for the benefit of her **neighbor** <note>original: "proximo"</note>. Not that she leaves the house of self-knowledge, but the virtues conceived through the affection of love go out from the house of the soul and she gives birth to them in the time of her neighbor’s need in many and various ways, having no regard for the love of not losing her own consolations, just as I told you above. But since they have come to perfect and liberal love, they go out in the manner described, abandoning themselves. And this joins them with the fourth state: that is, from the third state—which was a state of perfection, in which state one tastes and gives birth to charity toward the neighbor—one receives a final state of **perfect union** <note>original: "perfecta unione"</note> in me. These two states are joined together, because one is not without the other; just as there is no love for me without love for the neighbor, and no love for the neighbor without my love, for one cannot be separated from the other. Thus these two states are not one without the other, as I have been declaring and showing you through this third...

# Of Divine Providence: Chapter 75

[mort]al nature <note>The text begins with the second half of the word "mortale" (mortal), referring to Christ's human capacity to suffer.</note> to sustain pain and torments was finished: and because through a finite thing I could not show as much love as I possessed—for my love was infinite—I therefore willed that you should see the secret of the heart: showing it to you opened <note>This refers to the piercing of Christ’s side by the lance, revealing his heart.</note>: so that you might see that I loved more than I could demonstrate through finite suffering. And by shedding blood and water, I showed you the holy baptism of water, which you receive by virtue of the blood. And therefore I poured out blood and water.

It also showed the baptism of blood in two ways. One way is in those who are baptized in their own blood, shed for me <note>The "Baptism of Blood" traditionally refers to martyrs who die for the faith before being water-baptized.</note>. Certain others are baptized in fire: desiring baptism with an affection of love, and yet they are not able to have it <note>The "Baptism of Desire" (baptism of fire), where the intense love for God and the wish for the sacrament are considered sufficient for salvation if the physical ritual is impossible.</note>. And it is not a baptism of fire without blood: because the blood is infused and kneaded with the fire of divine **charity** <note>original: "charita"; the highest form of Christian love.</note>, because it was shed for love.

In another way, the soul receives this baptism of blood, speaking figuratively: and this was provided by divine charity, because, knowing the infirmity and the fragility of man—by which fragility he offends—not that he is forced by fragility or anything else to commit a **sin** <note>original: "colpa"</note> unless he wills it; but as a fragile being, he falls into the fault of **mortal sin** <note>original: "pctõ mortale"</note>. Through this fault, he loses the grace that he drew from holy baptism by virtue of the blood. It was therefore necessary that divine charity should provide a way to leave a "continuous baptism" of blood: which is received with **contrition** <note>original: "otritiõe"; sincere sorrow for one's sins.</note> of the heart and with holy **confession** <note>original: "oſeſſiõe"</note>.

This is done by confessing, when one is able, to my ministers, who hold the **keys of the blood** <note>original: "chiaue del ſangue"; refers to the authority of priests to grant absolution through the sacraments.</note>. They pour this blood during absolution upon the face of the soul. And when one is not able to have confession, the contrition of the heart is enough. Then the hand of my **mercy** <note>original: "clemẽtia"</note> gives you the fruit of this precious blood. But if you are able to have confession, I want you to have it: and whoever can have it and does not wish for it shall be deprived of the fruit of the blood. It is true that in the final extremity of life, if one desires it and is not able to have it, they shall still receive it. But let no one be so mad as to...

# Providence: Chapter 75

should not, however, with this hope <note>The hope of God's infinite mercy through the blood of Christ.</note>, intend to set his affairs in order only at the ultimate extremity of death: for it is not safe. For because of his obstinacy, my divine justice might say: "You did not remember me in life, in the time when you were able; and I will not remember you in death." So no one should take such confidence <note>The original "idusia" is likely a variant of "fiducia," here meaning a false or presumptuous confidence.</note>. Thus you see that this baptism is continuous, wherein the soul must be baptized even until the end in the manner described.

In this baptism, therefore, recognize that my suffering—that is, the pain of the cross—was finite; but the fruit of that pain, which you have received through me, is infinite. This is by virtue of the infinite **divine nature** joined with the finite **human nature**; which human nature sustained pain in me, the **Word** <note>original: "uerbo"; referring to Christ as the Logos, the second person of the Trinity.</note> clothed in your humanity. But because one nature is mixed and kneaded with the other, the eternal deity drew to itself the pain that I sustained with such a fire of love; and therefore this work can be called infinite. 

Not that the pain was infinite—neither the actual pain of the body, nor the pain of the desire that I had to complete your **redemption** <note>original: "redẽptione"</note>; for it had a term and an end on the cross when the soul departed from the body. But the fruit that proceeded from the pain and from the desire for your salvation is infinite, and therefore you receive it infinitely. For if it had not been infinite, it would not have restored the whole of human generation—neither those in the present, nor in the past, nor in the future. Nor could the man who offends rise again after the offense if this baptism of blood were not given to you as infinite: that is, that the fruit of the blood was infinite. This I manifested to you in the opening of my side, where the secret of the heart was found: showing that I love you more than I can show with this finite pain. I showed it to you, then, in[finitely...]

<summary>God explains that while Christ's physical suffering on the cross was finite in time, the "fruit" or saving power of that sacrifice is infinite because it is joined to his eternal divine nature. # Providence LXXVI

->Dialogue of Saint Catherine<-

...nature: in different ways: and each according to their state. I say that they eat the food of souls for my honor at the table of the most holy cross: for in no other way: and at no other table could they eat it perfectly in truth. I say that they chew it with the teeth: for in no other way could they swallow it: that is, with hatred and with love: which are the two rows of teeth <note>The original "dui figli de denti" likely refers to the two rows of teeth, representing the dual actions of the soul: rejecting sin (hatred) and embracing God (love).</note> in the mouth of holy desire which receives the food, chewing it with hatred of oneself: and with love of virtue in itself and in its neighbor. It chews, I say, every injury: scorn: insults: torments: and outrages with many persecutions: enduring hunger: and thirst: cold: and heat: and painful desires: tears: and sweat for the salvation of souls: all these it chews for my honor: bearing: and supporting its neighbor. And after it has chewed, the taste enjoys savoring the fruit of the labor: and the delight of the food of souls, tasting it in the fire of my **charity** <term>divine love (caritas)</term>: and that of its neighbor. And so this food reaches the stomach: which through the desire: and hunger for souls will be disposed to receive it: that is, the stomach of the heart, with cordial love, delight: and the affection of charity with its neighbor. Delighting in it: and consuming it in such a way: that it loses the tenderness of the corporal life <note>Meaning the soul becomes indifferent to physical comforts or pains in its pursuit of God.</note> in order to eat this food taken at the table of the cross of the doctrine of **Christ crucified**. Then the soul grows fat <note>In mystical tradition, "growing fat" signifies being filled with grace and spiritual strength.</note> in the true and real virtues: and it swells so much from the abundance of the food: that the garment of its own sensuality: that is, the body: which covers it, bursts as far as the sensory appetite is concerned; he who bursts, dies: and so the **sensitive will** <term>the part of the human will driven by physical senses and desires</term> remains dead. And this is because the will ordered by the soul is alive in me, clothed in the earthly will: but the sensitive will is dead. Now this soul: which in truth has arrived at the third step of the mouth: because it has killed its own will: it tastes the affection of my charity: and thus finds peace: and quiet in its soul at the mouth.

# Of the Divine Chapter
<meta>catchword: And this</meta>

You know that in the mouth, the kiss of peace is given: so in this third state, the soul finds peace: in such a way that no one can disturb it: because it has lost and denied its own will. This will gives peace and quiet only when it is dead <note>In Catherine’s theology, the "death of the self-will" does not mean the end of desire, but the perfect alignment of the human will with the Divine will.</note>. Such souls as these exercise virtues without pain toward their neighbor: not that pains are no longer pains to them, but there is no pain to the deadened will, because it voluntarily sustains pain for the sake of my name. These run without negligence through the doctrine of Christ crucified: and they do not slow their pace because of any injury done to them, nor for any persecution, nor for any delight—that is, any delight that the world might wish to give them. Now they pass through all these things with a strength and perseverance, having clothed their affection with the affection of **charity** <term>Divine love (caritas), distinguished from mere human affection</term>: tasting the food of the salvation of souls with true and perfect patience. This patience is a demonstrative sign: which shows the soul to me, its God, most perfectly and without any self-regard <note>original: "ſẽza alcũo riſpecto" - meaning without selfish motivation or looking back at one's own interests.</note>: because if the soul loved me and its neighbor for its own utility, it would be impatient and would become negligent in its journey. Now, because they love me for my sake—inasmuch as I am the supreme goodness and worthy of being loved—and if they love me for my sake and their neighbor for my sake—that is, to render glory and praise to my name—they are patient and strong to endure, and persevering.

### Of the operations of the soul after it has ascended to the third step. Chapter LXXVII.

These are those three glorious virtues founded on the one charity, which stand at the top of the tree of this charity: namely, patience, fortitude, and perseverance. The soul is crowned with the light of the most holy faith, with which light they run without darkness through the way of truth. And the soul is raised on high by holy desire: and therefore there is no one who can offend it. Not the demon with his temptations: because he fears the soul that burns in the furnace of **charity**. Not the slanders nor the injuries of men; but rather, despite everything—that is, though the world persecutes them—the world is afraid of them.

In this state of perfect charity, the soul becomes immune to the world's injuries and is feared even by the devil.</summary>

And this my goodness promises: that is, to strengthen them and make them great before me and in the world, because they have made themselves small through **humility** <term>For Catherine, humility is the "nanny" of charity, representing the soul's recognition that it is nothing and God is everything</term>. You see it well in my saints, who for my sake made themselves small; and I have made them great in me—in everlasting life—and in the **mystical body** <note>The "Corpo Mistico" refers to the spiritual union of all the faithful as one body with Christ as the head.</note> of the Holy Church, where mention is always made of them: for their names are written in me, the **Book of Life** <note>original: "libro di uita"</note>. Thus you see that the world holds them in reverence because they have despised the world.

Such people do not hide virtue out of fear, but out of humility; and if the neighbor has need of their service, they do not hide for fear of pain, nor for fear of losing their own consolation, but they serve manfully, losing themselves and not caring for their own interests. And in whatever way they exercise their life and their time, they rejoice in my honor and find peace and quiet in the mind. Why? Because they do not choose to serve me in their own way, but in my way; and therefore the time of consolation is as valuable to them as that of tribulation, and prosperity as much as adversity. 

One is as important to them as the other, because in everything they find my will; and they do not think of doing anything else but conforming themselves to that will of mine wherever they find it. They have seen that nothing is made without me, and they see that everything is made with mystery and with **divine providence** <term>The governance of God by which He guides all things in the universe toward their proper end</term>, except for sin, which is nothingness <note>original: "il peccato: che nõ e" - This reflects the theological idea that sin has no "being" or existence of its own; it is a privation or a turning away from God, who is Being itself.</note>; and therefore they hate sin, and they hold everything else in reverence. 

And therefore they are so firm and stable in their desire to walk the way of life and they do not slow down, but faithfully serve their neighbor. They do not look at his ignorance, nor at his ingratitude, nor do they slow down because sometimes a vicious man insults them and reproves their good works; for they cry out in my presence with holy prayer for him, grieving more for the offense he does to me and for the damage to his soul than for their own injury. These say the glorious saying of **Paul** <note>St. Paul the Apostle, frequently cited by Catherine as a model of the "herald" or preacher.</note>, my herald: "The world is..."

# Of Divine Providence: Chapter [LXXVII]

...they speak ill, and we bless; they persecute us, and we give thanks; we are cast out as the filth and sweepings of the world, and we bear it patiently <note>This passage paraphrases 1 Corinthians 4:12-13, where St. Paul describes the trials of the Apostles.</note>. So you see, most beloved daughter, the sweet signs—singularly above every other sign—of the virtue of **patience** <term>For Catherine, patience is the ultimate proof of love, as it demonstrates a soul's willingness to suffer for the beloved without murmuring.</term>. By this, the soul shows in her life that she has been lifted from imperfect love and has arrived at perfection, following the sweet and immaculate **only-begotten Lamb** <note>original: "agnello unigenito"</note>, my Son.

Who, while standing upon the **cross** held by the nails of love <note>Catherine frequently emphasizes that it was love for humanity, not iron nails, that kept Christ on the cross.</note>, did not draw back because of the words of the Jews who said, "descend from the cross and we will believe in you." Nor did he draw back because of your ingratitude; he did not fail to persevere in the **obedience** <note>original: "obediëtia"</note> that I had imposed upon him with such patience that his cry was never heard to murmur. 

In this way, these most beloved children and faithful of mine follow the doctrine and the example of my Truth. And although the world may wish to pull them back with flatteries or threats, they do not turn their heads back to look at the plow <note>A reference to Luke 9:62: "No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for service in the kingdom of God."</note>, but keep their gaze fixed only on the object of my life. These do not wish to leave the field of battle to return home for their "coat"—that is, for the coat of self-love <note>Catherine interprets the "garment" mentioned in Mark 13:16 as the soul's old habits of seeking human approval or self-interest.</note>, which they left behind—desiring to please creatures more, or fear them more, than me, their Creator. Instead, they remain in the heat of the battle with delight, inebriated by the blood of Christ crucified.

This blood is placed before you in the battle within the **mystical body** <note>original: "corpo mistico"</note> of the **Holy Church** <note>original: "sctā chiesia"</note> of my charity, to set on fire those who wish to be true knights and fight against their own sensuality, their fragile flesh, the world, and the devil. They fight with the knife of hatred for these enemies and with the knife of the love of virtue. This love is a piece of armor that shields against blows so that they cannot strike home, unless the knight strips the armor from his own back and hands the knife over to his enemies. This happens when one surrenders the weapons using the hand of **free will** <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note>, yielding voluntarily to his enemies. But these [perfected souls] do not do so...

# Of the Divine Chapter
<meta>catchword: to them</meta>

...[with such a] great desire to be able to endure pain for the glory and praise of my name. These people glory in the reproaches <note>original: "opbrīi" — insults or shames</note> of my only-begotten son, just as Paul the herald <note>Saint Paul the Apostle, frequently referred to in this period as the "herald" or "vessel of election."</note> said: *I glory in tribulations and in the shames of Christ crucified.* And in another place he says: *I do not think I should glory in anything else but in Christ crucified.* Wherefore in another place he says: *I bear the marks <term>Stigmata: literally "marks" or "brands." In this context, Catherine refers to both the physical wounds of Christ and the spiritual identification with his suffering.</term> of Christ crucified in my body.*

Thus, such as these—being in love with my honor and hungry for the food of souls <note>original: "ie," an abbreviation for "anime" (souls)</note>—run to the table of the most holy cross. They wish, through pain and much endurance, to be useful in preserving their neighbor and acquiring the virtues, bearing the marks of Christ in their bodies. This means that the crucified love which they possess shines forth in their bodies, showing itself through the despising of themselves and through delighting in reproaches, sustaining hardships and pains from whatever side and in whatever way I grant them. 

To these most dear children, pain is a delight, and [worldly] delight is a labor. They despise every consolation and pleasure that the world might sometimes wish to give them—and not only those things the world gives by my dispensation <note>The "dispensation" here refers to God's providence in allowing even worldly people to sometimes respect or assist his servants.</note> (that is, that the servants of the world are sometimes forced by my goodness to hold them in reverence and to help them in their physical needs and necessities). But even the consolation that they receive from me, the Eternal Father, in their minds, they despise out of humility and out of hatred for their own [selfish] selves. 

It is not that they despise the consolation and the gift and my grace itself, but rather the [selfish] pleasure that the soul's desire finds in that consolation. This is because of the virtue of true humility, acquired through holy hatred <note>A common medieval ascetic concept where one "hates" the selfish ego or "sensuality" to make room for divine love.</note>; this humility is the governess <term>original: "baila" — a wet-nurse or governess who rears and protects a child.</term> and nurse of the charity acquired with true knowledge of oneself and of me. 

So you see that virtue shines, and the marks of Christ crucified are in their minds. From these people, the feeling of being separated from me is taken away; unlike the others of whom I told you, where I seemed to "come and go" to them.

This sweet scent <note>original: "suitor" likely a transcription of "sentore," meaning a scent or sensation. In mystical literature, the "scent" of virtue or prayer is what rises to God.</note> carries, brings, and offers to me the pious and sweet amorous desires of them; and it carries to them the fruit of divine charity <term>charity: in this context, the highest form of love (Agape), representing the soul’s selfless union with God</term> from their labors in their soul, as they taste and nourish themselves on the sweetness of my love. So you see that I am the table for them, and my Son is their food, and the Holy Spirit serves them <note>original: "gli sue," likely "gli serve." See, therefore, that through feeling they always perceive me in their minds. 

And the more they have despised earthly delight and pleasure, the more they have lost the pain of suffering and acquired delight, because they are burned and inflamed in my charity where their own will is consumed. Wherefore the devil <term>demōio: the personification of temptation and spiritual opposition</term> fears the staff of their charity, and so he throws his arrows from afar and does not dare to approach. And the world <term>mōdo: the secular or material realm that opposes the spiritual life</term> strikes at the skin of their bodies, believing it causes offense, but it is the world itself that is offended. This is because the arrow, finding no place to enter, returns to the one who throws it. 

Thus the world, with the arrows of injuries, persecutions <term>psecutiōe: trials or harassment faced by the faithful</term>, and its murmurings, throws them at my most perfect servants. But there is no place on any side through which they can enter, because the garden of their soul is locked; and so the arrow returns to the one who throws it, poisoned with the venom of guilt. See then, that it can strike from no side; for in striking the body it does not strike the soul, but the soul remains both blessed and sorrowful. It remains sorrowful for the offense against its neighbor, and blessed for the union and affection of charity that it has received within itself. 

These follow the immaculate lamb <term>agnello unigenito: the "only-begotten lamb," referring to Jesus Christ</term>, my only-begotten Son, who while on the cross was both blessed and sorrowful. He was sorrowful carrying the cross of the body, enduring pain, and the cross of desire to satisfy the guilt of the human race. And he was blessed because the divine nature <term>natura diuia: the essence of God</term>, joined with the human nature <term>natura hūana: the essence of man</term>, could not suffer pain; it always made his soul blessed, showing itself to him without a veil. And so he was blessed and sorrowful: because the flesh suffered, but the divinity could not suffer, nor even the soul as to its higher part <note>original: "parte de sopra." In medieval theology, the "higher part" of the soul (the intellect and will) could remain in a state of beatific vision while the "lower part" (the senses) experienced agony.</note>.

Thus these beloved children who have reached the **third** and **fourth state** are sorrowful, bearing the **actual and mental cross**: that is, actually sustaining pain in their bodies according to what I permit; and the cross of desire, which they have from the crucified sorrow of the offense against me and the harm of their neighbor. So then, it is a nourishing pain and not an afflictive one, because no sorrow or pain can pull the soul out of the fire—just like a **firebrand** <note>original: "stizone," a piece of burning wood.</note> that is entirely consumed in the furnace; there is no one who can take it out to extinguish it, because it has become fire itself. And I never withdraw myself from them by **feeling** <note>original: "sentimento," referring to the internal perception or emotional awareness of God's presence.</note>, so that their mind does not feel me within itself, as I told you of the others, where I went and returned, departing by feeling but not by grace; and I did this to make them come to perfection. Having arrived then at perfection, I take from them the **game of love** <note>original: "zoco d'amore." This refers to the spiritual stage where a person feels God's presence "come and go," a cycle used to teach the soul not to rely on emotional highs.</note> of going and returning; it is called a "game of love" because for love I depart, and for love I return. Not that I, your immobile God, truly move, for I do not move; but the feeling that comes from my charity in the soul is that which goes and returns.

In another way I depart: because the soul <note>original: "lania," a contraction of "l'anima."</note>, which is bound in the body, is not sufficient to receive continuously the union that I make in the soul to see me; and because it is not sufficient, I withdraw—not by feeling, nor by grace, but by union. Because souls, rising with anxious desire, run with virtue across the **bridge** <term>the bridge: a central metaphor in Catherine's work, representing Christ as the link between humanity and God</term> of the doctrine of **Christ crucified**. And here they reach the gate, lifting their minds into me, fed and inebriated with blood, burned with the fire of love; they taste in me the **eternal deity**, which is to them a **peaceful sea**. In this sea, the soul has achieved such union that the mind has no movement other than in me. And being mortal, it tastes the good of the immortals; and being burdened with the weight of the body, it receives the lightness of the spirit. 

Hence, often the body is lifted from the earth because of the perfect conjunction that the soul has made in me, as if the heavy body becomes light. It is not, however, that its heaviness is taken away from it, but because the union that the soul has made in me is more perfect than the union between the soul and the body; therefore the strength of the spirit united in me lifts the weight of the body from the earth. The body remains as if immobile, completely overcome <note>original: "stracciato," literally "torn apart." In this mystical context, it refers to the body being rendered powerless or suspended by the sheer intensity of the soul's spiritual experience.</note> by the affection of the soul—so much so that, as you remember having heard regarding certain creatures, it would not be possible to live if my goodness did not surround them with strength. 

Hence I want you to know that it is a greater miracle to see that the soul does not depart from the body in this union than to see many dead bodies resurrected. And therefore, for some space of time, I withdraw the union, making it return to the **vessel of its body**: that is, the feeling of the body, which was entirely alienated by the affection of the soul, returns to its own senses. This is not because the soul actually departs from the body—for it does not depart except by means of death—but it is because the powers and the affection of the soul depart through love, being united in me. Therefore the memory is not found <note>the original Italian ends with "trova," matching the catchword "tro:"</note> at that time full of anything else:

His eye was bound so that it could not see me, the **Eternal Trinity**, nor the vision of the immortal blessed ones who always give glory and praise to my name.

But he found himself among mortals who always offend me, deprived of my vision—that is, of seeing me in my essence. and in the mortal body, there is a darkness compared to the sight that the soul has when it is separated from the body. Thus, it seemed to Paul <note>St. Paul the Apostle</note> that the sense of sight conflicted with the sight of the spirit; that is, that the human feeling of the body’s density hindered the eye of the intellect <term>intellect: the faculty of the soul used to perceive spiritual and divine truths</term>, which did not allow him to see me face to face. Therefore, it was with pain; for if the desire for that which was loved had been full, they would not have felt pain. But because love, while it is in the mortal body, does not perfectly possess what it loves, it therefore feels pain. But once the soul is separated from the body, its desire is fulfilled, and thus it loves without pain. Then it is satisfied, but boredom is far from that longing; and being satisfied, it still hungers, but the pain of hunger is far away. For once the soul is separated from the body, its vessel <note>original: "uasello," a metaphor for the soul as a container for divine grace</note> is filled in me, truly fixed and established in truth, so that it cannot desire anything it does not already have. Therefore, desiring to see me, it sees me face to face. And desiring to see the glory and praise of my name, it sees it in my saints, or in the angelic nature, or in the human nature.

# Providence LXXXI

of their glory and the praise of my name: that is, that in them shines my mercy and the abundance of my charity. I grant them time <note>God refers here to the "time of grace," the period of a human life during which repentance is possible</note>, and I do not command the earth to swallow them up for their failings. Instead, I wait for them, and I command the earth to give them its fruits, the sun to warm them and give them its light and heat, and the sky to move for them, as it does for all created things made for their sake. I exercise my mercy and charity, not withdrawing these things because of their failings, but giving them to the sinner just as to the righteous man. Indeed, I often give more to the sinner than to the righteous man, for the righteous man—who is fit to endure—is deprived of the goods of the earth so that I may give him more abundantly of the goods of heaven. Thus, my mercy and charity shine upon them. 

Sometimes also, in the persecutions that the followers of the world inflict upon my servants, the virtue of patience and charity is proven in them. By offering up their own selves—sustaining themselves in humble and continual prayer—glory and praise return to my name. So, whether the perverse <note>original: "puerfo," likely a variant of *perverso*</note> man intends it for good or not, glory returns to me, even though his own intention was not for that, but rather to bring me reproach.

### How even the demons give glory and praise to God. Chapter 81.

And I say that they increase them by exercising them in virtue through many troubles and temptations in diverse ways: by causing them to do injury to one another and to take things from one another—not solely for the sake of the objects or the injury itself, but to deprive them of charity. -># Of the Divine Chapter<-

...glory and praise to my name: and thus my life <note>original: "uita." In this context, God refers to His divine purpose or the "life" of His grace being fulfilled through the outworking of His plan.</note> is fulfilled in them. That is, I had created them for the glory and praise of me, the Eternal Father, and so that they might participate in my beauty; however, rebelling against me through their pride, they fell and are deprived of my vision. Therefore, they did not return glory to me, nor the delight of love. But I, Eternal Life, have set these demons as an instrument for the exercise of my chosen ones in virtue, and also as the ministers of justice for those who, through their failings, go to eternal damnation, and also for those who go to the pains of purgatory. So you see, that my life is fulfilled in them. That is, they return glory to me—not as citizens of eternal life, of which they are deprived by their own faults—but as my ministers of justice, manifesting through them my justice upon the damned and upon those in purgatory.

### How the soul, once it has passed from this life, fully sees the glory of God's name in every creature, and how in her the pain of desire has ended, but not the desire itself. Chapter 82.

Who is it that sees this, and who tastes it? That is, who sees the glory and praise of my name in every created thing—both in the demons and in the creatures who possess reason? The soul that is stripped of the body and has reached me, its final end, sees it clearly, and in its seeing, it knows the truth. Therefore, seeing me, the Eternal Father, it loves; loving, it is sated; sated, it knows the truth; and knowing the truth <note>original: "uita," life; the text equates knowing the Truth with possessing the Life</note>, it is fixed to my will. It is bound and established in such a way that in nothing can it suffer pain, because it possesses that which it desired to have: namely, to see through me the glory and praise of my name. 

The soul sees this fully in the life of my saints, and in the blessed spirits, and in all other creatures, and even in the demons, as I have told you. And although it sees the offense committed against me—which previously caused it sorrow—now it cannot feel sorrow, but only compassion without pain.

# Providence 83

...loving without suffering, and always praying to me with the affection of charity <note>In Catherine’s theology, "charity" (caritas) is the highest form of love—a selfless, divine love for God and others.</note> that I might show mercy to the world. So you see that in them, pain has ended, but charity has not. It is just as it was with the Word, <note>original: "uerbo." This refers to Jesus Christ as the "Logos" or Divine Word.</note> my Son, upon the cross; for in his death, the pain of his tormented desire ended—a desire he had carried as a suffering burden from the moment I sent him into the world until the very end in death for your salvation. 

But the desire for your salvation did not end; only the pain did. For if the affection of my charity, which I demonstrated through him, had ended and ceased toward you at that moment, you would not exist. You exist because you are made of love; therefore, if love were withdrawn from me—that is, if I did not love your very being—you would not be. But my love created you, and my love preserves you. And because I am one thing with my Truth, he, the incarnate Word, ended the pain of his desire along with me. 

See then: the saints, and every soul that has reached eternal life, have a desire for the salvation of souls without suffering. Their pain ended in their death, but the affection of their charity did not. Instead, like those drunken on the blood of the immaculate Lamb and clothed in the charity of their neighbor, <note>original: "pxīo" (prossimo). The text emphasizes that the saints enter heaven through their love for others, shown here as being "clothed" in that love.</note> they pass through the narrow gate bathed in the blood of Christ crucified. They find themselves in me, a peaceful sea, lifted from imperfection—that is, from dissatisfaction—and joined to perfection, satisfied with every good thing.

# Concerning the Divine Chapter

...doctrine of my Truth, the incarnate Word. The soul of Paul clothed itself through feeling and union with me, the Eternal Father, just as the blessed do in the life that lasts forever—except that his soul was not separated from his body, but [experienced it] through feeling and union. And since it pleased my goodness to make him a vessel of election <note>original: "uasello de electiõe" (vas electionis). A biblical title for Saint Paul from Acts 9:15, referring to him as a chosen instrument of God.</note> in the abyss of me, the Eternal Trinity, I stripped him of myself—because within me there is no suffering, and I wanted him to endure suffering for the sake of my name. 

Therefore, I placed Christ crucified as the object before the eye of his intellect, clothing him in the garment of his doctrine, bound and chained by the clemency of the Holy Spirit, which is the fire of charity. He, like a vessel prepared and reformed by my goodness—because he did not resist as much as he was able—said: "My Lord, what do you want me to do? Tell me what you want me to do, and I will do it." <note>A paraphrase of Paul’s conversion experience on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:6).</note> 

I taught him when I placed Christ crucified before his sight, clothing him in the doctrine of my Truth. I illuminated him most perfectly with the light of true contrition, with which he consumed his failings, founded in my charity. He clothed himself in the doctrine of Christ crucified and bound it to himself in such a way—just as he made clear to you—that it was never taken off his back: neither through the temptations of demons, nor by the thorn in the flesh <note>original: "stiolo de la carne" (stimolo). A reference to the "thorn in the flesh" mentioned by Paul in 2 Corinthians 12:7, traditionally interpreted as a physical ailment or persistent temptation.</note> that often attacked him. This was left to him by my goodness to grow him in grace and merit, and for the sake of humility, because he had tasted the height of the Trinity. 

Neither through tribulation, nor through anything else that happened to him, did he loosen the garment of Christ crucified—that is, the perseverance in his doctrine. Instead, he made it even more a part of his very being, <note>original: "se lo icarnaua" (incarnated it into himself).</note> and he held it so tightly that it gave him life; and in that garment, he returned to me, the Eternal God. 

Thus, Paul had experienced what it was like to taste me without the weight of the body, for I allowed him to taste it through the feeling of union, though not through actual separation [of soul and body]. Therefore, once he had returned to himself, clothed in the garment of Christ crucified to perfection...

# Providence 84
L

...of the love that it had tasted and seen in me. Compared to what the saints taste when separated from the body, its own experience seemed imperfect. And so it seemed to the soul that the heaviness of the body rebelled against it; that is, it hindered the great perfection of the "face of desire" <note>An image Catherine uses to describe the soul's yearning for God, which is fully satisfied and "unveiled" only after death.</note> which the soul receives after death. Wherefore the memory seemed imperfect and weak to it, as indeed it is. Because of this weakness and imperfection, the soul was prevented from being able to retain, contain, receive, and taste me in truth with that perfection with which the saints receive me. 

And so it seemed to him that everything, while he remained in his body, was a perverse law <note>original: "lege puersa" (lex perversa). This refers to the "law in my members" from Romans 7:23, describing the internal struggle between physical existence and spiritual goals.</note> that fought and rebelled against the spirit—not a battle of sin, because as I have already told you, I gave him assurance when I said: "Paul, my grace is sufficient for you." <note>2 Corinthians 12:9. God explains that Paul's struggle was not about falling into sin, but about the physical limits of human life.</note> Instead, it was a battle that served to hinder the perfection of the spirit—that is, the seeing of me in my essence, which sight was hindered by the law and the heaviness of the body. 

And therefore he cried out: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from my body? For I have a perverse law bound in my members that fights against the spirit." <note>A paraphrase of Romans 7:23–24.</note> And so it is the truth: because the memory is besieged by corporal imperfection, the intellect is hindered and bound by this coarseness of the body from seeing me as I am in my essential being <term>essence: the core reality of God's nature, which Catherine argues cannot be fully perceived by a living person.</term>; and the will is bound, such that it cannot reach, with the weight of the body, to taste me, the Eternal God, without pain, in the way I have told you. 

So Paul said that in his life he had a perverse law bound in the body that fought against the spirit. And likewise these servants of mine—of whom I told you, who had reached the third and fourth state of perfect union <note>Catherine describes four stages of the soul's ascent to God; the third and fourth represent the highest levels of mystical intimacy.</note> that they find in me—they cry out with him, wishing to be unbound and separated from the body.
