# Of the Divine Chapter

...and with true patience they carried out that which they were bound and obligated to do: that is, to distribute temporal substance for their needs, to the poor, and to the Holy Church. And they did not make a hoard <note>original: "disposito," referring to an accumulation of wealth or a private deposit</note>, and after their death no great sum of money remained; indeed, there were some who left the church in debt for the sake of the poor. 

This was because of the abundance of their <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charita," meaning the selfless, divine love of God</note> and the hope they had placed in my <term>providence</term> <note>original: "puidẽtia," God's sustaining care for the world</note>. They were stripped of <term>servile fear</term> <note>original: "timor suile"; a base fear of punishment or loss, rather than a fear born of love</note>, and therefore they did not fear that anything would fail them, whether spiritual or temporal. 

This is a sign that the creature hopes in me and not in itself: namely, when it does not fear with servile fear. But those who hope in themselves are those who tremble and are afraid of their own shadow, doubting and fearing that heaven and earth might fail them. And with this fear and perverse hope, which they place in their own meager wisdom, they take on such miserable anxiety in acquiring and in preserving temporal things that it seems spiritual matters are cast behind their backs, and no one is found who cares for them. 

And these miserable, unfaithful, and proud ones do not consider that I am he who provides for every single thing that is necessary to the soul and to the body; although with that measure that you hope in me, with that same measure will my providence be measured out to you. But the miserable, presumptuous ones do not look to see that I am He who Is, and they are those who are not; and their very being they have received from my goodness, as well as every grace that is added to that being. 

Therefore, he who guards the house may be considered to labor in vain if it is not guarded by me <note>original: "nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem..." a reference to Psalm 127</note>. Every labor will be vain if they believe they guard it through their own toil or through their own anxiety, for I alone guard it. It is true that regarding the being and the graces I have placed upon your existence, I desire that in this time you exercise them in virtue, using the <term>free will</term> <note>original: "libero arbitrio"</note> that I have given you with the <term>light of reason</term> <note>original: "lũe de la rasone"</note>; for I created you without you, but I will not save you without [you] <note>This is a famous reference to St. Augustine’s teaching: "He who created you without you will not justify you without you."</note>.

<header>Providence CXIX</header>

...toward you. I loved you before you existed; and this my beloved ones saw and recognized; and therefore they loved me ineffably. And because of the love with which they loved, they hoped with such great generosity in me that they feared nothing. **Sylvester** <note>Saint Sylvester I (Pope from 314–335 AD), often associated with the conversion of Constantine</note> did not fear when he stood before the Emperor **Constantine** <note>original: "constãtio," likely referring to Constantine the Great</note>, disputing with those twelve Jews before the whole crowd; rather, with living faith, he believed that since I was for him, no one could be against him. 

And so all the others lost every fear, because they were not alone, but accompanied. Since they stood in the delight of <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charita," meaning the selfless, divine love that comes from God</note>, they stayed in me, and from me they acquired the light of wisdom of my only-begotten Son. From me they received power, being strong and mighty against the princes and tyrants of the world, and from me they had the fire of the **Holy Spirit**, participating in the mercy and the burning love of that same Holy Spirit. 

This love was and is a companion to whoever wishes to partake of it, joined with the light of faith, with fortitude, with living patience, and with long perseverance even until the end in death. Thus you see that they were not alone, but were accompanied; therefore they did not fear. Only he, then, who feels alone—that is, who hopes in himself, being deprived of the delight of charity—is afraid, and every little thing causes him fear. This is because he alone is deprived of me, who give the greatest security to the soul that possesses me through the affection of love. 

These glorious and beloved ones of mine truly prove this: that nothing could harm them, but they instead harmed <note>In this context, "harmed" refers to the saints' spiritual victory over their opponents' evil intents</note> the men and the demons, and many times these remained bound by the power and virtue that I had given the saints over them. This was because I respond to the love, to the **faith**, and to the **hope** that they had placed in me. 

Therefore, your tongue would not be sufficient to narrate the virtues of these people, nor the eye of your intellect to see the fruit that they receive in the lasting life—and which anyone will receive who follows in their footsteps. They are like precious stones, and so they stand in my sight, because I have received...

<meta>This page continues the discourse of God the Father to Saint Catherine of Siena regarding the rewards and qualities of holy ministers. It follows the previous page's discussion on how these "anointed ones" lived without fear because they were accompanied by Divine Charity.</meta>

-># Of the Divine Chapter<-

...their labors, and the light they sowed and placed with the fragrance of virtue in the <term>mystical body</term> <note>original: "corpo mistico"; the theological concept of the Church as a living organism with Christ as its head</note> of the holy church. Therefore, I have placed them in the everlasting life in the greatest dignity, and they receive <term>beatitude</term> <note>original: "beatitudine"; the supreme, eternal happiness of heaven</note> and glory in my vision. This is because they gave an example of an honest and holy life, and with light they administered the body and the blood of my only-begotten Son, along with all the other <term>sacraments</term> <note>original: "sacramenti"; the sacred rites of the Church</note>. Therefore, they are very uniquely loved by me, both for the dignity in which I have placed them—for they are my anointed ones and ministers—and because they did not bury the treasure I placed in their hands through negligence or ignorance. Instead, they recognized it as coming from me, exercising their duty with care, profound humility, and with true and real virtue.

And because I had placed them in such excellence for the salvation of souls, they never ceased, like good <term>shepherds</term> <note>original: "pastori"; a metaphor for clergy who care for the "flock" of the faithful</note>, to bring back the little sheep to the fold of the holy church. Driven by the affection of love and a hunger for souls, they would face death to draw them from the hands of the demon. They became "infirm"—that is, they made themselves weak with those who were weak—often so as not to overwhelm them in their despair, and to give them more freedom to reveal their own weaknesses. They would show this by saying: "I am weak together with you." They wept with those who wept, and rejoiced with those who rejoiced, and thus they knew how to sweetly give to each one their proper food. 

They preserved the good, rejoicing in their virtues, for they were not gnawed by envy; rather, they were expanded by the greatness of <term>charity</term> <note>original: "charita"; selfless, divine love</note> toward their neighbor and those under their care. ### On the defects and the evil life of wicked priests and ministers. Chapter 110.

Now pay close attention, my dearest daughter: so that my other servants may have more reason to offer themselves to me for them through humble and continual prayer. I want to show you and tell you of their wicked life: although whichever way you turn—whether toward the laity or religious clerics, the small or the great, the young or the old, or any other kind of people—you see nothing but offense; and all already cast me aside through <term>mortal sin</term> <note>a grave sin that "kills" the life of grace in the soul and separates it from God</note>, the stench of which does me no harm at all, but brings harm and injury to themselves.

I have told you until now of the excellence of my ministers and of the virtue of the good ones: both to provide refreshment to your soul and so that you may better recognize the misery of these wretched ones, and so you may see how they are worthy of greater rebuke and of suffering more intolerable pain. Just as my chosen and beloved ones, who have exercised in virtue the treasure given to them, are worthy of a greater reward and to be placed like pearls <note>original: "margarite"</note> in my sight—the opposite is true for these wretches, who receive cruel punishment.

Do you know, dearest daughter—and listen with sorrow and bitterness of heart—where they have made their beginning and their foundation? And to me they return shame and offense, whereby they attribute to themselves that which is not theirs and give away that which is not mine. 

To me should be given glory and praise for my name; and to themselves they should attribute the [shame] of their own <term>sensuality</term> <note>the lower, physical nature and its desires</note> with true self-knowledge, deeming themselves unworthy of such a great <term>mystery</term> <note>the sacred power of the priesthood, particularly the ability to consecrate the Eucharist</note> as they have received from me. O temples of the devil! I placed you so that you might be **earthly angels** in this life, and you are demons; and therefore you hold the office of the devil. The demons give darkness; and from that which they have for themselves, they minister; and with excruciating torments, they withdraw souls from **grace** with many troubles and temptations to lead them into the guilt of **mortal sin**, striving to do to them whatever they can. Although no sin can fall upon the soul unless it so wills, they do what they can. 

Thus these wretches, unworthy of being called ministers, are **incarnate demons**, because through their own fault they have aligned themselves with the will of the demons. Therefore, they perform their office, ministering Me—the true Light—with the darkness of mortal sin; and they minister the darkness of their disordered and wicked life to their subjects and to the other creatures who are under their authority. Wherefore, causing confusion, they minister pain into the minds of creatures who see them living so disorderedly; and they are also the cause of ministering pain and confusion of conscience in those who often withdraw from the state of grace and from the way of **truth**. 

By leading them into guilt, they make them go by the way of the lie; although he who follows them is not thereby excused from his own guilt, because no one can be forced into the guilt of mortal sin, neither by these visible demons nor by the invisible ones; because no one should look at their life, nor follow what they do.

**¶ How in the aforesaid wicked ministers injustice reigns, and especially by not correcting their subjects. Chapter cxxii.**

I told you that in my elect the **pearl of justice** shone. Now I have told you that these wretches carry manifest injustice in their breasts; this injustice proceeds from and is joined with their own **self-love**. Today it is not so; it is the opposite. Because the shepherds are wicked, the subjects are wicked. Therefore, this spouse is full of various thorns of many and varied sins. This is not to say that she herself can receive the stench of sin—that is, that the virtue of the **holy sacraments** could receive any offense. But those who feed at the breast of this spouse receive the stench in their souls <note>original: "ia" is a likely OCR error for "anima" (soul)</note> by forfeiting the dignity in which I placed them. It is not that the dignity itself diminishes, but it diminishes in regard to them. 

Thus, through their defects, they have debased the **Blood** <note>The Blood of Christ, which priests administer through the Eucharist.</note>. By this I mean that the secular people <note>The "seculars" or laity.</note> lose the due reverence they ought to show the ministers for the sake of the Blood. Although the laity should not lose this reverence—and if they do, their fault is no less despite the defects of the shepherds—nonetheless, these miserable ministers are mirrors of misery, though I placed them there to be **mirrors of virtue**.

# Providence 123

->R iv<-

<meta>Catchword: Dialogues of St. Catherine</meta>

The soul of these wretches, my dearest daughter, receives such a stench from their own **sensuality**, which they have made their mistress <note>original: "madona"; here used to mean they have enslaved themselves to their physical desires as if to a noble lady</note> with **self-love**. With their own suffering, and with holy and great desire—following my **Truth**—they should take up the food of your souls.

Yet they have taken the taverns for their table. There, swearing and forswearing with many miserable defects publicly, and like blinded men without the light of reason, they have become animals through their defects. They exist in acts, in deeds, and in words lasciviously. And not...

# Of the Divine Chapter

->R iv<-

<meta>Catchword: [Continues]</meta>

...they do: whatever the office might be; and if indeed they sometimes say it with their tongue, their heart is far from me. They remain **scoundrels** <note>original: "ribaldi"</note> and **swindlers**; and after they have gambled away their own souls and placed them in the hands of the demons, they gamble with the goods of the Church. Thus, the temporal substance—which they receive in virtue of the **Blood** <note>In Catherine’s theology, all Church property and authority are "the Blood of Christ" because they were earned by His sacrifice.</note>—they gamble and barter away. Wherefore the poor do not receive what is due to them, and the Church is left destitute, lacking those furnishings which are necessary to her. And because they have made themselves a temple of the **devil**, they no longer care for the temple of stone.

### How because of the aforementioned defects the subjects are not corrected, and regarding the defects of the religious; and how by not correcting the aforementioned evils many others follow. Chapter 125.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring interlaced geometric knotwork patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

In what way, then, can these men, full of so many defects, correct and do justice, and rebuke their own defects and those of their subjects? They cannot, because their own defects take away their boldness and the zeal for holy **justice**. And if they should ever try to do it, the wicked subjects say to them: <note>original: "medico: medica ināzi te medesmo: & poi medica me". I do not say that he should not rebuke evil—whether he himself is good or bad—when it exists in the subject; but I say he does wrong because he does not correct it through a holy and honest life. 

And he does much worse who, in whatever way the rebuke is given—whether by a good or bad pastor—does not receive it humbly, correcting his own wicked life; for such a person does more harm to himself than to others, and he is the one who will suffer the punishment for his own defects. # Concerning the Divine Chapter

...maintaining them in the eyes of the <term>seculars</term> <note>Laypeople; those living in the world rather than in a cloistered religious order.</note>: wishing to please them and to hammer at their own defects. So then you see: that they do not fulfill the first mode of obedience, which is to observe the <term>Order</term> <note>The specific Rule (such as Dominican or Franciscan) they swore to follow.</note>; I will speak to you of this obedience in another place. 

They also make a vow to observe voluntary poverty and to be <term>continent</term> <note>Practicing self-restraint, specifically regarding sexual chastity.</note>. As for how they observe this poverty: look at the possessions and the great wealth they keep for themselves individually, separated from the common <term>charity</term> <note>Here, the practice of communal ownership where resources are shared among all members.</note>—that is, sharing temporal and spiritual goods with their brothers, as the way of charity and their Order requires. 

And they wish to fatten nothing but themselves and their animals; so that while one stall feeds another animal, their poor brother dies of cold and hunger. And since he is well-clothed and has good food, he does not think of his brother, nor does he want to be found with him at the poor table of the <term>refectory</term> <note>The communal dining hall of a monastery or convent.</note>; his delight is in being able to stay where he can fill himself with meat and satisfy his gluttony. 

Therefore, for such a person, it is impossible to observe the third vow, that is, of <insert>continence</insert>, because a full belly does not make for a chaste mind; instead, it becomes lascivious with disordered heat, and so they go from bad to worse. And much evil also comes to them through possessing property: for if they had nothing to spend, they would not live so disordered a life; and they would not have those curious friendships, because having nothing to give, love is not maintained, nor is the <unclear>state of friendship</unclear>, which is founded on the love of the gift and on some delightful pleasure that one draws from the other, and not on perfect charity. 

O wretches, placed in such misery by their own defects, though by me they were placed in such dignity! They flee from the <term>choir</term> <note>The part of the church where the Divine Office is chanted by the community.</note> as if it were poison; and even if they stay there, they cry out with their voice, but <note>Original: "il core loro e dlonga da me." A reference to Isaiah 29:13 and Matthew 15:8: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me."</note> their heart is far from me. At the table of the altar, they have taken up the habit of going there without any devotion, just as if going to a physical table for a common meal. All these evils, and many others, of which I do not wish to tell you more...

Providence CXXVI
S
<meta>catchword: Dialogue of St. Catherine</meta>

...not to annoy your ears, they continue through the defect of the wicked pastors: who do not correct, nor punish the defects of their subjects; and they do not care, nor are they zealous, that the <term>Order</term><note>The specific rules and lifestyle of a religious community, such as the Dominicans.</note> be observed, because they themselves are not observers of the Order. They will certainly place the stones of great obedience upon the heads of those who wish to observe them, punishing them for the faults which they have not committed; all this they do because the pearl of <term>justice</term><note>In medieval theology, "justice" (iustitia) often refers to "righteousness" or the proper moral order of things.</note> does not shine in them. Rather, they act out of injustice, and therefore they unjustly give penance and hatred to the one who deserves grace and benevolence; and to those who are members of the devil, as they themselves are, they give love and delight and status, committing to them the offices of the Order. Thus they live as if blinded; as blinded men they grant offices and govern their subjects; and if they do not correct themselves from this blindness, they arrive at the darkness of eternal damnation. It is necessary for them to render an account to me, the Supreme Judge, for the souls of their subjects; but being truly bound <note>Meaning bound by their own sins and worldly attachments.</note>, they cannot render it, and therefore they receive from me justly that which they have deserved.

### How in the aforementioned ministers avarice reigns: lending at interest: and especially selling: and buying benefices: and prelacies: and of the evils that by this cupidity have come into the church. Chapter 127.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' containing a portrait of a tonsured cleric or saint in profile, holding a book.</image-desc> **P**ince I have told you of the first <note>The "first column" refers to Pride, discussed in the preceding section.</note>, let us come to the second: that is, to **avarice**. ### Providence CXXVII

S iiii

<meta>catchword: Dialog.de.S.catha</meta>

But, daughter, how much reason I have to lament over these ministers <note>original: "mi si", an abbreviation for *ministri*</note> of mine: and what largesse I have used toward them: and they use toward me such narrowness <note>The text contrasts God's "largesse" (generosity/abundance) with the "narrowness" (stinginess or spiritual poverty) of the clergy.</note>: so that, as I told you: some will act like those who lend at usury—not that they keep a shop like public usurers: but with many subtle ways they will sell time to their neighbor for their own greed: which thing is not lawful by any means in the world. Wherefore, if a gift of some small thing were given to him: and he with his intention received it as a payment above the service he performed for that person by lending his own goods: this is usury: as is every other thing he might receive for that time mentioned. I have placed the minister so that he may watch over the seculars <note>The "seculars" refers to the laity, or people living in the world rather than in religious orders.</note>: and he is that same [type of person]: and even more so when someone goes to him for counsel on this matter: because he shares that same defect: since he has lost the light of reason: the counsel that he gives is dark, clouded by that passion that is within his soul. This, therefore: and many other defects arise from his narrow, greedy, and avaricious heart. Whence he can say that word which my Truth <note>A title Catherine uses for Jesus Christ.</note> spoke when he entered the temple: where he found those who were selling and buying: whom he drove out with a scourge of cords, saying: "Of the house of my Father, which is a house of prayer, you have made a den of thieves" <note>original: "spelūca de latrōi", quoting Matthew 21:13.</note>. You see well, my sweetest daughter, that it is so within my Church: that instead of a place of prayer, it is made a den of thieves: because they sell and buy, and have made merchandise of the grace of the Holy Spirit. Wherefore you see that those who desire prelacies <note>High-ranking offices in the Church, such as bishoprics.</note> and the benefits of the Holy Church buy them with many presents: offering goods and money to those who surround them. And the miserable ones do not consider whether they are good rather than evil, but to please them: and for love of the gift they have received, they will strive to put this rotten plant in the garden of the Holy Church.

### Providence CXXVII

-><meta>catchword: de:</meta><-

...since he has lost the light of reason and has clouded the eye of his intellect. In that light of reason—together with the supernatural light—the **Holy Scripture** was explained and understood, just as I told you more clearly in another place. So then, you see that **knowledge** <term>knowledge: the original Italian "scientia" refers to formal, scholarly, or theological learning</term> is good in itself, but not in the one who does not use it as it ought to be used; for such a person, it will even be a punishing fire if they do not correct their life. And therefore, they <note>meaning the people or the faithful</note> ought to look more toward a holy and good life than toward a learned man who leads an evil life.

But they do the opposite: for those who are good and virtuous but simple in their **knowledge** are considered fools and are despised by them; and they avoid those poor ones because they have nothing to give. Thus, you see that in my house—which ought to be a house of prayer—where the **pearl of justice** <note>a favorite metaphor of Catherine's, representing the beauty and integrity of divine law</note> and the light of **knowledge** ought to shine alongside an honest and holy life, and where the scent of truth ought to be, there instead falsehood abounds. They ought to possess voluntary poverty and, with true care, preserve **souls** <note>original: "laie," a contraction for "l'anime"</note> and draw them from the hands of the devil; but instead, they crave riches. They have taken such great care for temporal things that they have completely abandoned the care of spiritual things. They attend to nothing other than gambling, laughter, and the increasing and multiplying of their temporal possessions.

The wretches do not realize that this is the very way to lose them. For if they abounded in virtue and took care of spiritual things as they ought, they would also abound in temporal ones; and my **bride** <note>The Church</note> would not have suffered the many rebellions she has had. They ought to **let the dead bury the dead** <note>A reference to Matthew 8:22, implying that those spiritually dead should focus on worldly, passing matters, while the living follow Christ</note> and they should follow the doctrine of my Truth and fulfill my will in them—that is, to do that for which I have placed them there. But they do exactly the opposite: for they set themselves to burying dead and transitory things with disordered affection and worry, and they take the office from the **hands** <note>original: "mãe," a contraction for "mani"</note>...

-># Providence CXXVIII<-

<meta>Catchword: corre</meta>

Now it remains to speak of the third column: that is, of **pride**. And although I have placed it last for you, it is actually the first, for all vices are seasoned by pride, just as the virtues are seasoned and receive life from **charity**. Pride is born from and nourished by **sensory self-love** <term>sensory self-love: a disordered obsession with one's own physical desires and worldly ego, rather than spiritual growth</term>, which I told you was the foundation of these three columns and of every evil that creatures commit. For whoever loves themselves with a disordered love is deprived of my love; because they do not love me, they offend me, failing to observe the commandment of the law: which is to love me above all things, and one's neighbor as oneself. This is the reason: by loving themselves with sensory love, they do not keep the law nor do they love, because sensory love and the love of the world have no conformity <note>original: "conformita," meaning alignment or harmony of nature</note> with me. Therefore, having no conformity together, it must be that whoever loves the world with sensory love and serves it through their senses must hate me; and whoever loves me in truth, hates the world. And so my Truth <note>Referring to Jesus Christ, "the Way, the Truth, and the Life"</note> said: "no one can serve two opposing masters, for if he serves one, he will despise the other" <note>original Latin: "nemo potest duobus dominis servire," from Matthew 6:24</note>. So you see: self-love deprives the soul of my charity and clothes it in the vice of pride, from which every defect is born through the principle of self-love. 

Therefore, I grieve over every creature endowed with reason who is in this defect, and I lament over them; but I grieve singularly over **my anointed ones** <note>original: "uncti mei," referring to priests and clergy who are anointed with oil at their ordination</note>. They ought to be humble, both because every man should possess the virtue of **humility**—which nourishes charity—and because they are made ministers of the humble and **immaculate Lamb**, my only-begotten Son. And yet they—and all human generation—are not ashamed to be prideful, even seeing me, God, humbled to the level of man by giving you the **Word** <note>original: "ubo/verbo," referring to Christ as the Logos</note> of my Son in your own flesh. And they see this Word, through the **obedience** I placed upon him, running—

# Regarding the Divine Chapter

<meta>catchword: inestimable</meta>

...the fragility of the world: in its little stability. If they recognized it, they would not make themselves gods. Who has taken away their discernment? Pride. To remove every curb of fear regarding their evil-doing, having risen in the morning from impurity <note>original: "mūditia," likely referring to sexual impurity or lack of ritual washing</note> and in the evening from disordered eating and drinking, they find it necessary to satisfy the people. 

And as they consider their iniquity, they see that they neither ought to nor can celebrate with a good **conscience** <note>original: "conscientia"</note>. See then, **dearest daughter** <note>God is addressing St. Catherine of Siena</note>, how blind such a man is: he does not run to **contrition of heart** <note>original: "ɔtritiōe del core," the sincere sorrow for sin required for forgiveness</note> or to the displeasure of his failing with the intent to correct himself. Instead, he takes this remedy: he will not consecrate. And by this he does not see that the error and the failing afterward is greater than the one before. For he makes the people idolaters, making them adore that **host** <note>the bread used in the Eucharist</note> which is not consecrated as if it were the body and the blood of my only-begotten Son—wholly God and wholly man—as He is when He is consecrated; but at that time, it is only bread because it is not consecrated. 

Now see how great is this abomination and how great is my patience, that I tolerate them. But if they do not amend themselves, every **grace** <note>original: "gratia"</note> will turn to judgment against them. But what should the people do, so that they do not fall into that impropriety? They should adore with a condition, and say thus: "If this minister has said that which he ought to say, I truly believe that you are Christ, the Son of the living God, given to me as food from the fire of [charity]..."

### Regarding many other defects: which are committed through pride: and through self-love. Chapter 129.

<meta>This page continues the discourse of God the Father to St. Catherine of Siena. In the previous section, the Father spoke of the "blindness" of priests who fail to consecrate the Eucharist out of malice. Here, the focus shifts to how the corruption of the Church starts with the leaders (pastors) and trickles down to the people (subjects), and how ignorance leads to the appointment of unfit priests.</meta>

<header>Of the Divine Chapter <note>original: "De la diuina Capitolo"</note></header>
<meta>catchword: Now how</meta>

...[reforming it with the abun]dance of good and holy pastors. And by reforming it with good pastors, the subjects will necessarily be corrected; for almost all the evils committed by the subjects are the fault of the wicked **pastors** <note>original: "pastori"; here referring to bishops and clergy who shepherd the faithful</note>. Because if they corrected themselves, and the **pearl of justice** <note>original: "margarita de la iustitia"; a common metaphor for the purity and integrity of the judicial and moral office</note> shone in them with an honest and holy life, the subjects would not act this way. And do you know what comes of these perverse ways? One follows in the footsteps of the other; thus the subjects are not obedient, because when the **prelate** <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop</note> was once a subject himself, he was not obedient to his own superior. Therefore, he receives from his own subjects exactly what he gave of himself; because he was a bad subject, he is now a bad pastor. The cause of all this and every other defect is pride, which is founded upon self-love. 

Wherefore, he was ignorant and proud as a subject, and he is much more ignorant and proud now that he is a prelate. And so great is his ignorance that, like a blind man, he will grant the office of the priesthood to an **ignorant man** <note>original: "hõ idiota"; in this period, "idiota" referred to someone unlettered or lacking formal theological training</note> who can barely even read, and does not know his office. And often through his ignorance, not knowing how to say the sacramental words, he will not **consecrate** <note>The act of turning the bread and wine into the Body and Blood of Christ</note>. Thus, because of this ignorance, they commit the same fault of failing to consecrate as those others who do not do it out of malice—failing to consecrate, but making a show of doing so. 

Where they ought to choose experienced men, grounded in **virtue** <note>original: "uirtu"</note>, who know and understand what they say, they do the exact opposite. For they do not look to see if they are wise, and they do not look for maturity <note>original: "tẽpo"; literally "time," implying age and experience</note>, but only for their own pleasure. It seems they choose children <note>original: "fãciuli"</note> rather than mature men. And they do not look to see if they are of honest and holy life, nor whether they recognize the dignity to which they are called, nor the great **mystery** <note>original: "myſterio"; referring to the Sacrament of the Eucharist</note> that they must perform; rather, they look only to increase the number of people, and not to increase in virtue. They are blind, and they are gatherers of the blind. They do not see that I will demand an account from them for this and for all other things at the final extremity of death. And after they have made such "darkened" priests—as has been said—they give them the care of souls, even though they see that these men do not even know how to take care of themselves.

# Providence CXXIX

<meta>catchword: Dialogue of St. Catherine T</meta>

Now how could these men, who do not recognize their own defect, correct it or recognize it in others? They cannot act against themselves. Wherefore the **little sheep** <note>The faithful laity, often described as a flock in need of protection</note>, who have no shepherd to care for them or who knows how to guide them, easily wander off; and many times they are devoured and scattered by the wolves. And because the shepherd is wicked, he does not care to keep the dog that would keep watch upon seeing the wolf approach; instead, he keeps a dog just like himself. 

Now, in this way, these ministers and pastors have no solicitude; they have neither the **dog of conscience** <note>A signature metaphor for Catherine: conscience is a watchdog that should "bark" to warn the soul of approaching sin</note> nor the staff of justice, nor the rod for correction. Their conscience does not reprimand them, nor do they reprimand the little sheep when they see them wandering. They do not walk in the way of truth—that is, by not observing my commandments—wherefore the **hellish wolf** <note>Satan or the influence of mortal sin</note> comes and devours them. 

But if they had this dog, and if they turned their own defects upon themselves with the rod of holy justice as has been said, they would save their sheep. But because he is a shepherd without a rod and without the dog of conscience, his sheep perish, and he does not care; for the dog of his conscience is weakened, and therefore it does not bark, because he has not given it food. 

The food that must be given to this dog is the food of the **Lamb** <note>Jesus Christ</note>, my Son, <unclear>full of mercy</unclear> <note>original: "poch piẽa"; likely a contraction for "pietà" (mercy) or "piena" (full)</note>, which is the memory of the **Blood** <note>Refers to the Blood of Christ shed in the Passion, a central theme in Catherine's theology as the source of salvation and spiritual strength</note>. Just as a vessel of the soul, the conscience is nourished by it; that is, through the memory of the Blood, the soul is moved to the hatred of vice and the love of virtue. This hatred and love purify the soul from the stain of mortal sin and give such vigor to the conscience that it guards the soul. 

Thus, as soon as any enemy of the soul—that is, sin—wishes to enter, not only into the heart's affection but even into the thought, immediately the conscience, like a dog, barks with a <unclear>stinging</unclear> prick <note>original: "stimulo punto"</note> that awakens reason. And then such a person does not commit injustice, because he who has conscience has justice; and therefore such wicked men, unworthy of being called...

# Of the Divine Chapter

<meta>catchword: for</meta>

...called not so much ministers, but irrational creatures: for they have made themselves into animals through their defects. They have no dog <note>The "dog of conscience," a recurring metaphor in Catherine’s writing for the internal voice that should "bark" a warning against approaching sin.</note>, because it could be said that they lack its strength; and not having the dog of **conscience**, they have no rod of holy **justice**. Their own defects have made them so timid that even a shadow causes them fright—not a holy fear, but a **servile fear** <note>original: "tiore fuile." In medieval theology, "servile fear" is the dread of punishment, whereas "filial fear" is the dread of offending God out of love.</note>. They ought to offer themselves to death to pull **souls** out of the hands of the demon, yet they instead place them into those hands by failing to give them the doctrine of a good and holy life, and by being unwilling to endure a single injurious word for their salvation.

Wherefore, many times the **soul** of the subject will be entangled in the gravest **mortal sins**, and will have to make restitution to others; but because of the disordered love these ministers have for their own family <note>Nepotism and the desire to protect the financial standing of their relatives often prevented priests from demanding that wealthy sinners pay back what they had stolen or gained through usury.</note>, so as not to strip them of wealth, they do not make the subject render what is due. But the miserable priest goes to do what he must do, and if an injurious word is said to him, or he receives a bad look, he will no longer trouble himself out of fear. And sometimes a gift will be made to him; thus, between the bribe and his servile fear, he lets that soul remain in the hands of the demons. He even gives them the **sacrament** of the body of Christ <note>original: "corpo de xpō" (Corpus Christi). The text uses the Greek abbreviation 'xp' for Christ.</note>, my only-begotten Son, even though he sees and knows that this soul is entangled in the darkness of mortal sin.

[They are] called not so much ministers, but irrational creatures, having become beasts through their defects. They have no dog <note>original: "cane." # Concerning the Divine Chapter
<meta>catchword: lives</meta>

As has been said: it is a very weak thing for a man to find himself unarmed in the time of battle among many enemies.

## Concerning many other defects which the aforementioned wicked ones commit. Chapter CXXX

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>**C**haringest daughter, these wretched ones of whom I have told you have no consideration; for if they had it, they would not fall into so many defects—neither they nor others. Instead, they would act like the others who lived virtuously, who chose death before they would ever choose to offend Me, or to stain the face of their **soul** <term>anima: the spiritual essence of a person</term> and diminish the dignity in which I had placed them. Rather, the dignity and the beauty of their souls increased. Not that the dignity of the **priesthood** <term>sacerdotio: the holy office and sacramental power of a priest</term> can purely increase through **virtue** <term>uirtu: moral excellence and spiritual strength</term>, nor diminish through defect, as I have told you <note>Catherine refers to the theological doctrine that the validity of a priest's sacraments does not depend on his personal holiness, but on the office itself</note>; but virtues are an adornment and a dignity that they give to the soul beyond the pure beauty that the soul had from its beginning, when I created it in my image and likeness.

These [virtuous ones] recognized the truth of my goodness, beauty, and their own dignity, because pride and self-love had not clouded them, nor taken away the light of reason—for they were not deprived of it—and they loved me and the salvation of souls. But these poor wretches mentioned above, because they are entirely deprived of light, do not care about going from vice to vice until they reach the pit; and of the temple of their souls and of the **Holy Church** <term>chiesa: the community of believers and the institution of the faith</term>—which is a garden—they make a den for beasts. 

O dearest daughter, you know how abominable it is to me that their houses, which ought to be a shelter for my servants and for the poor, and where they ought to hold the **Breviary** <term>breuiario: the liturgical book containing the daily public prayers of the Church</term> as their spouse and the books of **Holy Scripture** <term>sancta scriptura: the Bible</term> as their children—delighting in them to give teaching to their neighbor for leading a holy life—instead, they are shelters for filth and for wicked people. His spouse is no longer the Breviary; rather, he treats the said spouse, the Breviary, as if she were an adulteress <note>original: "tracta la dicta sposa dl breuiario come adultera," implying he has abandoned his commitment to prayer for worldly or carnal distractions</note>, but [his true companion] is a miserable she-devil who lives filthily.

# Providence CXXX
T iiii
<meta>catchword: Dialogue of Saint Catherine</meta>

...lives with him. And his children <note>The original OCR reads "libri" (books), but the context and the word "figlioli" (little children) confirm this is a typo for "liberi" (children).</note> are his only company; children whom he has fathered in such filth, and in this misery he delights without any shame. On the feast days and solemn days, in which he ought to give glory and praise to My name through the **divine office** <term>diuīo officio: the daily cycle of prayers and psalms that clergy are required to recite</term> and offer Me the incense of humble and devout **prayer** <term>oratiōe: the lifting of the mind and heart to God</term>, he instead spends his time in games and amusement with his she-demons <note>The original "demonie" likely refers to the priest's concubines or mistresses, viewed by the author as agents of temptation</note>. He carouses with worldlings, hunting and fowling as if he were a layman or a lord of the court. 

O wretched man, what have you become? You ought to hunt and fowl for souls for the glory and praise of My name, remaining in the garden of the **Holy Church** <term>ſctā chieſia: the spiritual and institutional body of the faithful</term>, and yet you wander through the woods. Because you have made yourself a beast, you keep the animals of many **mortal sins** <term>pctī mortali: grave sins that lead to the death of the soul's relationship with God</term> within your soul; and therefore you have become a hunter and a fowler of beasts. Because the garden of your soul has grown wild and is full of thorns, you have taken delight in wandering through desolate places, searching for wild animals. 

Be ashamed, man, and look upon your defects! For you have cause to be ashamed whichever way you turn; but you do not feel shame, because you have lost the holy and true fear of Me. Like a shameless prostitute, you boast of maintaining a great status in the world, and of having a fine household and a company of many children. And if you do not have them, you seek to have them so that they may remain heirs to your property. # Providence 131

...his enemies in life have been defeated by them. Therefore, the world cannot accuse him, because he recognized its deceits and then renounced the world and all its delights. His fragile **sensuality** <term>sensualita: the physical appetites and inclinations toward worldly things</term> and his body do not accuse him, because he keeps them as a servant held by the bridle of **reason** <term>rasone: the faculty of logical and moral discernment</term>, wearing down the flesh through **penitence** <term>penitentia: acts of self-denial or atonement</term>, through **vigils** <term>vigilia: staying awake for prayer or meditation during the night</term>, and through humble and constant **prayer** <term>orone: (orazione) communication with the Divine</term>. 

The sensitive will looks upon itself with hatred and displeasure for **vice** <term>vitio: a habit or tendency toward sin</term> and with love for **virtue** <term>virtu: moral excellence and alignment with God’s will</term>. All the tenderness for its own body is lost—that love which naturally exists between the **soul** <term>lania: (l'anima) the spiritual essence of a person</term> and the body, which naturally makes death seem bitter, and which causes man to naturally fear death. 

But because virtue in a perfect just man surpasses nature—that is, he overcomes the fear that is natural to him and moves beyond it with holy hatred <note>In this mystical context, "holy hatred" refers to a rejection of the selfish ego and sinful impulses rather than malice toward people.</note> and the desire to return to his final end—his natural tenderness cannot wage war against him. His **conscience** <term>conscientia: the internal sense of right and wrong</term> remains quiet, because during his life it kept good watch, barking whenever enemies approached to seize the city of the soul. 

Wherefore, just like a dog at the gate who barks when he sees enemies and by barking awakens the guards, so too the dog of conscience awakens the guard of reason. Then reason, together with **free will** <term>libero arbitrio: the power of the human will to choose between good and evil</term>, recognized through the light of the **intellect** <term>intellecto: the capacity for spiritual understanding and reasoning</term> who was a friend and who was an enemy. 

To the friend—that is, to virtue and the holy thoughts of the heart—they gave **delight** <term>dilectione: a deep, spiritual love or choice</term> and an **affection** <term>affecto: the orientation of one’s feelings or will</term> of love, practicing them with great diligence. To the enemy—that is, to vice and perverse thoughts—they gave hatred and displeasure. And with the knife of hatred and love, by the light of reason and with the hand of free will, they struck down their enemies. Thus, at the moment of death, the conscience does not gnaw at him, because it kept good watch; instead, it remains at peace. 

It is true that even the just soul, out of **humility** <term>humilita: the virtue of recognizing one's true state before God</term> and because at the time of death it better recognizes the treasure of time and the precious stones of the virtues, reproaches itself, feeling it has made too little use of its time;

...but this is not a painful suffering; rather, it is a suffering that nourishes <note>original: "pena che ingrassa." The **demons** <term>demonii: fallen angels or evil spirits who attempt to tempt or terrify the soul at the moment of death</term>, because they cannot reproach the soul for sin—since during its life it conquered their malice with wisdom—still come, wanting to see if they might acquire anything. But because the **soul** <term>lania: (l'anima) the spiritual essence of the person</term> has no stain of sin, their appearance does not cause it that dread, nor does it instill fear in it as it does in another who has lived viciously in the world. When the demons see that the soul has entered into the Blood with most burning **charity** <term>charita: divine love, the highest of the theological virtues</term>, they cannot endure it; they stay at a distance, casting their arrows. As I told you in another place, with the **eye of the intellect** <term>lochio de lintellecto: the faculty of spiritual understanding</term>—which has the pupil of most holy **faith** <term>fede: the light that allows the soul to see spiritual truths</term>—it sees its infinite and eternal Good, which it expects to receive through grace, not by right, through the virtue of **Christ** <gloss>Christ</gloss> my Son. 

Thus, it stretches out the arms of hope and, with the hands of love, it embraces Him, entering into possession [of God] before it has even departed [the body], as I have said to you in another place. Suddenly, then, drowned in the Blood, passing through the narrow gate of the **Word** <term>uerbo: the Logos, or Christ, described as a "bridge" or "gate" between humanity and God</term>, it arrives in Me, the **peaceful sea** <term>mare pacifico: a metaphor for the infinite, calm essence of God the Father</term>; for we are united together, I the Sea with the Gate, because I and my Truth, my only-begotten Son, are one and the same thing. 

How much joy the soul receives, seeing itself arrive so sweetly at this crossing! For it tastes the good...

# Providence CXXXII

...in the hope of mercy: so that at the end of death they might have something to cling to, and not entirely fail in the face of the reproach <note>The internal accusation or "worm" of conscience that wakes up at the moment of death.</note>, and not arrive at **despair**. But the sin of <term>despair</term> <note>original: "desperatione"—in medieval theology, despair is the refusal to believe God can or will forgive, making it the ultimate barrier to salvation.</note> does not move them because of human frailty, for they find no delight in it, but only intolerable pain.

And in despair, the soul despises my mercy, judging his sin to be greater than my mercy and goodness. Once he has fallen into this sin, he does not repent, nor does he have true sorrow for the offense against me; he should grieve for the loss of such a sweet good [God], but he does not grieve for the offense he has committed against me, and thus he receives eternal damnation.

So you see that this sin alone leads him to hell; and in hell he is tortured by this, and by all the other faults he has committed. But if he had grieved and repented of the offense he had done to me, and had hoped in my mercy, he would have found mercy; because, beyond any comparison—as I told you—my mercy is greater than all the sins that any creature could possibly commit. # On the Divine Chapter
<meta>catchword: darkness</meta>

...this sweet deception: that is, making them hope broadly in my mercy. For when they are nourished within this hope, upon arriving at death they are not so inclined to abandon it because of the harsh reproaches <note>The "reproaches" refer to the sudden awakening of a guilty conscience at the moment of death.</note> they hear, as they would be had they not been nourished within it. All this is given to them by the fire and the abyss of my inextinguishable charity; but because they have used it with the darkness of **self-love**, from which every defect proceeds, they have not known it in truth. Therefore, it is counted as great presumption, just as much as the sweetness of mercy was in their affection.

And this is another reproach that conscience gives them in the presence of the demon: reproaching them for the time and for the abundance of mercy in which they hoped. They should have expanded in charity and in the love of virtue, and spent the time that I gave them out of love [wisely]; yet they, with that time and that broad hope of mercy, offended me miserably. O blind above the blind! You buried the pearl and the <term>talent</term> <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), where a servant is punished for burying the money entrusted to him rather than investing it for his master.</note> that I placed in your hands, so that you might gain with it; and you, in your presumption, did not want to do my will, but you buried it under the earth of the disordered self-love of yourself, which now renders to you the fruit of death.

O miserable one, how great is the pain which you now receive at the very end; and your miseries are not taken from you: because the **worm of conscience** <note>A common medieval metaphor for the persistent, gnawing guilt that torments the soul.</note> now no longer sleeps, but gnaws. The demons cry out to you and render to you the "reward" they are accustomed to rendering to their own: that is, offense and reproach. So that at the point of death you do not escape their hands, they want you to arrive at **despair**. Therefore, because you did not do so, you are held accountable; and to your greater pain and confusion, you have before your conscience and the light of your intellect that which you have done, which you should not have done, and that which you should have done, which you have not done.

# On the Divine Chapter
-> v <-
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

their conscience places before them the faults they have committed and the virtues they ought to have practiced. These virtues are presented for their greater shame; because when vice is placed beside virtue, the soul recognizes its failings more clearly through the light of that virtue, and the more it recognizes them, the greater the shame it feels. And so, through its own defect, it recognizes better the perfection of virtue, which causes greater sorrow; for the soul sees that its life has been lived outside of all virtue. 

I want you to know that in this recognition of virtue and vice, the soul sees all too well the good that follows from virtue for the virtuous man, and the punishment that follows for one who has remained in the darkness of <term>mortal sin</term> <note>A grave sin that, according to Catholic doctrine, separates the soul from God's grace.</note>. I grant this knowledge so that the soul may come to a perfect knowledge of itself and feel shame for its faults, yet with hope—so that with this shame and knowledge it may atone for its defects and appease my wrath by humbly asking for <term>mercy</term> <note>In this context, mercy is the compassionate forgiveness offered by God to a repentant sinner.</note>. 

The virtuous person, by contrast, grows in joy and in the knowledge of my <term>charity</term> <note>The theological term "charity" (caritas) refers to the highest form of love: the reciprocal love between God and humanity.</note>. Because they have received the grace to follow the virtues and walk according to the doctrine of my Truth <note>The "doctrine of my Truth" refers to the life and teachings of Jesus Christ.</note>, they recognize that this grace comes from me and not from themselves. Because of this, they exult in me with this true light and knowledge, and they taste and receive their sweet end in the manner I described to you in another place. 

So, then, the one exults in joy—that is, the just soul who has lived with most ardent charity—while the dark and wicked soul is confounded in pain. To the just, the darkness and the vision of the <term>demons</term> <note>In Catherine’s visions, demons often appear at the deathbed to tempt or terrify the soul, but they have no power over the righteous.</note> do not cause any harm, nor do they fear them; for sin is the only thing they fear and the only thing that can cause harm. But those who have led their lives lasciviously and with many miseries receive harm and fear at the sight of the demons. This is not the harm of despair—if they are willing to turn to me—but the pain of reproach, the stinging reminder of their conscience, and the dread and fear at their horrible sight. See then, how great the difference is, my dearest daughter...

### Of the Divine Chapter

...loving charity; which you gave to us through the door of the Word <note>original: "uerbo," referring to Christ as the Logos or Word of God</note>: I know already that you open before we even knock: few, with the affection and the love that you have given to your servants, knock and call to you, seeking your honor and the salvation of souls. # On the Divine Chapter
<meta>catchword: ci [certainly]</meta>

...my only-begotten son: with great providence: for your necessity. This my providence performed with a finite operation [the suffering of the flesh]: since finite was the pain of the cross: yet in the Word you have received infinite fruit in virtue of the divinity: as was said.

# Providence CXXXV

...heaven was made. Wherefore he had lost all hope; which hope, if he could have grasped it, would have been a refreshment to him. ### How God provides through hope in his creatures; the more perfectly one hopes, the more one tastes his providence. Chapter 136

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' with interlaced knotwork patterns.</image-desc> I have also given him the refreshment of **hope** <term>Hope (spanza): In this context, the theological virtue of looking forward with confidence to God's help and the attainment of eternal life.</term>; if with the light of most holy faith he regards the price of the blood, which is paid for him, it gives him firm hope and certainty of his salvation. You know that hope cannot be placed in two contrary things; this is what the Truth wanted to say to you...

# Providence CXXXVI

...truth in the **holy Gospel** <note>original: "facto euangelio." Referring to Matthew 6:24: "No one can serve two masters."</note> when it said: no one can serve two masters; if he serves one, he holds the other in contempt. Serving is not without **hope** <term>Hope (speranza): Not merely a wish, but a confident expectation of a future good based on trust in the master.</term>; for he who serves, serves with hope—the hope he has in the reward and the utility he expects to draw from it. It is with hope that he intends to please his master, for he would not serve his master’s enemy at all, as such service could not be performed without some hope of gain. Thus, by fearing and hoping, he would see himself deprived of what he expected from his master. 

Now think then, **dearest daughter** <note>God the Father is addressing Saint Catherine of Siena directly.</note>, of what happens to the soul. It must necessarily serve and hope either in the world or in itself. It serves the world through **sensual service** <term>Sensual service (seruitio sensuale): Serving the "sensuality" or lower nature; acting based on physical desires and ego rather than the spirit.</term> outside of me, in as much as it serves and loves its own sensuality. From this love and service, it hopes to have delight, pleasure, and sensory utility. But because its hope is placed in things that are finite, vain, and transitory, its hope eventually fails it, and it does not reach the outcome it desired. 

Therefore, while the soul hopes in itself and in the world, it does not hope in me. For the world—that is, the worldly desires of man—is hateful to me. Such desires were held in such abomination by me that I gave my **only-begotten Son** <note>original: "unigenito mio figliolo."</note> to the shameful death of the cross; therefore, the world has no conformity with me, nor I with it. 

But the soul that perfectly hopes in me and serves me with all its heart and all its affection, must immediately and by necessity—for the reason stated—**despair of itself** <note>To "despair of oneself" in mystical theology means to lose all confidence in one's own power or worldly merit in order to rely entirely on God.</note> and of the world, and of the hope placed in its own fragility. This true and perfect hope is either lesser or more perfect according to the perfection of the **love** <note>original: "amore."</note> that the soul has for me; and whether perfect or imperfect, it thus tastes my **providence** <note>original: "puidētia."</note>. 

But those who serve and hope only to please me taste and receive it more perfectly than those who serve with hope of the fruit or delight they might find in me. These first ones are those of whom I spoke to you in the final state of the soul...

And how they are so very mad, oh **dearest daughter**! How can they think that I, the supreme and eternal Goodness, could want anything other than their good? Even in the small things, all of which I permit for their **salvation**, they find that I want nothing other than their satisfaction. Even in the great things, which with all their blindness they cannot fail to see—at least with a little **natural light** <note>The "natural light" refers to basic human reason, which even without divine revelation should be able to recognize a Creator's care.</note>—they should see my goodness and the benefit of my providence. This they find, and they cannot deny it, in the first **re-creation** that man had in the **Blood**, re-creating him in grace, as I have told you. This is a thing so clear and so manifest.

# Of the Divine [Providence] Chapter
<meta>catchword: salvation</meta>

...will provide at the last. This is generally given to every **creature** <term>Creature: In Catherine’s theology, this refers to any created being, but specifically human beings who possess "the light of reason."</term> who has reason within them: so that they would want to reap the fruit of this providence. In particular, I say to you: that I give them everything through my providence: both life and death in whatever manner it may be. Whether it be hunger, thirst, the loss of worldly status, nakedness, cold, injuries, scorns, or insults: I permit all these things to be done or said by men. I do not create the malice of the evil will of the one who commits these acts and the injury; nor for this purpose does he have time and his being—which he received from me—which being I gave to him, not so that he should offend me or his neighbor, but so that he might serve me and his neighbor with the delight of **charity** <note>original: "charita." This refers to *agape*, or selfless, divine love.</note>. 

But I permit that act, either to prove the virtue of **patience** <note>original: "patientia"</note> in the soul of the one who receives the injury, or to make them recognize their own state. Sometimes I will allow the whole world to be against the just man: and in the end, he will meet such a death as will cause great wonder to the men of the world. Wherefore it seems to them an unjust thing to see a just man perish, sometimes in water, sometimes in fire, sometimes strangled by an animal, and sometimes by the falling of a house upon him, in which he will lose his bodily life. 

Oh, how strange these things will seem to that eye which does not have within it the light of most holy **faith** <note>original: "fctissma fede"</note>! But not so for the faithful soul, because she has proved and tasted through the affection of love my providence in the great things mentioned above. And thus she sees and holds that with **providence** <note>original: "prouidentia"</note> I do whatever I do, and only to procure the **salvation** <note>original: "salute"</note> of man; and therefore she holds everything in reverence. She is not scandalized in herself, nor in my works, nor in her neighbor; but passes through everything with true patience. My providence is not taken away from any creature: because all things were created with it. Sometimes it will seem to man that either a great storm or a **lightning bolt** <note>original: "faeta" (saetta), meaning a lightning bolt or arrow.</note> that I send upon the body of the creature is an act of cruelty, almost judging that I have not provided for their

...salvation of that person: and I have done it to save him from eternal death; and he believes the opposite. And thus the men of the world in every thing want to defame my works and understand them according to their low understanding.

# How that which God permits is solely for our good and salvation: and how they are blind who judge the contrary. Chapter 138.

**D** <note>Initial D: The woodcut depicts Saint Catherine of Siena, the author of this text, who was a 14th-century mystic and diplomat known for her influential "Dialogue" with God.</note>earest daughter, I want you to see with how much **patience** <note>original: "patientia"</note> I must bear with my **creatures** <term>Creatures: Throughout this text, this refers to human beings as the created works of God.</term> whom I have created, as I told you, in my image and likeness, with such sweetness of love. And therefore open the eye of your **intellect** <note>original: "lochio de lintellecto." In Catherine's theology, this is the faculty of the soul that perceives spiritual truth through the light of faith.</note> and look into me, as I set before you a particular case that occurred, which if you remember well, you prayed to me that I might provide for; and I provided, as you know, and without danger of death, he regained his status. And as it is in this particular case, so it is generally in everything.

I have told you of this particular case; now I return to the general: you could never see how great is the ignorance of man. He is without any sense or knowledge, having taken it from himself by hoping in himself and by trusting in his own wisdom <term>sape (sapere): here referring to human ingenuity or intellect as opposed to divine wisdom</term>. O foolish man: do you not see that you do not have your wisdom from yourself, but my goodness, which provides for your need, has given it to you? Who shows this to you? It is shown to you by that which you experience in yourself: because at certain times you want to do a thing that you cannot do, nor will you know how to do. Sometimes you will have the knowledge but not the power, and sometimes the power but not the knowledge; sometimes you will not have the time; and if you have the time, you will lack the will. All this is given by me through **providence** for your salvation, so that you may know you are not of yourself, and have reason to humble yourself and not to be proud; wherefore in all things you find change, because they are not within your own liberty. Only my grace, then, is that which is firm and stable, and which cannot be taken away or changed—that is, it cannot be made to depart from you and return you to guilt—unless you yourself change it.

Therefore, how can you raise yourself up <note>original: "leuare el corpo" (to lift the body), a metaphor for prideful rebellion</note> against my goodness? You cannot, if you wish to follow **reason**. Nor can you have wisdom in yourself, nor trust in your own wisdom, for you have become an animal without reason. Do you not see that everything changes except my grace? And why do you not trust in me, who am your creator? Why do you trust in yourself? Am I not faithful and loyal to you? Certainly I am; and this I have not hidden from you, because you have proof of it continually. O sweetest and dearest daughter, man was not loyal nor faithful to me when he transgressed the **obedience** I had imposed on him, through which he fell into death; and yet I was faithful to him, fulfilling for him that for which I had crea[ted him]...

## Providence

->**and [in] my likeness:**<- and I placed it in this garden: which garden, because of the sin of Adam, sprouted thorns: where before there were fragrant flowers of innocence: and of its very great life. At that time everything was obedient to man: but through the <margin>43. Is-</margin> <note>Likely a reference to Isaiah 43</note> fault: and through the disobedience committed, man then found <margin>Jo. 3. 5-</margin> <note>Likely a reference to John 3:5</note> rebellion within himself: and in all creatures: whereby the world became wild <note>original: "insaluadichi," meaning to grow wild or lose cultivation</note>: and man [likewise], which man is another world <note>A reference to the "microcosm," the idea that a human being contains the complexity of the entire universe</note>. 

But I provided: for having sent my truth into the world, the Word incarnate, he took away that wildness: and pulled out the thorns of original sin: and made it a garden watered by the blood of Christ crucified, planting there the plants of the seven gifts of the **Holy Spirit** <term>Spirito Sancto: the third person of the Trinity</term>, extracting from it mortal sin: and this was after the death of my **only-begotten** <term>unigenito: the only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ</term> son: but not before. 

Just as it was prefigured in the Old Testament: when **Elisha** <term>Helyseo: the biblical prophet Elisha</term> was begged to resuscitate the youth who was dead. Elisha did not go himself then: but sent **Gehazi** <term>Giezi: Gehazi, the servant of Elisha</term> there with his staff, saying: that he should place it upon the boy. And Gehazi going: and doing that which Elisha told him: he did not then raise him. And Elisha seeing: that he had not been resuscitated: went there in his own person: and conformed himself entirely to the boy: that is, with all his limbs <note>This refers to 2 Kings 4:34, where Elisha lay upon the child, putting his mouth on his mouth and eyes on his eyes</note>. And breathing seven times into his mouth: the boy breathed seven times as a sign that he was resuscitated. 

This was prefigured by **Moses** <term>Moyse: the biblical prophet and lawgiver</term>: whom I sent with the staff of the Law over the dead body of the human generation <note>the human race</note>: but through this Law there was no life. Wherefore I then sent the Word of my only-begotten son: who was prefigured by Elisha: who conformed himself to this dead son through the union of the **divine nature** <term>natura diuina: the essence of God</term> joined with your **human nature** <term>natura humana: the physical and spiritual essence of mankind</term>. With all the limbs this divine nature joined itself: that is, with the power of the Father: with the wisdom of the Son: and with the clemency of the Holy Spirit: all of me, God, abyss of the **Trinity** <term>Trinita: the Three-in-One Godhead</term>: conformed: and united with your human nature.

### How God provides that we are troubled for our salvation, and concerning the misery of those who do not trust in this providence.

See then, dearest daughter—**Chapter 141**—that through my providence I recreated the second world, that is, man. From the first world <note>Likely referring to the physical world or the state of nature before grace</note>, it was not taken away that it should sprout the thorns of many tribulations, nor that man should find rebellion in all things. This is not without providence, nor without your own good; rather, it is with great providence and for your benefit, to take away man's hope in the world and to make him run and turn toward me, who am his end. Thus, at least through the persistence of troubles, he might lift his heart and his affection to me. 

And man is so ignorant that he does not know the truth, and so fragile in spreading himself out in the world, that even with all these labors and thorns that he finds there, it does not seem that he wishes to leave it, nor does he care to return to his homeland <note>The "homeland" (patria) refers to Heaven, the soul's true place of origin and rest</note>. Now consider, daughter, what he would do if he found perfect delight and rest in the world without any suffering! 

And therefore, with providence, I permit and grant that the world should sprout many tribulations for him, to test virtue in them; and through the pain, effort, and violence they do to themselves <note>The "violence" refers to the spiritual struggle against one's own lower impulses</note>, I might have reason to reward them. So you see that in everything, my providence has ordered and provided with great wisdom. I have given to him, then, as has been said; for I am rich and I was able and am able to give, because my wealth is infinite. Furthermore, everything is made by me, and without me nothing can exist. 

Thus, if he desires goodness, I am **Goodness**, for I am supremely good. I am **Wisdom**; I am kind, I am compassionate, I am a just and **merciful** God. I am generous and not stingy. I am he who gives to whoever asks me, who opens to whoever knocks in truth, and I respond to whoever calls me...

He describes His nature as the source of all goodness, wisdom, and mercy, available to all who seek Him.</summary>

### Of the Divine [Providence] - Chapter

And he teaches you to seek first the kingdom of heaven: that is, the good: and perfect life. For regarding these smallest things, I, your Father in heaven, well know: that you need them, and thus I have made them: and I have commanded the earth: that it give you its fruits. But this miserable person: who through his lack of trust has tightened his heart: and his hands against charity for his neighbor, has not read this doctrine: which my Word, my Truth, has given you: because he does not follow it.

...lives incorporeally by my word. And thus the spiritual sacraments are given to the soul, although they are presented and given through the instrument of the body; because they would not give the soul the life of grace solely in that physical act if that soul did not dispose itself to receive them with a spiritual, holy, and true desire.

Which desire is in the soul and not in the body. And therefore I told you that they were spiritual, and that they are given to the soul because it is an incorporeal <term>incorporea: existing without a physical body</term> thing; notwithstanding that they are administered by means of the body, as has been said. To the desire of the soul it is granted that it may receive it sometimes to increase its growth in me; and through holy desire I will make the soul long for it, and yet it will not be able to have it; and in not being able to have it, its hunger grows, and this brings the soul to the knowledge of itself, as it considers itself unworthy through humility.

And then I make the soul worthy, providing many times in diverse ways for this sacrament <note>The Eucharist</note>, as you know to be true. And if you remember correctly, you have heard and experienced this in yourself: because my clemency, through the <term>Holy Spirit</term> given to them by me out of my goodness, will inspire the mind of some minister to give the soul this food. Constrained by the fire of my charity, that same Holy Spirit—who gives the minister a prick of conscience—moves him to feed the hunger and fulfill the desire of that soul.

And sometimes I will cause a delay until the very last moment; and when the soul has entirely lost hope, it will receive what it desires. Could I not have provided it at the beginning just as well as at the end? Indeed I could. But I do it to increase the soul in the light of faith, so that it may never fail to hope in my goodness, and to make it cautious and prudent, so that it does not imprudently turn its head back <note>original: "uolti el capo adrieto," an idiom for retreating or losing faith</note>.

## How the providence of God serves those who are in mortal sin. Chapter 144.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring floral motifs within a square frame.</note>

**L**athe soul: either it is in a state of mortal sin <term>mortal sin: in Catholic theology, a grave sin that "kills" the life of grace within the soul, separating it from God</term>, or it is imperfect in grace, or it is perfect. And with everyone I use my providence generously, but in diverse ways and with great wisdom, according to what I see is needed. Wherefore the people of the world who lie in the death of mortal sin, I desire to awaken with the sting of conscience, or with hardships that they will feel in the midst of their hearts in new and diverse ways. Wherefore, through this persistence of pains and the sting of conscience which is within the soul, they often depart from the guilt of mortal sin. 

And sometimes, from among the thorns I draw the rose <note>original: "poche de le spine trago la rosa"; a metaphor for God bringing forth something beautiful or virtuous out of a painful or sinful situation</note>, occupying the heart of man. When he has a love for mortal sin or for a creature <note>original: "creatura"; referring to any created thing or person as opposed to the Creator</term> outside of my love, I will take away from him the place and the time so that he cannot fulfill his will. So much so that with the weariness of the heart's pain—which the soul has acquired through its own defect—and not being able to fulfill its disordered desires, it returns to itself with compunction <term>compunction: a feeling of guilt or moral scruple that prevents or follows the doing of something bad</term> of heart and with stings of conscience; and with these, it casts to the ground its frantic love. 

This love may rightly be called "frantic," because believing it places its affection in something, when it comes to see it, it finds it was nothing. The creature <note>the object of the person's affection</note> was and is indeed something, which they loved with a misaligned love; but that which the soul took from it was nothing, because sin is nothing. This door of the **will**, which is free: I do not give permission to the enemies <note>referring to demons or temptations</note> to open it. I do give permission to the demons and the other enemies of man to knock at the other doors, but not at this one, which is the principal one; for it preserves the **city of the soul**. It is true that she is under the guard of **free will** <term>free will: the human capacity to choose between different possible courses of action unimpeded</term>, which stands at this door; and I have given it freedom to say "yes" or "no" as it pleases. Many are the doors of this city, but there are three principal ones: one is the **will**, which always holds itself firm if it so wishes, and it is the guardian of the others. These doors are: the **memory**, the **intellect**, and the **will**. Therefore, if the **will** consents, the enemy of **self-love** <note>original: "amōr pprio"</note> enters, along with all the other enemies that follow after him. Immediately after the doors are opened, the "wickets" <note>small side-doors or gates</note> of the bodily senses are opened, which are all instruments that respond to the soul. Thus you see that the disordered affection of a person who has opened their doors responds with these organs. Hence all sounds are spoiled and contaminated—that is, their choices—and so the eye provides nothing but death; for it is positioned to see dead things with a disordered gaze, looking where it should not. For to look with unity of heart and with joy, rather than with dishonest manners and glances, is the cause of giving death to oneself and to others. O miserable one!
