...tion: <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing "afflic-tion" from the previous page.</note> so that then she may taste eternal life; and the soul <note>original: "aia," a contraction of "anima"</note> remains so serene that whatever she sees, it seems to her that she cries out to God, all inflamed with loving fire through the considerations that my **providence** <term>providence: "providentia" refers to God's proactive care and orchestration of events for the soul's salvation</term> makes then; because she sees herself having emerged from such a great ocean, not by her own effort—since the light came unexpectedly and not through her striving—but came only through my inestimable **charity**, which wished to provide for her necessity in the time of need. So then you see that the imperfect soul, by striving in these battles, comes to perfection; because in those battles she proves my divine providence, receiving what she believed in before she had the proof. Hence, once I have certified her with the proof, she has conceived **perfect love**; because she has known my goodness in my divine providence; whereby she has raised herself from **imperfect love**.

Furthermore, I use with them a **holy deception** <note>original: "sancto ingano"</note> solely to lift them from imperfection: which is this, that I will make them conceive love for some **creature spiritually in particular** <gloss>a specific person loved for the sake of their soul</gloss> beyond the general love [for all people]. Whereby through this means the soul exercises itself in virtue and removes its imperfection, and it makes the heart strip itself of every other creature that it might have loved sensually—such as the love for father, mother, sisters, and brothers. It draws out every personal passion and loves them through me, the eternal God; and with this ordered love of the "means" <note>The "means" refers to the specific spiritual person God provided as a bridge</note> that I have placed there, it drives out the disordered love with which it previously loved creatures. Thus you see that this removes imperfection.

But take heed that no other thing does this love of this "means" accomplish: for it serves to prove whether she perfectly loves me and the means I have given her, or not; and therefore I gave it to her, so that she might prove it...

This pain causes her to enter into the knowledge of herself.

Therefore, if she wishes to walk with light and with **prudence**, as she ought, she should love that means with a more perfect love; because through self-knowledge and the hatred she will have conceived for her own selfish feelings, the imperfection is removed. And having then been made perfect, there follows a more perfect and greater love for creatures in general, and for the particular means provided by my goodness. ### Of the Divine Providence Chapter 145

...[chari]ty <note>The text begins with "ta:", the final syllable of "charità" (charity) from the previous page.</note>: there can be no good, even if their acts were virtuous. And so also evil is done through this means, by the deprivation of **charity** <term>charity: "charita," the supernatural love of God and neighbor, which Catherine views as the soul's essential life-force</term>. So you see that through this means I have established, they demonstrate their perfection and the pure love they have for Me, always seeking the salvation of their neighbors through much endurance. Therefore, I purge them so that they may produce greater and sweeter fruit through many tribulations; from which their **patience** <term>patience: "patientia," the virtue of enduring suffering with a peaceful heart, which Catherine describes as a fragrant incense to God</term> sends up a great fragrance to Me. 

Oh, how sweet and pleasant is this fruit, and of what utility is it to the soul who suffers without fault! If she could see it, there is no soul who would not seek to carry [this weight] with great diligence and joy. Therefore, to give her this great treasure, I provide for her by placing her under the weight of many labors, so that the virtue of patience does not become rusted <note>original: "ruzene"; Catherine uses the metaphor of rust to describe how a virtue can decay if it is not put into practice through trials</note> in them. So when the time comes in which they must be tested, they would not find it rusty—finding there, for not having practiced it, the rust of impatience, which gnaws at the soul. 

And sometimes I use a pleasant deceit <note>original: "piaceuole ingano"; a theological concept where God "tricks" the soul's senses into a state of peace to allow for growth in humility</note> with them to preserve them in the virtue of **humility** <term>humility: "humilita," the honest recognition of one's own nothingness apart from God</term>. The deceit is this: I will make their feelings fall asleep, so that it will seem that neither in their will nor in their feelings do they sense any adverse thing, except like sleeping people; for the sensory feeling sleeps in the perfect soul, but it does not die. For as soon as the soul slackens her exercise and the fire of holy desire, it would be felt more strongly than ever. And therefore let no one trust themselves, no matter how perfect they may be; for everyone must remain in My holy love, because through self-trust, many fall miserably who otherwise would not have fallen. So then I say: it seems to them that their senses are sleeping, and while sustaining and carrying great weights, it does not seem that they feel them; and little by little, in a small consolation—which will be nothing—they will make fun of themselves, since they will feel themselves in such a way that they will become stupefied. And this does

<column-break/>

My providence, so that the soul may grow and so that she may walk in the valley of humility; because then, like a prudent woman, she rises above herself, not pardoning herself, but with hatred and reproach, she chastises the feeling—which chastising is a way of making it fall asleep. 

More perfectly, I sometimes provide for My great servants by leaving them a thorn <note>original: "stimulo"; likely referring to the "thorn in the flesh" mentioned by St. Paul (2 Corinthians 12:7)</note>, just as I did for the sweet Apostle Paul, the **vessel of election** <term>vessel of election: "uasello de electione," a biblical title for St. Paul, indicating he was a chosen instrument for God's work</term>. Having received the doctrine of My Truth in the abyss of Me, the Eternal Father, I nonetheless left him the thorn and the battle of his flesh. Could I not have acted—and can I not still act for Paul and for others in whom I leave the thorn in various ways—so that they would not have it? Yes, indeed. Why then does My providence do it? I do it to make them earn merit and to preserve them in the knowledge of themselves, from which they draw true humility. 

And I also do it to make them merciful <note>original: "piatosi"; having pity or compassion</note> and not cruel toward their neighbor, and so that they are compassionate toward their neighbor's labors; for those who are troubled and suffering have much more compassion when they feel suffering in themselves than if they did not have it. And through this, they grow in greater love and run to Me, all anointed with a humility and burned in the furnace of divine **charity**. Thus, by these means and infinite others, they reach perfect union, just as I told you—that is, in such conjunction and knowledge of My goodness that, being in the mortal body, they taste the good of the immortals, and while remaining in the person of the body, they seem to be outside of it. 

And because they have much knowledge of Me, they love Me much; and whoever loves much, grieves much. Thus, as love grows, sorrow grows. But in what sorrow and pain do they remain? Not in the sorrow of injuries done to them, nor in sorrow for bodily pains, nor for the molestations of the devil, nor for any other thing that could come specifically to them that would have to give them...

### Of the Divine Providence Chapter 145

...pain <note>original: "pena"; this completes the sentence from the previous page regarding the nature of the soul's suffering.</note>. But they only grieve for the offenses committed against me, seeing and knowing that I am worthy of being loved and served; and they grieve for the loss of souls, seeing them walk through the darkness of the world and remain in such blindness. Because of the union that the soul has made in me through the affection of love, she looks [into me] and knows how ineffably I love my creature. And seeing that they represent my image <note>The "imago Dei" or Image of God; Catherine emphasizes that the soul's love for others stems from seeing God's likeness in them</note>, she fell in love with them for love of me; and therefore she feels intolerable pain when she sees them distancing themselves from my goodness. 

And these pains are so great that they cause her to diminish and fade away within herself; she prizes herself as nothing, as if it were not she herself who was receiving [the suffering]. 

Furthermore, I provide for them. With what? With the manifestation of myself to them, making them see in me, with great bitterness, the iniquity and misery of the world, and the damnation of souls—both in general and in particular—according as it pleases my goodness. I do this to make them grow in **love** and in pain, so that, spurred on by the fire of **desire** <term>desire: "desiderio," in Catherine's theology, this is the "hunger" for the salvation of souls which drives the spiritual life</term>, they cry out to me with firm hope and with the light of most holy faith, asking for my aid to succor their many needs. 

Thus, in this way, I provide through **Divine Providence** <term>Divine Providence: "diuina prouidentia," God's guidance and care for all creation, which Catherine describes here as being "constrained" by the prayers of the saints</term> to assist the world, letting myself be constrained by the sweet suffering and the anxious desires of my servants. And I provide for them, nourishing them and increasing them thereby in a greater and more perfect **knowledge** and union with me. 

See, then, that I provide for these perfect ones in many ways and in diverse manners. For while you are alive, you are always capable of increasing in the state of **perfection** and in merit. Therefore, I deprive them of all self-centered and disordered love, whether spiritual or temporal; and I strike them with many tribulations so that they may produce greater and more perfect fruit, as has been said. And through the great tribulations they endure—seeing me offended and the soul deprived of grace—[the soul’s self-love]

is extinguished <note>catchword: "si smorza"</note>

# Concerning the Divine Chapter
<meta>catchword: the mysteries</meta>

it was so in truth: but prefigured through that which I have told you: you will find that it belongs to you: and I make it known to you: that all the **mysteries** <note>original: "mysterii"; referring to the events and hidden meanings of the life of Christ.</note> and the ways that my life held in the world: both with disciples and without disciples, were prefigured within the souls of my servants in every manner of people: so that in everything you might have a **rule** and **doctrine**, reflecting yourselves with the light of **reason**: both the simple and the subtle, and those who have low understanding and high: everyone can take their part, provided they wish to. 

I told you that **Peter**, at the command of the **Word** <note>original: "uerbo" [Verbo]; Catherine uses this term specifically for Jesus Christ, the Eternal Word of the Father.</note>, cast the **net**: so you see that he was **obedient**, believing with living faith that he could catch them: and therefore he took many: but not in the time of the night. Do you know what the time of the night is? It is the dark night of **mortal sin**, when the soul is deprived of the light of **grace**: in this night nothing is caught, because it casts its affection not into the living sea, but into the dead one: where it finds guilt, which is nothing. In vain then it labors: and with great and intolerable pains: and without any utility: wherefore they make themselves martyrs of the devil, and not of **Christ crucified**. 

But when day appears: that is, when they come out of guilt: and return to the state of **grace**, the commandments of the law appear in their mind: which command: that you cast this net in the word of my **Word**, loving me above all things: and your neighbor as yourself. # Of the Divine Chapter

...the great ones, that is, the <term>powers of the soul</term> <note>In Thomistic and Catherine’s theology, these are the Intellect, Memory, and Will.</note>, are also joined by the small ones: that is, the senses of the body. Wherefore, just as I told you when speaking of wicked men—that they all sounded a note of death toward their enemies—so these souls sound a note of life. They receive the [notes] of true and royal virtues, and they play their instruments with sanctity and good operation. 

Wherefore every member performs the work that it was given to do, each one perfectly in its own degree: the eye in its seeing, the ears in their hearing, the sense of smell in its smelling, the taste in its tasting, the tongue in its speaking, the hands in touching and working, and the feet in walking. So they are all tuned in one and the same sound to serve their neighbor for the glory and praise of my name, and to serve the soul with good and virtuous operation; and they are all obedient to the soul, responding as they ought. 

Wherefore these souls are pleasing to the "living tasters" <note>Those who have a spiritual "taste" for divine things and can recognize grace in others.</note>, who wait with great joy and happiness, where they benefit well from one another. Many, indeed, are caught by this sound as if by an instrument, and they are pulled back from death and come to life. All the senses are captured by this "organ" <note>The human person acting as a musical instrument for God's grace.</note>.

And the first who played this sound of life was the sweet and loving **Word** <note>original: "uerbo"; referring to Jesus Christ, the Logos.</note>, taking up your **humanity**; and with this humanity joined to the **deity**, He made a sweet sound upon the **cross**. He captured the children of the human generation, and He captured the demon; for He took away his lordship, which he had possessed for so long because of man's sin. 

All of you others play your music by learning from this Master. Wherefore, by learning from Him, the **apostles** took [souls] by sowing His word throughout the whole world; then the **martyrs**, and **confessors**, and **doctors**, and **virgins**—all of them captured souls through His sound. ### On the providence of God in general, which He uses toward His creatures in this life and in the next. Chapter 148.

Enlarge, then, my daughter, your heart; open the eye of your intellect with the light of faith to see with how much love and providence I have created and ordered man, so that he might enjoy my supreme and eternal good. In everything I have provided, as I have told you: in the soul and in the body; in the imperfect and in the perfect; for the good and for the wicked; spiritually and temporally; in heaven and on earth; in this mortal life and in the immortal one. 

Wherefore, in this mortal life, while you are wayfarers <note>From the Latin *viatores*, a traditional theological term for humans on their journey toward eternity.</note>, I have bound you in the bond of <term>charity</term> <note>Christian love; the selfless love of God and neighbor.</note>. Whether man wants it or not, he is bound by it; so much so that if he unbinds himself through his affection—that is, if he does not live in charity toward his neighbor—he is still bound to him by necessity. 

Wherefore, so that man might practice charity in both act and affection, I providently chose not to give to any one man, nor to everyone, nor to an individual, the knowledge of how to do everything necessary for human life. Instead, one has one part, and another has another, so that each one has a reason, through his own need, to have recourse to the other. 

Even if you lose the affection of charity through your iniquity, you are at least constrained by your needs to perform the act of it. Thus you see that one craftsman has need of another, because one does not know how to do what the other does. Likewise, the cleric and the religious person have need <note>The text breaks off here; "cleric" refers to secular priests, while "religious" refers to those in monastic orders.</note>...

### Of the Divine [Providence] Chapter
<meta>catchword: of</meta>

...of the secular world, and the secular person to the religious; and the one cannot do anything without the other; and so it is with every other thing. I could indeed have given everything to everyone; but I willed with **providence** that one should humble himself to the other, and that they should be constrained to use the affection and the act of <term>charity</term> <note>In Catherine’s theology, charity (caritas) is the glue of creation; God purposefully made people interdependent so they would be forced to love one another.</note> together. Wherefore I have shown my magnificence, goodness, and providence in them; but they let themselves be guided by the darkness of their own fragility.

Thus, the members of your own body put you to shame, because they use charity together, and you do not. For when the head hurts, the hand helps it; and if the finger, which is so small, hurts, the head does not disdain to help it, although it is greater and more noble than all the other parts of the body. Instead, it helps with hearing, with seeing, with speaking, and with all that it has; and so do all the other members.

The proud man does not do this. Seeing his poor member <note>The "poor member" refers to a fellow human being, following the metaphor that all humanity forms one body.</note> sick and in necessity, he does not help him—and not only with that which he loves [his wealth], but not even with a single kind word. Instead, with reproach and disdain, he turns his face away. He abounds in riches and lets the other die of hunger; but he does not see that his misery and cruelty cast a stench up to me even to the depths of hell; to there his stench goes.

But I provide for that poor little one, and for his poverty, he shall be given supreme wealth; and to the other, there will be great reproach from my **Truth** <note>Catherine frequently uses "my Truth" as a proper name for Jesus Christ.</note>, if he does not correct himself while in the world. As I said in the holy <term>Gospel</term> <note>A direct reference to the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats in Matthew 25:35-45.</note>: *I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me nothing to drink; I was naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.* And it will not avail him in that final moment to excuse himself by saying: "I did not see you; for if I had seen you, I would have done it." The wretched man knows well—and so my Truth said—that whatever is done to his little poor ones, is done to him. And therefore eternal punishment with the demons will justly be given to him. So you see that on earth I have provided so that they do not go to eternal sorrow. And if you look...

# Providence CXLVIII

...from above, [they have] in me lasting life in the angelic nature:
and in the citizens <note>The "citizens" are the souls of the redeemed who now dwell in the Heavenly City.</note> who are in that same lasting life: who by vir-
tue of the blood of the Lamb <note>original: *lagnello*</note> have obtained eternal life: I have
ordered their <term>charity</term> <note>From the Latin *caritas*; here meaning the supernatural love that binds the soul to God and neighbor.</note> with such order: that is, I have not ordained
that one should taste only his own specific good in the blessed life
which he receives from me, without it being shared by the others.
I have not willed it so: but I have ordered and perfected their charity
in such a way that the great tastes the good of the small, and the small that of the
great. I say "small" in terms of measurement: not that the small soul
is not as full as the great; everyone is full in their own degree,
just as I described to you in another place. <note>Catherine frequently uses the metaphor of different-sized vessels (like a glass and a pitcher) both being dipped into the ocean; both are completely full, even if they hold different amounts.</note> O how fra-
ternal is this charity, and how it is unitive in me, and one with the
other! Because they have it from me, and they recognize it as coming from me with that
holy fear and due reverence which I have given them; where-
fore, seeing themselves, they reflect in me: and in me they see and
know their own dignity, in which I have placed them. The an-
gel communicates with man—that is, with the souls of the blessed—and
the blessed with the angels. So that everyone in this delight
of charity, enjoying the good of one another, ex-
ults in me with jubilee and with joy without any sadness: be-
cause while they lived, and even in their death, they tasted me
through the affection of love in charity for their neighbor.
Who has ordered this? My wisdom, with admirable and sweet **pro-
vidence**. And if you turn your gaze toward purgatory,
you will find my sweet and inexhaustible providence in those poor souls
who, through ignorance, lost their time; and because they are now
separated from the body, they no longer have time to be able to earn merit.
Wherefore I have provided for them by means of you, who are still in the
mortal life and who have time to act for them: that is, through

### ¶ Of the providence that God uses toward his poor servants: helping them in their temporal needs. Chapter 149.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring floral motifs and vines within a square border.</image-desc>

Now, dearest daughter, I want to tell you a small portion of the ways: that I use to help my servants: who hope in me in their bodily necessity. They receive this help as perfectly or imperfectly as they themselves are perfect or imperfect—stripped of themselves and of the world—but I provide for everyone. Therefore, for my little poor ones, poor in spirit <note>original: "di spō," short for *spirito*</note> and in will: that is, through spiritual intention: I do not mean simply poor, because many are poor and do not wish to be. These such people are rich as far as their will is concerned: and they are <term>beggars</term> <note>Catherine draws a distinction here between the "spiritually poor" (who choose poverty) and "mendicants" or beggars (who are poor by circumstance and resent it).</note>: because they do not hope in me; they do not carry voluntarily the poverty that I have given them as a medicine for their soul <note>original: *medecina de lania*</note>; because wealth would have done them harm: and would have been their damnation. But my servants are poor and not beggars. The beggar often does not have what he needs: and suffers great necessity: but the poor person does not overflow, yet has his needs filled: because I never fail him: as long as he hopes in me. I sometimes lead them even to the extreme: so that they may better know: and see what I can: and want to provide: and so that they fall in love with my providence: and embrace my bride, true poverty: wherefore their servant, the Holy Spirit <note>original: *spirito sancto*</note>—my clemency—seeing that they do not have what they need for the necessity of the body: falls in love with a desire, placing a sting in the hearts of those: who are able to help: so that they will go...

This is just as it happened to the <term>philosophers</term> <note>Likely referring to ancient Greek philosophers like Diogenes or the Stoics, who were famous for giving up possessions to focus on thought.</note>, who, because of the love they had for knowledge <note>original: "scientia"; here referring to human wisdom or academic study.</note> and the desire to learn it, despised riches and made themselves poor voluntarily. But because this virtue of poverty was not spiritual, nor done for the glory and praise of my name, they did not have the life of grace, nor perfection, but eternal death.

This rule has its own kingdom in which there is never war, but always peace and tranquility. It abounds in <term>justice</term>, because whatever offends justice is separated from it. The walls of its city are strong, because the foundation is not made upon the earth, but upon the living stone, sweet Christ Jesus, my only-begotten son. And she took her as a bride with the light of most **holy faith**, with firm **hope**, and with prompt **obedience**, having become obedient to the commandments and to the counsels <note>The "counsels" refer to the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience followed by monastics and dedicated religious.</note> which my Life <note>original: "mia uita"; Catherine often refers to Christ as "the Truth" or "the Life."</note> gave them in deed and in spirit, as has been said. These people hold **death** in desire and life in displeasure and impatience—not to escape toil or fatigue, but to be joined with me, who am their end. And because they do not fear death, which man naturally fears, they do not fear it because the bride they have taken, **poverty**, has made them secure by taking away from them the love of **riches**. Whereby through virtue they have trampled underfoot their natural self-love and have received that light and that divine love which is supernatural. 

How could a man who is in this state grieve over his own death? He desires to leave this life; it is a pain for him to endure it when he sees it prolonged so much. And how could he grieve at leaving the riches of the world, which he has despised with such great desire? This point is no great feat; for he who does not love does not grieve, and he even delights when he leaves the thing he hates. So, from whichever side you look, you find in them perfect peace, quiet, and every good. 

But in the miserable ones who possess **riches** with such disordered love, you find nothing but supreme evil and intolerable pains, although to outward appearances the contrary might seem true. But in life it is truly so. Who would not have judged that poor **Lazarus** was in extreme misery, and the **damned rich man** <note>Traditionally known as Dives from the parable in Luke 16:19–31.</note> in great joy and rest? And nonetheless, it was not so, nor was it ever so; because that rich man sustained greater pain with his riches than poor Lazarus, who was tortured by **leprosy**. This is because in the rich man, his self-will was alive—from which all pain proceeds—and in Lazarus, his will was dead <note>In Catherine’s theology, a "dead will" means a human will that has been completely surrendered to God’s will, resulting in inner peace regardless of external circumstances.</note> and was alive in me. Therefore, even in his pain, he had refreshment and consolation. And why is it that a man surrounded by riches, taking such great care of his body and with many servants, will always be sickly? Yet another, despising wealth and embracing poverty for love of me, keeping only enough clothing to cover his body, becomes strong and healthy. Nothing seems to harm him; neither cold, nor heat, nor coarse foods seem to damage that body. Why is this? It comes from my providence; for I took it upon myself to care for him because he left everything for me. So you see, most beloved daughter, in what rest and delight these, my beloved poor ones, dwell.

...but eternal greatness: and transformed in the abyss of the supreme and inestimable providence. Like one drunk on the thought of her salvation, you go seeking her while she flees from you. Now I give thanks to you, supreme and eternal Father, for your boundless goodness shown to me, a miserable woman unworthy of any grace. But because I see that you are the fulfiller of holy desires, and because your Truth cannot lie, and because I so desire it, I ask that you now speak to me a little of the virtue of obedience, and wherein its excellence lies.

# Providence

...if it falls, let him pick it up. Do you believe that you can go to the wedding with torn and foul clothing? Do you believe that by sitting down and binding yourself in the chains of **mortal sin** <term>A grave sin committed with full knowledge and consent that separates the soul from God's sanctifying grace.</term>, you can go there, or that you can open the door without a key? Do not imagine that you can, for your imagination would be greatly deceived.

It is necessary for you, then, to be unbound; so step out of mortal sin through holy **confession**, **contrition**, and **satisfaction**, <note>These are the three necessary parts of the Sacrament of Penance: confessing sins to a priest, feeling true sorrow for them, and performing an act of penance to make amends.</note> and with the firm resolve <note>original: "cõpponimento." A formal intention or promise made during confession to avoid future sin.</note> to offend no more. And then you will cast to the ground that foul and filthy garment, and you will run with the wedding garment, with the light, and with the key of **obedience** in your hand to unlock the gate.

Tie this key with the cord of **humility** <term>original: "uilta." While literally meaning "lowliness" or "vileness," in this spiritual context, it refers to the humble recognition of one's own unworthiness before God.</term> and with displeasure for yourself and for the world; and attach it to the pleasure of me, your Creator. You should make a belt <note>original: "cingulo." This refers to a liturgical girdle or belt, symbolizing readiness, purity, and the binding of one's will to God.</note> of this pleasure and gird yourself with it, so that you do not lose the key.

But know, my daughter, that there are many who have taken this key of obedience, because they have seen by the light of **faith** that they cannot escape eternal damnation in any other way; yet they hold it in their hands without the belt girded and without the strap around it. That is to say, they do not clothe themselves perfectly in my pleasure, but they still please themselves. Nor have they put on the cord of humility, for they do not desire to be held as lowly, but rather they delight in the praise of men. 

And therefore, such as these are prone to losing the key; it only takes a little excess of toil, or some mental or physical tribulation. For if this happens—unless they take great care—by loosening the hand of holy desire, they would often lose it. This losing is a straying <note>original: "ſmarire." To lose one's way or lose possession of something through wandering or negligence.</note>. For they can find it again while they live, if they wish to; but if they do not wish to, they will never find it again. And what will manifest that they have lost it? **Impatience**; because **patience** was united with obedience. Thus, where there is no patience, it is demonstrated that obedience is not in the soul. 

Oh, how sweet and glorious a virtue this is!

Who placed them in so much good? The blood of the Lamb. You exercise cruelty toward your neighbor, and commit robberies and betrayals, following the disordered pleasure and delights of the world. 

Cut off the **horn of pride** <term>original: "supbia." A metaphor for the arrogance that makes a person feel superior to others and to God's law.</term>; once it is cut off, you will extinguish the hatred that you have in your heart toward those who do you injury. Measure the injuries that you do to Me and to your neighbor against those that are done to you, and you will find that, compared to the ones done to Me and to them, your own injuries are as nothing. ...you <note>The text likely completes a thought from the previous page regarding the contrast between the holy life of the Order and the failings of its leaders.</note> and miserable shepherds and prelates placed by the Master <note>original: "patrone"; referring to God as the captain or owner of the ship.</note> of this little ship; but she <note>The "little ship" (nauicella), a metaphor for a religious Order.</note> in herself is of such delight that your tongue could not recount it. And if it enters there imperfectly, it is not because it cannot reach perfection—for it does indeed reach it there—provided it wishes to exercise the virtue of obedience within itself; for the majority of those who enter are imperfect. Thus, some enter with perfection, some enter in their childhood, some enter through fear, some through fear of punishment, and some through flatteries <note>original: "losenghe"; refers to being drawn to religious life by the "sweetness" or "attractions" of God's grace or the promise of peace.</note>. And therefore, everything depends on exercising oneself in virtue and persevering until death; for no judgment is made based on the entry, but only on the perseverance. Many have appeared to have started perfectly who have later turned their heads back, or have remained in the Order with much imperfection. 

So then, the manner and the act with which they enter the little ship—which are all ordained by me, calling them in diverse ways—cannot be judged; one can only judge the affection of the one who perseveres with true obedience. This little ship is rich, for the subject need not have any thought for what he needs, neither spiritually nor even temporally. For if he is truly obedient and a keeper of the Order, he is provided for by the Master through the Holy Spirit <note>original: "spõ sctõ" (spirito sancto).</note>—just as you know I told you when I spoke to you of my Providence: that if my servants were poor, they were not beggars <note>original: "mendici"; referring to the promise that those who seek the Kingdom of God will have their basic needs met.</note>. 

So it is with these souls, for they find their needs well provided for, provided they are observers of the Order. Thus you see that in the times when the Orders were governed in the flower of virtue, with true poverty and fraternal charity, temporal substance never failed them; rather, they had more than they required.

Wherefore he took up the office of the Word <note>Jesus Christ, the "Logos" or Word of God.</note>, my only-begotten son. Directly in the world, he appeared as an apostle; with such life and light, he sowed my word, removing the darkness and giving the light.

Because Mary gave him the habit <note>Refers to the tradition that the Virgin Mary revealed the specific design of the Dominican habit (the white tunic and black mantle) to the order.</note>, since that office was committed to her by my goodness. Dominic does not want his children to attend to anything else but to remain at this table, in the light of knowledge <note>original: "lume de la scientia"; refers to the study of theology and sacred scripture as a path to God.</note>, seeking only the glory and praise of my name and the salvation of souls. And so that they might attend to nothing else, he removes from them the care of temporal things and wishes them to be poor. It is true that some lacked faith, fearing they would not be provided for; however, he himself did not fail, for he was clothed in faith and, with firm hope, trusted in my providence.

He also wishes them to observe obedience and be obedient in their actions; for a base, carnal life <note>original: "vivere brutamente"; literally "living like a beast," referring to a life led by animal instincts rather than spiritual reason.</note> obscures the eye of the intellect. And it is not only the eye of the intellect that is clouded; because of that miserable, base vice <note>A reference to lust or lack of chastity.</note>, even physical sight is impaired—that very light by which they might better and more perfectly acquire the light of knowledge. Therefore, he established the third vow of continence; and in all things, he wishes them to observe it with true and perfect obedience.

Although today this is poorly observed by many—indeed, they pervert the light of knowledge into darkness through the darkness of pride—it is not that this light receives darkness into itself, but rather it is darkened within their souls. For where there is pride, there can be no obedience. I have already told you that a man is only as humble as he is obedient, and as obedient as he is humble. When one transgresses the vow of obedience, it is rare that he does not also transgress that of continence, whether in thought or in deed.

Thus, he has organized his little ship <note>The religious Order.</note> and bound it with these three cords: namely obedience, continence, and true poverty. He made his Order entirely royal, not binding its rules under the penalty of mortal sin <note>Saint Dominic famously declared that the Order's constitutions do not bind the friars under pain of sin, but rather under pain of discipline, to foster a spirit of love rather than fear.</note>. Wherefore I, the Eternal Father, illuminated him with the true light of providence to provide even for those who might be less perfect. For although all who strictly observe the Order are "perfect" <note>Meaning they have entered a "state of perfection" or consecrated life.</note>, nonetheless, even in this life, one person is more perfect than another. Yet, both the perfect and the "imperfect" find a place within this little ship. He aligns himself with my Truth, showing that I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live <note>original: "non volere la morte d’ l’ peccatore: ma che se puertisse: & viuesse"; a paraphrase of Ezekiel 33:11.</note>. # Of the Divine Chapter

...passing through, they would bypass obedience: because they would not observe the promise of poverty; because of this, they would also fall into pride, following the lead of their own will. And if it happens that they must obey at times, they do not bow out of humility, but they pass with pride, bowing the head by force—which force breaks the head of the will, performing that obedience with displeasure toward the Order and their superior.

Now, little by little, they see themselves ruined in the other [vow]: that is, transgressing the vow of continence. For he who has not hated his own appetite and has not stripped himself of temporal substance, takes part in many conversations <note>The Italian "conversazione" here refers to social interactions and worldly associations that distract a monk or nun from their vows.</note> and finds plenty of associates who love him for their own utility. From these conversations, they then come to close friendships, and they keep their bodies in delights. And because they do not have the nurse of humility, nor her sister, lowliness <term>lowliness: "vilità," the spiritual practice of embracing a humble, "lowly" status and rejecting worldly honor.</term>, they remain in their own self-pleasure, dressing neatly and delicately—not like religious, but like lords; not with vigils, nor with prayer. 

Wherefore, because they have money to spend—and through these things I have told you, and many others which happen and which they do (and if they did not have money to spend, this would not happen to them)—they fall into impurity, whether physical or mental. For if sometimes, out of shame or lack of opportunity, they abstain bodily, they will not abstain mentally; because it would seem impossible for one who engages in much conversation and in bodily delicacy, taking food immoderately without vigils and without prayer, to keep their mind pure.

The perfect obedient soul, however, sees from afar with the light of most holy faith the evil and the harm that would come from possessing temporal substance and from walking with the weight of their own will. They see well that they must pass through this wicket-gate <term>wicket-gate: "sportello," the narrow door of specific religious rules within the larger gate of Christian obedience.</term>, and see that they would pass through it with death and not with life, because they would not have unlocked it with the key of obedience.

<summary>The Father explains how the possession of private property and self-will leads religious souls to pride and the eventual breaking of their vows of obedience and continence. In contrast, the "perfectly obedient" soul uses the light of faith to avoid these traps and successfully navigate the narrow "wicket-gate" of the Order.</summary>

The obedient man does not abandon the refectory <term>refectory: "refectorio", the communal dining hall of a monastery</term>, but visits it continually; and he delights in being at the table with the poor. And as a sign that he delights in it, in order to have a reason to stay away [from worldly matters], he has stripped himself of temporal substance, perfectly observing the vow of poverty <term>poverty: "pouerta", the renunciation of personal ownership</term>. He does this so perfectly that the body's necessity comes with a sense of reproach; thus his cell is full of the fragrance of poverty, and not of bread <note>Meaning it is empty of hoarded food or material luxuries, filled instead with the "scent" of holiness.</note>. 

Therefore, he has no worry that thieves might come to steal from him, nor that rust or moths might damage his garments. And if something is given to him, he has no thought of storing it away, but generously shares it with his brothers, not thinking of tomorrow. Instead, he takes only what is necessary for the present day, thinking only of the kingdom of heaven and of true obedience, and how best he may observe it. And because the way of humility is best followed this way, he submits himself to the small as to the great, and to the poor as to the rich, and makes himself the servant of all, never refusing labor.

# Divine Providence
### On the Virtue of Obedience

...everyone he serves charitably. The obedient man does not wish to practice obedience in his own way, nor to choose his own time or place; rather, he acts according to the way of the Order and of his superior <term>superior: "p̄lato" (prelate), referring to the head of a religious house</term>. The truly obedient and perfect man does all this without pain and without weariness of mind. He passes with this key <note>The "key of obedience" mentioned on the previous page.</note> in his hand through the narrow door of the Order fittingly and without violence, because he has observed and continues to observe the vow of poverty, of unique obedience, and of continence.

He has removed from himself the loftiness of pride and has bowed his head to obedience through humility <term>humility: "hūilita", the act of lowering oneself before God and others</term>; and therefore he does not "break his head" <note>original: "nō rōpe el capo"; an idiom meaning he does not lose his peace or suffer mental anguish</note> through impatience. Instead, he is patient with fortitude and long perseverance, which virtues are friends of obedience. He bypasses the snares of the demons by mortifying and macerating his flesh, stripping it of delights and pleasures, and clothing it with the labors of the Order with faith. He acts without indignation and with compunction <note>original: "eputio"; likely a variant of "compunzio" or "epunzio", referring to a state of humble sorrow or patient endurance.</note>, for he does not hold in his mind the strike of the father <note>referring to a disciplinary action by a superior</note> nor any injury that might be done to him.

Thus, this little obedient one does not dwell upon injuries, nor labors, nor strikes that he might receive in the Order from his superior; but when called, he humbly returns to him, not impassioned by hatred, anger, or rancor, but with gentleness and benevolence. These are those "little ones" of whom my Truth <note>original: "mia uita" (my life); God the Father often refers to Christ as His "Truth" or "Life" in this text.</note> spoke when he said to the disciples who were contending among themselves as to which of them was the greatest. There, having a little child <term>little child: "putino", an archaic Italian term for a young boy or toddler</term> come to Him, He said: "Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven <term>reame del cielo: the kingdom of heaven</term> belongs to such as these." And whoever does not humble himself like this little child—that is, by adopting his condition—shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, whoever humbles himself, my dearest daughter, shall be exalted, and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, as my Truth himself said. Thus, it is only right that these humble little ones—who for love have humbled themselves and made themselves subjects with true and holy obedience, not kicking against the Order nor against their superior—are exalted by me, the highest and eternal Father, alongside the true citizens of the blessed life <term>uita beata: the state of eternal happiness in heaven</term>, where they are rewarded for every...

# Divine Providence
### Chapter [on the Reward of Obedience]

...without fatigue; and in this life they taste eternal life.

¶ How the truly obedient receive a hundredfold and eternal life, and what is meant by that "one" and by that "hundred." Chapter

IN these, most beloved daughter, is fulfilled that which was spoken in the Holy Gospel by the sweet and loving Word <note>original: "ũbo" (verbo); referring to Jesus Christ as the Word of God.</note>, my only-begotten Son, when he replied to Peter. Peter had asked him: "Master, behold, we have left everything for your love, and we have followed you; what shall we have?" Then my Truth <note>original: "mia uerita"; in Catherine's writings, God the Father refers to Jesus as "My Truth."</note> replied: "I will give to you a hundredfold, and you shall possess eternal life." It was as if my Truth wished to say: "You have done well, Peter, because in no other way could you follow me; therefore, in this life, I will give you a hundredfold."

But what is this hundred, most beloved daughter, which is followed by eternal life? My Truth did not speak of temporal substance <term>temporal substance: "substãtia temporal"; material wealth or worldly goods</term> specifically—although I do sometimes cause the goods of those who give alms to multiply—but of what, then, did he speak? He intended to speak of that which comes from one's own will <term>own will: "ppria uolũta"; the individual’s ego or desires as opposed to God's will</term>, which is "one." For this "one," I return to them a hundred. And why do I use the number of one hundred? Because a hundred is a perfect number <note>In medieval numerology, 100 represented completion or perfection.</note>, and you cannot add more to it unless you begin again from the first.

Thus, just as this is a perfect number, so charity <term>charity: "charita"; the highest form of divine love (Caritas)</term> is most perfect above all other virtues. One cannot climb to perfect virtue unless one begins again with the knowledge of oneself <note>Self-knowledge is a core theme in Catherine's spirituality; one must know their own nothingness to understand God's greatness.</note> and grows to the number of a hundred in merit. Yet, you still reach the number of a hundred. Now this, then, is that hundred which is given to those who have given the "one"—that is, their own will—both in general obedience and in this particular obedience.

And with this hundred, they possess eternal life afterward; for charity alone is that which enters as mistress, bringing with her the fruit of all the other virtues. The virtues themselves remain outside—I mean they bring the fruit as a lasting life in which they taste eternal life; for...

<summary>God explains to Saint Catherine that the "hundredfold" reward promised in the Gospels represents the perfection of Charity, which is granted to those who sacrifice their "one" thing: their own self-will.</summary>

# Chapter on the Divine [Providence]
<meta>catchword: & the</meta>

...[I have told] you about true obedience, and how can this wretch be in anything but pain, since he is deprived of charity? He is forced to bow the head of his own will by necessity, while pride keeps him stiff-necked. Thus, all his desires are out of harmony with the will of his religious Order. For the Order commands him to be obedient, but he loves disobedience; it commands him to practice <term>voluntary poverty: the vow to own nothing personally, relying entirely on the community.</term>, yet he tires of it and flees from it, possessing and desiring wealth. It requires that he maintain continence and purity, yet he desires impurity. 

By violating these three vows <note>The three traditional vows of religious life: Poverty, Chastity (continence), and Obedience.</note>, my daughter, the religious man falls into ruin and into so many miserable defects that his appearance no longer seems like that of a man of God, but like an incarnate demon. I have spoken to you about this more extensively in another place, but I will not fail to tell you something of their deception, and of the fruit they harvest from disobedience—which leads to condemnation—in contrast to the exaltation of obedience. 

Therefore, you should know that this wretch is deceived by <term>self-love: in Catherine’s writings, "amore proprio" is the root of all sin, where the soul loves itself apart from God.</term>. The eye of his intellect is fixed, with a dead faith, upon the pleasure of his own sensuality and the things of the world. Therefore, although he has left the world in body, he has remained there in his affections. Because obedience seems like a great labor to him, he wants to disobey to escape the struggle, yet he falls into a much greater labor. For he must obey eventually, whether by force or by love. It would have been better and less exhausting for him to obey out of love than without it. 

Oh, how deceived he is! And there is no one who deceives him except himself. In wanting to please himself, he becomes displeasing to himself, for he finds the very tasks imposed upon him by obedience to be painful. He wishes to live in great delight and create an "eternal life" for himself in this world, whereas our Order wants him to be a pilgrim <note>A common medieval spiritual theme: the "homo viator" or human as a pilgrim who has no permanent home on earth.</note> and constantly reminds him of this. For when he has settled himself in a place where he wishes to stay for his own pleasure and the delight he finds there, he is moved to another place. In this change he suffers, because his will was set on not wanting to move. If he does not obey willingly, he is forced to endure the discipline...

->Providence 160<-

...and the labor of the Order, and thus he remains in continual torment. See, then, how he deceives himself: by wishing to flee pains, he enters into pain, because his blindness does not allow him to know the way of obedience. This is a way of life founded upon the obedient Lamb, my only-begotten Son, who takes away the pain. And who guides him? The love he has for his own passion to disobey. Like a madman, he wishes to sail in this tempestuous sea using only his own arms, trusting in his own wretched knowledge <note>original: "miso sape," likely a contraction for "misero sapere."</note>. He does not wish to sail upon the arms of the Order and of his <term>superior: the "prelato," the head of the religious community to whom the monk owes obedience.</term>. He has left it in desire, not observing the regulations, nor the customs of the Order, nor the three vows <note>The vows of Poverty, Chastity, and Obedience.</note> he promised to keep at his profession. 

Wherefore, he remains in the sea of the tempest, struck by winds very contrary to the little ship. He stays attached to it only by his clothes, wearing the habit upon his body but not in his heart. Such a person is not a friar, but a man dressed in the form of a man, yet not a man in effect; for in his way of living, he is worse than an animal. He does not see that it is much more labor for him to sail with his own arms than with the arms of others. He does not see that he stands in danger of eternal death; if his cloth <note>Referencing his superficial attachment to the Order.</note> were torn from the ship, he would have no more remedy once death occurred. He cannot see this because the ship of <term>self-love: "amore proprio," which Catherine describes as the root of all sin and spiritual blindness.</term>—from which his disobedience sprang—has deprived him of light and does not let him see his own woes. See, then, how miserably he is deceived.

What fruit does the tree of this wretch produce? The fruit of death, because he has planted the root of his affection in pride, which he has drawn from pleasure and from self-love. Therefore, everything that grows from it is corrupt: the flowers, the leaves, the fruit, and the branches of the tree.

All are ruined: that is, the branch of obedience, of <term>poverty: "pota," a shortened form of "povertà."</term>, and of <term>chastity: "otinentia," meaning continence or self-restraint.</term>. These are the three branches held by the trunk of <term>disordered affection: "affecto," referring here to self-centered love or desire.</term>, which is poorly planted, as was said. And the leaves that this tree produces are corrupt words, spoken in such a way that they would not even be found in the mouth of a worldly scoundrel <note>original: "ribaldo seculare."</note>. And if he must proclaim my word, he casts it with polished but dishonest speech; that is, he does not intend to feed souls with the seed of my word, but only aims to speak elegantly. And if you look at the flowers of this tree, they give off a stench: that is, they are the various and diverse thoughts which he voluntarily receives with delight and pleasure. He does not flee the places or the paths that bring them to him, but rather seeks them out so he can reach the fulfillment of the sin. And it is a fruit that kills him, taking away the life of grace and giving him eternal death.

And what a stench this sin, born from the flower of the tree, gives off! It gives off the stench of disobedience; with the thoughts of his heart, he wishes to investigate and judge as evil the will of his <term>superior: "prelato," the head of the religious community.</term>. It also casts out impurity, as he delights in frequent conversations with those who bear the wretched name of <note>original: "deuote," referring to laywomen who lived lives of private devotion, here implying improper or distracting relationships for a monk.</note> the "devout women." O wretch! You do not see that under the guise of devotion, you are joined with a crowd of [sinful] offspring. This is what your disobedience gives you: for you have not embraced the children of the virtues as a truly obedient person does. He seeks to deceive his superior when he sees that what his perverse will desires is denied to him, using the "leaves" of flattering or harsh words, speaking irreverently and with reproach. He cannot bear his brother, nor can he endure even a small word or correction addressed to him. Instead, he suddenly brings forth the poisoned fruit of impatience, of rage, and of hatred toward his brother, judging as evil that which his brother did for his good. ### On the imperfection of those who live lukewarmly in religious life, although they keep themselves from mortal sins; and on the remedy against their lukewarmness

<margin>Chapter 162</margin>
O dearest daughter, how many are these miserable disobedient ones who today nourish themselves in this little ship? They are many, but few are their opposites—that is, the truly obedient. I tell you that even among the "perfect" <note>Here, "perfect" refers to those who have taken formal vows in a religious Order, not necessarily those who have reached spiritual perfection.</note> there are these miserable ones. There are many who live in the Order in a common, mediocre way; few among them are as they should be. Nor are they truly wicked—meaning they still preserve their conscience enough that they do not sin mortally—but they remain in lukewarmness <term>tepideza; a state of spiritual indifference or "room temperature" faith, neither hot nor cold</term> and in coldness of heart. Therefore, if they do not exercise their life a bit with the observances of the Order, they stand in great danger. 

And so they have great need of diligence and must not sleep, but rather rise from their lukewarmness. For if they remain in it, they are prone to fall; and even if they do not fall, they will live according to their own opinion and human pleasure, "colored" with the color of the Order. They strive more to observe the ceremonies <note>external rituals and formal rules</note> of the Order than the essence of the Order itself. Often, because they lack light, they will be prone to judge those who observe the Order more perfectly than they do, but who perhaps show less perfection in the specific ceremonies of which these lukewarm ones have made themselves observers. Thus, in every way, it is harmful for them to remain in this state of "common" obedience—that is, passing through their obedience coldly, with much fatigue and much pain, because to a cold heart, any burden seems heavy to carry.

<summary>God explains that disobedience leads to the same fate as the fallen angels, then shifts focus to "lukewarm" religious members who follow rituals without heart, warning that they are in danger of falling away.</summary>

to carry: <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the burdens of the disobedient.</note> hence they carry great fatigue with little fruit; and they offend their state of perfection, into which they have entered and are bound to observe. And although they do less evil than the others of whom I have told you, they still do poorly; because they do not depart from the world to remain with the **general key of obedience**, but rather to unlock heaven with their **little key**. <note>original: "chiauicella." This refers to their own private will or personal devotion, rather than the communal Rule of the Order.</note> This key should be attached to the cord of self-abasement, by abasing oneself, and with the girdle of humility as has been said; and one must hold it tight in the hands of burning love. 

And therefore know, dearest daughter, that they are well suited to reach great perfection if they so desire, because they are closer to it than the others I have mentioned; but in another way, it is more difficult to raise these people from their imperfection within their state than it is to raise the wicked man from the misery of his state. And do you know why? Because the wicked man clearly sees that he does evil, and his conscience manifests it to him; but because of the self-love he has, which has weakened him, he does not force himself to leave that fault. Yet he sees with a **natural light** <note>The basic human capacity to distinguish right from wrong, even without special grace.</note> that what he does is evil; so if someone were to ask him, "Are you not doing wrong by doing this?" he would answer, "Yes, but my fragility is such that it seems I cannot leave it." Although he does not speak the truth—for with my help he can leave it if he wills—he nonetheless recognizes that he does evil, and with this recognition, it is easy for him to leave it if he chooses.

But these **lukewarm** ones <term>tepidi; those who are spiritually indifferent or "room temperature," neither hot with love nor cold with manifest sin</term>, who do no great evil nor any great good, do not recognize the coldness of their state, nor in what danger they stand. Thus, not recognizing it, they do not care to rise, nor do they care to be shown their state, because of the coldness of their heart; and so they remain bound in their long-accustomed habits. What way, then, shall there be for these people to be made to rise? The way is this: that they should take the wood of **self-knowledge** <note>A central theme in Catherine's spirituality: the soul must know its own nothingness to experience God's everything.</note> with hatred of their own pleasure and their own reputation, and put it into the fire of my divine...

### ¶ On the excellence of obedience: and of the benefits it gives to those who receive it in truth. Chapter CLXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring floral and foliate motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

**This, then, I have told you: it is that true remedy** which the truly obedient person holds. And every day they hold it anew, increasing the virtue of **obedience** with the light of faith, always desiring insults and vileness <note>In the context of 14th-century spirituality, "desiring insults" refers to the practice of humility—seeking to be lowly in the eyes of the world to be closer to the suffering of Christ.</note>, and wishing that great burdens be imposed on them by their **prelate** <note>original: "prelato." Referring generally to a religious superior or anyone in a position of authority within the Church or a monastic order.</note>; this is so that the virtue of obedience and its sister, **patience**, do not grow rusty. They seek this so that in the time when these virtues must be put to work, they do not fail or prove too difficult to use. Instead, the instrument of desire actively sounds, and the soul does not let time pass, because it has a hunger for it [obedience]. 

Obedience is a diligent bride who does not wish to remain idle. O pleasant obedience! O sweet obedience! Delightful obedience! Illuminating obedience! For you have removed the darkness of **self-love**. O obedience that gives life, granting the soul the life of **grace**! You have chosen the soul for a bride and have stripped away the death of the **own-will**, which brings war and death to the soul. 

You are generous, for you make yourself subject to every creature that possesses reason <note>Catherine emphasizes that the truly obedient person humbles themselves before everyone for the sake of God, not just their direct superiors.</note>. You are kind and merciful, because with kindness and gentleness you carry every great burden; for you are accompanied by **fortitude** and true **patience**. You are crowned with **perseverance**. You do not fail because of the persistence of the prelate, nor because of the great burdens he might place upon you without **discretion** <note>original: "discretione." The spiritual gift of discernment or moderation; here, it refers to a superior giving orders that might seem unreasonable or unbalanced.</note>; rather, with the light of faith, you carry everything. 

You are so bound to **humility** that no creature can pull you from the hands of the soul’s holy desire that possesses you. And what shall we say, most beloved and dearest daughter, of this most excellent virtue? We shall say that it is a good without any evil; it stays hidden in the ship <note>The "ship" is a common metaphor in Catherine’s writing for the religious orders or the Church itself, providing safety on the stormy sea of the world.</note>, where no contrary wind can harm it.

Referring to one's personal judgment or subjective desires that contradict a command.</note>; which sensory feeling seeks the things of others and not its own; just as the disobedient person does, who wishes to investigate the will of the one who commands him, and judge it according to his own pleasure and dark sight; but he does not wish to investigate his own perverse will, which gives him death. 

But the truly obedient person, with the light of faith, is to judge the will of his superior as good; and therefore he does not seek his own will, but bows his head with the fragrance of true and holy obedience, which nourishes his soul; and this virtue grows in the soul just as much as it bathes itself in the light of most holy faith. # Of the Divine Chapter

I reply to you: that the merit of obedience is not measured by the act, the place, nor the person: that is, [it is not] more in a good [superior] than in a bad one, nor more in a secular person than in a religious, but according to the measure of the **love** <note>original: "lamore." Catherine emphasizes that the internal disposition of the heart is more important than external status.</note> that the obedient one has. With this measure it is measured: because for the truly obedient, the imperfection of a bad **prelate** <note>In this context, "prelate" refers to any religious superior or person in authority over another.</note> does not harm them; rather, sometimes it helps them. Because through the imperfection and the indiscreet weights of a heavy obedience, one acquires the virtue of obedience and of patience, its sister. Nor does an imperfect place harm them—I say "imperfect" because **religion** <note>original: "religione." Here meaning the formal religious life or joining a monastic order, which was considered a "perfect" state of life compared to the world.</note> is a more perfect, more firm, and more stable thing than any other state. Therefore, I deem "imperfect" the state of those who have the **small key** of obedience, observing the counsels outside of an order; but I do not deem their obedience imperfect, nor of less merit, because every obedience (as has been said) and every other virtue is measured by the measure of love.

And it is indeed true that in many other ways—both because of the **vow** <note>original: "uodo" / "voto." A formal, legal promise made to God through a superior.</note> that he makes in the hands of his prelate, and because he sustains more—obedience is better proven within an order than outside an order. For in every physical act he is bound to this **yoke** <note>original: "zouo," archaic for "giogo." This refers to the "sweet yoke" of Christ mentioned in the Gospels.</note>, and he cannot untie himself whenever he wishes without the guilt of mortal sin: because it is approved by the Holy Church and he has made a vow.

But this is not the case for the other; for he has bound himself voluntarily for the love he has for obedience, but not with a solemn vow. Thus, without the guilt of mortal sin, he could depart from the obedience of that creature, having a legitimate reason—that is, provided he does not depart because of his own defect [sinful impulse]. But if he should depart through his own defect, he would not do so without very grave fault; yet he is not properly bound to mortal sin specifically for that departure. But see how much difference there is between the one and the other: as much as between him who takes what belongs to another, and him who has lent it, and then takes back that which he had given for love with the intention of not asking for it back, but he has no **contract** <note>original: "carta," literally "paper" or "document."</note> for it.

# Providence CLXV

affirmatively: but that one has given [the gift], and the **document** <note>original: "carta." Refers to the legal or formal record of the religious profession.</note> is drawn up in the **profession** <note>original: "p̄fessiōe." The formal act of entering a religious order by taking vows.</note>. Thus into the hands of the **prelate** <note>A religious superior, such as an Abbot or Mother Superior.</note> he renounces himself and promises to observe obedience, continence, and voluntary poverty; and the prelate promises to him that, if he observes these until death, he will be given eternal life. 

So then, regarding observance in place and in manner: that [religious life] is more perfect, and this [secular life] is less perfect; that one is more secure, and if one falls, it is easier to rise again because it has more help; and this one is more doubtful and less secure. It is easier, if he happens to fall, to turn his head back, because he does not feel bound by a **vow** made in profession. Thus he remains like a **religious** <note>original: "religioso." Someone belonging to a formal monastic or mendicant order.</note> before he is professed, who until the profession is made can leave, but afterwards cannot. 

But I have told you about the **merit**, and I say it again: that it is given according to the measure of the **love** <note>original: "lamore."</note> of the truly obedient person, so that everyone, of whatever state they may be, can perfectly have the merit, since I have placed it only in love. Thus I call some to one state and others to another, according to what each is suited to receive; but everyone always receives with this stated measure of love. And so, if the **secular** <note>original: "seculare." A person living "in the world" rather than in a monastery.</note> person loves more than the religious, and if the religious loves more than the secular, they merit more; and so it is for all the others.

### ¶ How God does not reward according to the labor of obedience, nor according to the length of time, but according to the greatness of charity and promptness; and of the miracles God has shown for this virtue; and of discretion in obeying; and of the reward of the truly obedient. Chapter 165.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' decorated with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

O where I have placed all in the **vineyard** <note>A common biblical metaphor for the Church or the spiritual life where souls labor for God.</note> of obedience to work in various ways: and to everyone the **price** <note>original: "precio." The spiritual reward or "wage" of eternal life.</note> shall be given according to the measure of love, and not according to the suffering, nor according to the measure of time—that is, that he who came early should have more than he who came late—just as it is contained in the **Holy Gospel** <note>A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16), where those who started late received the same wage as those who started early.</note>

### Of Divine Providence

...[offering you] My life as an example of those who were idle and were sent by the Lord to work in **His vineyard** <note>original: "uigna foa." A reference to the Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard from Matthew 20.</note>. And He gave as much to those who went late to work as to those who went at the hour of **Prime** <note>original: "prĩa." The first of the "canonical hours" of prayer, observed at sunrise.</note>; and as much to those of **Terce** <note>original: "tertia," the third hour, or 9 a.m.</note>, and to those who went at **Sext** <note>original: "sexta," midday</note>, and at **None** <note>original: "nõa," the ninth hour, or 3 p.m.</note>, and at **Vespers** <note>original: "uespro," evening</note>, as to those of the first hour. By this, I am showing you My life: that you are rewarded not according to the time, nor according to the work, but according to the measure of **love** <note>original: "laore," an archaic form of "amore."</note>.

Hence many are set to work in this vineyard in their **childhood** <note>original: "pueritia."</note>; and some enter later, and some in their old age. Nevertheless, these [who come late] will sometimes walk with such a fire of love—because they see the brevity of the time—that they catch up to those who entered in their childhood, because those [who started early] have walked with slow steps. Therefore, in the love of obedience, the soul receives its merit and fills its vessel in Me, the **peaceful sea** <note>A recurring metaphor in Catherine's writing for the infinite nature of God.</note>.

And there are many who have so proven this obedience, and have so embodied it within their souls, that they do not even stop to seek the reason why a thing is commanded of them by the one who commands. Instead, they hardly wait for the word to leave the mouth, because with the **light of faith** <note>original: "lũe de la fede."</note> they understand the intention of their **prelate** <note>A religious superior, such as an Abbot or Bishop.</note>.

Wherefore the truly obedient person obeys the intention of their prelate more than the **word** <note>original: "pola," likely "parola."</note>, judging that the will of the prelate exists within My will, and that I command him through My dispensation and will. And therefore I told you that such a one obeyed the intention more than the word; he obeyed that word because he first obeyed the prelate's will with affection, seeing it with the light of faith and judging his will to be in Me.

This was well shown by the one of whom we read in the **Lives of the Fathers** <note>original: "uita patrum." A famous collection of hagiographies and sayings of the early desert monks.</note>, who first obeyed with affection: for when an act of obedience was commanded by his prelate, and he had at that hour begun to write an **O** <note>original: "uno o." The letter of the alphabet.</note> or some other small thing, he did not give himself enough space even to want to finish it, but was immediately ready for obedience.

# Providence CLXV (226)

### Divine Providence CLXV

Wherefore, to show how pleasing it was to Me, I gave them the sign: and I completed My other writing in gold, that is, **My clemency** <note>original: "clemẽtia mia." Catherine often describes God's attributes as being written upon the soul or the world.</note>. This glorious virtue of obedience is so pleasing to Me that there is no other virtue in which so many signs and testimonies of miracles are given by Me as in it; for it proceeds from the **light of faith** <note>original: "lume de la fede." A central concept for Catherine: faith provides the spiritual vision necessary to obey without questioning.</note>.

And to demonstrate how much it pleases Me: the earth is obedient to this virtue, and the animals are obedient to it—just as you yourself were in your obedience. Wherefore, if you turn to the earth, you see how it obeyed the obedient man. As you know—if you well remember having read in the **Lives of the Fathers** <note>original: "uita patrũ." Referring to the *Vitae Patrum*, a famous collection of the lives and sayings of the early desert monks.</note>—about that disciple who, having been given a dry piece of wood by his abbot, was commanded through obedience that he should plant it in the earth and water it every day until it bore fruit. And he, as a truly obedient man with the light of faith, did not stop to ask how it would be possible; but without wishing to know the possibility, he fulfilled his obedience. In such a way, by the virtue of obedience and faith, the dry wood **turned green** <note>original: "ſeverdi."</note> and bore fruit.

This was a sign that the soul, truly raised up from the **dryness** <note>original: "fecheza." This likely refers to *secchezza* (spiritual dryness) which is contrasted here with the "greenness" of grace.</note> of disobedience and made green again, was sprouting the fruit of obedience. Wherefore the **fruit** <note>original: "pomo," literally "apple," but used generally for fruit.</note> of that wood was called by the Holy Fathers the "fruit of obedience." And if you look at the animals likewise, you find that they obey the obedient man. Wherefore that disciple, sent by obedience, through his purity and obedience took a lioness and led her to his abbot. But the abbot, like a wise physician—so that the disciple would not be carried away by the wind of **vainglory** <note>original: "uana glia." Pride or seeking human praise for spiritual gifts.</note> and to test him in patience—drove him away with insults, saying: "You beast, you have brought a beast bound to me."

And if you look at the fire likewise: wherefore you have it in Holy Scripture that many, in order not to transgress My obedience and to obey Me promptly, being placed in the fire, the fire did not harm them. Just as those **three youths** <note>original: "tre zoueneti." Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel.</note> were, who were in the furnace and the fire did not harm them, and many others of whom much could be said.
