# Of the Divine Chapter

Being sent by obedience to save that disciple, he went across the water. Wherefore he did not think of himself, but through the **light of faith** <note>original: "collūe d la fede."</note> to fulfill the obedience of his superior <note>original: "p̃lato." Literally "prelate," but used here to mean a religious superior or abbot.</note>; and he went over the water just as if he were walking upon the land, and he saved the disciple <note>A reference to St. Maurus saving St. Placidus from drowning at the command of St. Benedict. Maurus was so focused on obeying that he did not realize he was walking on water.</note>. In all things, therefore, if you open the **eye of the intellect** <note>original: "lochio de tellecto." Catherine’s frequent term for the soul's capacity to perceive spiritual truths through grace.</note>, you will find that I have shown you the excellence of this virtue; and therefore every other thing should be left for the sake of obedience.

Wherefore, if you were raised in such contemplation and in such vision of mind in Me that your body was suspended from the earth <note>Catherine is describing a state of ecstatic levitation, which she herself was said to experience.</note>, and obedience was imposed upon you—speaking generally and not of a specific thing which does not impose a law—I say to you that you should force yourself to rise to fulfill the imposed obedience. Think that you should never rise from prayer when it is the hour for it, except for necessity, or for charity, or for obedience. This I tell you so that you may see how much I desire it to be prompt in its members <note>original: "prõpta ne li ſui me." Likely referring to the "members" or practitioners of the religious life.</note> and how pleasing it is to Me. 

Wherefore, whatever the obedient man does is meritorious. If he eats, he eats with obedience. If he sleeps, he sleeps with obedience. If he goes, if he stays, if he fasts, if he wakes—everything he does with obedience. If he is in the choir, or in the refectory, or stays in his cell, it is obedience that guides him or makes him stay there. In the light of the **most holy faith** <note>original: "ſctiſſia fede."</note>—with which light he has cast himself down, humbled and with hatred for his own will—he is held in the arms of the Order and of his superior. 

With this obedience, remaining within the **ship** <note>original: "naue." Catherine frequently compares a religious order to a ship that carries the soul safely through the storms of life.</note> and allowing himself to be guided by his superior, he has navigated the tempestuous sea of this life with great calm <note>original: "bõaccia." Referring to a "bonanza" or a dead calm at sea.</note>, with a sincere mind and with tranquility of heart; because obedience with faith draws away all darkness. Wherefore he stands strong and secure, because he has removed weakness and fear by taking away his **own will** <note>original: "ppria uolũta." The surrender of the individual ego is the central goal of Catherine’s asceticism.</note>, from which comes every weakness and disordered fear. 

And what does this **bride of obedience** <note>original: "ſpoſa de lobediẽt." The soul that is "wedded" to the virtue of obedience.</note> eat and drink? She eats by the knowledge of herself and of Me, knowing herself to be nothing and recognizing her own defect, and knowing Me, who am—

# Providence 166

They are the ones who taste and eat my life, which they have known in my Truth, the **Incarnate Word** <note>original: "uerbo icarnato." This refers to Jesus Christ as the Word of God made flesh.</note>; and those who drink: they drink the blood. In this blood, the Word has shown them my truth and the ineffable love I have for them. In that same blood, He reveals His **obedience** <note>original: "obedientia." A central theme for Catherine, where Christ's death on the cross is seen as the ultimate act of obedience to the Father.</note> placed in Him for your sake by Me, His eternal Father.

And so the soul becomes inebriated; and once it is drunk on the blood and the obedience of the Word, it loses itself and all its own self-will and self-taste. It possesses Me through grace, tasting Me through the affection of love with the **light of faith** <note>original: "lume de la fede." The spiritual insight granted by God to see beyond the physical world.</note> in holy obedience. Thus, its entire life gives it peace, and in death it receives what was promised by its superior <note>original: "prelato." Referring to the head of a religious order who receives a monk or nun's vows.</note> at their profession: that is, eternal life, the vision of peace, and supreme, eternal tranquility and rest. This is an inestimable good that no one can fully value or comprehend, because it is infinite. Therefore, this infinite good cannot be contained by any finite thing, except in the way a vessel is placed in the sea. The vessel does not contain the whole sea, but only that quantity which it can hold within itself; yet it is the sea that contains the vessel.

In this same way, I—the peaceful sea—am the only one who can comprehend and value Myself. From My own self-valuation and comprehension, I enjoy Myself. And the soul enjoys the good that I share with you from within Myself; I fill each person according to their own measure, and I do not leave them empty, giving them perfect beatitude. Thus, the soul comprehends and knows of my goodness as much as is given to it to know by Me.

The obedient one, therefore, with the light of faith in this life—burning in the **furnace of charity** <note>original: "fornace d' la charita." A common metaphor in Catherine’s writing for the intense, purifying love of God.</note>, anointed with humility, inebriated by the blood, accompanied by the sister of patience and by self-contempt (lowering themselves through fortitude), and with long perseverance and all the other virtues (that is, with the fruit of the virtues)—has received their final end from their Creator, which is Me.

...-m of **obedience** <note>original: "lobediẽtia." The text likely refers to the "consummate state" or "mode" of obedience mentioned at the end of the previous section.</note>: wherefore if you well remember, in the beginning you asked Me with anxious desire—just as I made you ask in order to make the fire of My **charity** <note>original: "charita." Divine love, which Catherine describes as a fire that transforms the soul.</note> grow in your soul—you asked Me, I say, for four petitions. One of these was a part to which I have satisfied, illuminating you with My **Truth** and showing you in what way you might know this life, which you desired to know: that is, that with the knowledge of yourself and of Me, with the **light of faith** <note>original: "lue d̃ la fede."</note>, I leveled for you the way in which you came to the knowledge of life.

<margin>I: I-</margin>The second petition that you asked was that I should show **mercy to the world**. The third was for the **mystical body of the holy Church**, praying Me that I would take away its darkness and its persecution, you wishing that I would punish their iniquities upon yourself. Wherefore in this I declared to you: that no pain given in finite time can satisfy for the guilt committed against Me, the infinite Good, purely as pure pain; but it does satisfy if the pain is joined with the desire of the soul and with the contrition of the heart.

<margin>36: 1g- I: 24-</margin>The way, I have declared it to you; I have also answered you that I wish to show mercy to the world, showing you that mercy is My primary attribute. In order to show Him to you very clearly, I placed Him before you in the likeness of a **bridge**, which reaches from heaven to earth through the union of My divine nature with your human nature.

<margin>20: 3-</margin>I also showed you, to illuminate you further regarding My life, how the bridge was ascended by **three steps** <note>original: "tre scalõi." These represent the three powers of the soul (memory, intellect, and will) and the three stages of spiritual growth.</note>: that is, with the three powers of the soul. And of this same bridge I have shown you, I also figured these three steps in His body as you know: by the **feet**, by the **side**, and by the **mouth**. In these I placed three states of the soul: that is, the **imperfect state**, the **perfect state**, and the **most perfect state**, where the soul reaches the excellence of **unitive love**. And in each one I have shown you clearly: what that thing is which takes away imperfection and makes it reach perfection, and by what way it goes, and of the hidden deceptions of the devil, and...

I have also answered you the **fourth petition** of that which you prayed of me: that is, that I should provide for a particular case that occurred, for which I provided just as you know. And concerning this I have declared my **providence** to you in general and in particular, from the beginning of the creation of the world until the end; how I have done and do everything with divine providence, giving and permitting what I give—tribulation and temporal and spiritual consolation—I do everything for your good, and so that you may be sanctified in me, and so that my life may be fulfilled in you; since my life was that with which I created you, so that you might have eternal life, which truth was made manifest to you with the blood of the **Only-begotten Word** <note>original: "uerbo unigenito." Refers to Jesus Christ as the Word of God.</note>

unlocked. Now I invite you to weeping—you and my other servants: 
and with weeping, and with humble and continuous prayer <note>original: "orōne" (oratione)</note>, I wish to show

that you are not rebuked for going slowly: because more will be 
demanded of you by me now than before, because I have manifested myself 
to you in my life. Look then, that you never leave 
the cell of self-knowledge: but in this cell consume and 
spend the treasure that I have given you: which is a doctrine of life 
founded upon the living rock, Christ <note>original: "xpō"</note> sweet Jesus: and it is clothed in 
light, which discerns the darkness; in this, therefore, clothe yourself, 
most beloved daughter, in life. 

¶ How this devout soul, thanking God, makes prayer <note>original: "orōne" (oratione)</note> for all the world, and for the Holy Church, and commending the virtue of faith, makes an end to this work. Chapter CLXVII.

->**Providence CLXVII**<-

**THEN** that soul, having seen with the eye of the **intellect** <term>intellect: in Catherine’s theology, the "eye" of the soul that perceives spiritual truth through the light of faith</term> and known through the light of most holy faith the life and the excellence of **obedience**; and having seen it with feeling and tasted it through affection with a yearning <note>original: "spasimato," implying a desire so intense it causes a physical or spiritual pang</note> desire, as she contemplated the divine majesty, she rendered thanks to him, saying: "Grace and thanks be to you, Eternal Father, that you have not despised me, your creature, nor have you turned your face from me, nor despised my desires. O Eternal Light, you have not looked upon my darkness; you, Life, have not looked upon me, who am death; nor you, Physician, upon my grave infirmities. You, Eternal Purity, have not looked upon me, who am full of mud and of many miseries; you who are infinite upon me, who am finite; you, Wisdom, upon me, who am foolishness. From all these and many other infinite evils and defects that are in me, your wisdom, your clemency, your goodness, and your infinite good have not despised me. But in your goodness you have given me light; in your wisdom I have known the life; in your clemency I have found your charity and the love of neighbor."

"What has constrained you? Not my virtues, but only your charity. Therefore, let that same love constrain you to illuminate the eye of my intellect in the light of faith, so that I may know and understand your life manifested to me. Grant that my memory may be capable of receiving your benefits; let my will burn in the fire of your charity, which fire makes the body sprout and shed blood <note>A reference to the soul's mystical participation in the sacrifice of Christ</note>; and with that blood, given for love of Blood <note>original: "sangue dato per amore di sangue," meaning the soul's life offered in return for Christ’s sacrifice</note>, and with the key of obedience, let me unlock the gate of heaven. This same thing I ask of you cordially for every creature who possesses reason, both in common and in particular, and for the **mystical body of the holy Church**. I confess and do not deny it: that you loved me before I existed, and that you love me ineffably, like one 'mad' <note>original: "pazo" (pazzo). Catherine famously uses this term to describe God’s "extravagant" or "irrational" love for humanity that exceeds human logic</note> for your creature. O eternal Trinity! O Deity! Which Deity, through your divine nature, gave value to the price of the blood of your Son; you, eternal Trinity, are a sea..."

### Chapter XIV Of the Divine [Providence]

<meta>The catchword "fon" refers to the word "fondo" (depth) which begins the first paragraph.</meta>

**depth**: for the more I enter into it, the more I find of you. You are **insatiable**: for the soul, sating itself in your **abyss** <term>abyss: Catherine uses this to describe the infinite, bottomless nature of God's love and being</term>, is not sated, because it always remains in hunger for you, and thirsts for you, **Eternal Trinity**, desiring to see you with light in your light. Even as the deer desires the spring of living water <note>A reference to Psalm 42: "As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul pants for you, my God."</note>, so my soul desires to exit the prison of the dark body and see you in truth. O, how long will your face be hidden from my eyes? O **Eternal Trinity**, fire and **abyss of charity**: dissolve now the little vessel of my body; for the knowledge <note>original: "cognoſcimētō" (cognoscimento)</note> that you have given me of yourself in your life constrains me to desire to be freed from the weight of my body, and to give my life for the glory and praise of your name; since I have tasted and seen with the light of the **intellect** in your light, your **abyss**, **Eternal Trinity**, and the beauty of your creature.

Thus, looking at myself in you, I saw myself to be your image: gifted by you, **Eternal Father**, with power, and with your wisdom in the **intellect**, which wisdom is attributed to your only-begotten Son; and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from you and from the Son, has given me a will by which I am able to love. You, **Eternal Trinity**, are the **Maker**, and I am your **handiwork** <note>original: "factura," implying something crafted with care</note>: I have known in the [re]creation that you made of me in the blood of your Son, that you are in love with the beauty of your handiwork. 

O **abyss**, O Eternal Deity, O deep sea! And what more could you give me than to give yourself? You are **fire** that always burns and is not consumed; you are **fire** that consumes in its heat all self-love of the soul; you are **fire** that takes away all coldness; you are **fire** that illuminates, and with your light you have made me known your will. You are that light above every light, who gives to the eye of the **intellect** supernatural light in such abundance and perfection that you clarify the light of **faith**. By this **faith** I see that my soul has life, and in this light it receives you, the Light; thus in the light of **faith** I acquire wisdom in the wisdom of the Word, your Son. In the light of **faith**

# Providence CLXVII, 230

->Providence CLXVII<-

I am strong, and constant, and persevering; in the light of faith I hope, and it does not let me faint <note>original: "uenire ameno" (venire meno), meaning to grow weak, falter, or lose consciousness</note> on the path. This light teaches me the way, and without this light I would walk in darkness; and therefore I said to you, **Eternal Father**, that you should illuminate me with the light through most holy faith. Truly this light is a sea, since it nourishes the soul in you, **peaceful sea**, **Eternal Trinity**. The water of this sea is not troubled, and therefore the soul has no fear, because it knows the truth. It is distilled <note>original: "ſtillata," suggesting the light is pure, clear, or filtered like water</note>, because it manifests hidden things; for where the most abundant light of your faith abounds, it renders the soul certain of what it believes. 

It is a mirror, even as you, **Eternal Trinity**, make me know; for looking into this mirror, and holding it with the hand of love, it represents me in you—who am your creature—and you in me through the union <note>original: "cōiūctiōe" (congiunzione)</note> that you made of the divinity <note>original: "dita" (deità)</note> with our humanity. In this light I know [you], and it represents you to me as the supreme and infinite **Good**. **Good** above every good, happy **Good**, incomprehensible **Good**, and inestimable **Good**. Beauty above every beauty; wisdom above every wisdom; indeed, you are that very **Wisdom**. You, food of the angels given to men with the fire of love; you, the garment that covers every nakedness; you feed the hungry in your sweetness; you are sweet without any bitterness. 

O therefore, **Eternal Trinity**, in your light—which you gave to me, and which I receive with the light of most holy faith—I have known through many and admirable declarations, breathing into me the way of great perfection, so that with light and not with darkness I may be with you, and may be a mirror of a good and holy life. Lift me out of my miserable life, for I have always served you in darkness through my own defect; I have not known your life, and therefore I have not loved it. Why did I not know you? Because I did not see you with the glorious light of most holy faith, since the cloud of self-love <note>original: "lãore pprio" (l'amore proprio)</note> darkened the eye of my intellect; and you, **Eternal Trinity**, with your light dissolved the darkness. And who will be able to reach your height, and give you thanks for such an immeasurable gift and generous benefits as those you have...

### Saint Catherine

...in her body: so much so that her whole manner of living was changed: little [remained of] that act: which she used to perform of tasting food <note>referring to her inability to eat</note>, which became to her such an object of hatred: that it was a singular pain for her to endure it: and if even she did endure it: she did not swallow the substance of the food: but to force herself she moved the food about in her mouth: but nothing passed her throat: rather she spat it out. And also even from a drop of water she could have no refreshment: and she had a very great thirst: and painful: and a fire in her throat: that it seemed as if fire was pouring from her mouth. For all this, however, it did not happen: that she was not in good health <note>original: "p̃ſpita," meaning physical vigor or prosperity</note> in her body, cheerful: and fresh as she was accustomed: and in this way we reached Sexagesima Sunday <note>The second Sunday before Ash Wednesday</note>: and she had that evening at prayer <note>original: "orõne"</note> so strong a seizure <note>original: "accidente"</note>: that briefly from that day forward: she was never healthy. Then on the following Monday night: after we had written a letter, she had another more terrible [seizure] to the extent: that everyone wept for her as dead: and for a great space of time she remained: so that we could never see: that there was life in her: then for the space of several hours she rose up: and she did not seem to be the same person: from then onward every day began to come new pains: and cruel torments in her body. And having already come to Lent <note>original: "q̃drageſima"</note>: she, notwithstanding her infirmity: began to apply such study to prayer: that it was a great feat: with those humble sighs: and painful weeping: that it pulled at our hearts: I believe you know: that her prayers were of such force: that one hour of prayer consumed that little body more: than another person [suffering] on the rack <note>original: "la corda," a common instrument of torture where the victim is suspended by the arms</note> for two days. Wherefore every morning with weeping they lifted her from Communion in such a state: that whoever saw her: judged her dead: and they carried her to her little bed. And staying for the space of an hour: or two, she would rise up: and we would go to Saint Peter's <note>St. Peter's Basilica in Rome</note>: which is a full mile away: and there she would place herself in prayer: and she would stay until near Vespers <note>The evening liturgical office</note>: then she returned home in such a state that she seemed dead: and so also...

# The Passing Of

...continuing to do so: every day in the same manner until the third Sunday of **Lent** <note>original: "q̃drageſima"</note>. Then she laid down, overcome by the innumerable pains: and every day they had increased in that little body: and also because of the immeasurable mental pains that she suffered for the offenses she saw committed against God: and for the "little ones" <note>This likely refers to the "little sheep" or the simple faithful of the Church, or perhaps young souls being led astray during the Western Schism</note> she saw growing today in the **Holy Church**: for which she suffered so much and labored both inwardly and outwardly. 

Already in this way [it had been] eight weeks that she never raised her head, full of intolerable torments from the soles of her feet to the top of her body: so much so that she said several times: "These are not bodily or natural pains, but it seems that I have given leave to the demons to torment this body as they please." And truly it indeed seemed so, for she had the most severe <note>original: "strete," literally "tight," implying constricting or intense pain</note> pains that were ever heard of: and to tell you of her patience, it would seem to me to spoil what I have already said: but I will tell you this: that when a new pain arrived, with joy she raised her eye to God and said: "Thanks be to you, Eternal Spouse, who grants so many gifts and so many graces every day anew to me, your miserable and unworthy servant:" 

And thus she went on consuming that body until the Sunday which was before the **Ascension**. And it had reached such a point that she appeared like one of those bodies that are painted as dead; I do not speak of the face, which even to the grave was angelic and devout, but the torso and other limbs were nothing but bones covered with a thin skin: and she remained paralyzed <note>original: "p duta" (perduta), meaning her lower body had lost all function</note> from the waist down, so that she could not even turn herself a little. 

The night before the said Sunday came, more than two hours before daybreak, and she had a very great change, and it seemed that she was approaching the end; then the whole family <note>The "family" refers to her "Caterinaia," the circle of disciples and spiritual children who followed her</note> was called: and she, with humility and devotion, made a sign from nearby without speaking, that she wanted the holy **absolution** from guilt and punishment <term>absolution from guilt and punishment: a specific plenary indulgence, the "Apostolic Blessing," typically granted to the dying to remit the temporal punishment of sin</term>; and so it was done. She then went on in this way until daybreak, performing almost no action except for a continuous, painful, and weak sighing. Therefore it was decided to give her the extreme

# Saint Catherine

...unction: and so it was done by the hand of our Abbot of **Sant'Antimo** <note>Giovanni di Gano da Orvieto, a close friend and spiritual associate of Catherine</note>. She remained as if she felt nothing. Then, shortly after the said unction, she began to change completely, and to make various gestures with her face and with her arms, as if showing she was under a great siege by demons. She stayed in this cruel battle for more than an hour and a half; and after half of this time had passed in silence, she then began to say:

> "I have sinned, Lord, have mercy on me" <note>original: *peccavi domine misere mei*</note>.

And she said this, I believe, more than sixty times, raising her right arm each time and striking it upon the bed. Then she changed her words and said just as many times:

> "Holy God, have mercy on me" <note>original: *Sancto Dio habi di me misericordia*</note>.

without striking her arm. Then she changed to several ways of speaking, humble and devout, always making different gestures. And after the time I told you of, in an instant her face was completely transformed; from dark and gloomy, it became angelic and joyful. Her eyes, which before seemed pained and extinguished, all cleared and brightened, and it seemed as if she had emerged from a vast ocean <note>original: *generale pelago*, suggesting a deep sea of suffering or spiritual trial</note>. By this, the sorrow of the drowning hearts of us sons and daughters who stood around her, as afflicted as you can imagine, was much mitigated. 

She was lying in the lap of **Lady Alessia** <note>Alessia Saracini, one of Catherine's most devoted companions and a member of the Mantellate</note>, and then she wished to raise herself; and helping her enough that she sat up, she leaned against Lady Alessia. We then placed before her a devout tablet <note>likely a small portable altarpiece or reliquary</note> where there are many relics of saints and certain figures. She then fixed her physical eyes upon the **Crucifix** and began to worship, speaking of the loftiest things regarding the goodness of God; and while praying, she confessed her guilt in the presence of God for all her sins generally, and specifically she said:

> "My fault, Eternal Trinity, that I have offended you miserably with much negligence, ignorance, and ingratitude; in disobedience, and in many other defects. Have mercy on me, for I have not kept your general commandments, nor those specifically made by your goodness for me, miserable as I am."

And many times she beat her breast, declaring her fault. Similarly, she added:

> "I have not observed that commandment which you told me..."

# The Passing of Saint Catherine

### The Confession of the "Pure Dove"

...that I should always seek to give honor to you, and the labor to my neighbor; yet I have fled from labor in the time of need. You, O God, did not command me to abandon myself entirely and only seek the glory and praise of your name in the salvation of beloved souls; you asked me to take this food <note>the "food" of souls for whose salvation she hungered</note> upon the table of the most holy cross, and I have instead sought my own consolations. 

You have always invited me to bind you with agonizing, sweet, and loving desires—with tears and with humble and continuous prayer for the salvation of the whole world and for the reformation of the **Holy Church** <term>Holy Church: The Catholic Church, which Catherine spent her life trying to reform, urging the Pope to return to Rome from Avignon</term>, promising that through these means you would show mercy to the world and reform your Bride <note>original: *sposa tua*, a common mystical metaphor for the Church</note>. And I, wretched as I am, have not answered you, but have stayed asleep in the bed of negligence. 

Woe is me! You placed me to guide souls, giving me so many beloved children <note>the *Caterinaffati*, her circle of spiritual disciples</note>, that I might love them with a singular love and with diligence direct them to you along the way of life; and yet I have been a mirror of misery to them. I have not taken solicitous care of them, nor nurtured them with continuous and humble prayer before you, nor have I given them an example of a good and holy life, nor the doctrine of the word. Alas, wretch that I am! 

I have not held in reverence the innumerable gifts and graces of so many sweet torments and pains which it pleased you to place within this fragile body; and therefore I have not borne them with that burning desire, nor with that burning love with which you gave them to me. 

Alas, my Love: you through your goodness chose me as your bride in the end of my **childhood** <term>childhood: original *pueritia*. Catherine's mystical experiences began at age six, and she made a private vow of virginity shortly after</term>; and I have not been faithful to you, but unfaithful. My memory—I have not kept it filled only with you and your most high benefits. My intellect I have not kept fixed and firm upon your will, nor in seeking your will; and my will has not disposed itself to love you with all its strength without mediation, just as you require of me. 

For these and many other defects, that most pure dove <note>a reference to Catherine herself</note> accused herself—I believe more for our example than for her own need. Then she turned to the priest and said: 

> "Absolve me, for the love of **Christ crucified** <note>original: *Christo crucifixo*</note>, of these..."

# Saint Catherine

...sins which I have confessed in the sight of God and of all the other children I do not remember: and so it was done. Afterward, she desired once more the absolution from guilt and punishment <term>absolution from guilt and punishment: known in Latin as *a culpa et a poena*, this refers to a plenary indulgence, the total remission of temporal punishment for sins</term> saying that she had received it from **Pope Gregory** and **Pope Urban**. This she said as one hungry for the blood of Christ <note>original: *affamata dl sãgue d xp̃o*. Catherine’s mysticism often focused on the "Blood of Christ" as a symbol of divine mercy and salvation</note>. Her will was done; and she, with her eyes always fixed on the **Crucifix**, began again to pray devoutly, speaking of most sublime things which my sins did not merit for me to understand, both because of the great sorrow I felt and because of a pain she had in her chest which did not allow her voice to come out clearly. Even while standing right beside her mouth, I could not understand her, except for two words here and two more there. 

During this prayer, she turned to some of the children who had not been present at a notable sermon <note>original: *notabile smõe*</note> which she had given us many days before, showing us the way of perfection and imposing on each of us individually what she wished us to do after her life. So then, she did the same for those individuals. 

Asking everyone’s pardon with great humility for the little diligence she felt she had shown for our salvation, she then finally spoke a few words to another disciple and to me, a wretched man. After this, she returned to her prayer. Oh, if you had seen with what humility and reverence she received multiple times the blessing of her sorrowful mother <note>Lapa Di Puccio Piagenti, Catherine’s mother, who was also one of her followers</note>! Truly I tell you that it was a **sweet bitterness**. 

Oh, what devotion it was to see that afflicted mother commend herself to her blessed daughter, and go to her to receive her blessing! It truly drew the hearts from our chests. In particular, the mother asked the daughter that she might obtain grace from God, so that in such hard adversity she would not offend Him. 

All these things did not tire her from her prayer; instead, she prayed continually, speaking of God. And drawing near to the end, she made a singular prayer for the **Holy Church**, for which she reaffirmed that she was giving her life. She prayed for **Pope Urban VI**, whom she effectively confessed as the true Supreme Pontiff, encouraging her children to lay down their lives for this truth. Then with great fervor...

# The Passing of Saint Catherine

...she continued to pray for all her beloved children whom God had given her to love with a singular love: using many of those words which our Savior used when he prayed to the Father for his disciples: praying so cordially that not only our hearts but even stones should have broken. Making the sign of the cross, she blessed us all: and so she approached that so-greatly desired end, persevering continually in prayer, saying: "Lord, you call me, and I come to you; and I come to you not by my own merits, but only by your mercy, which mercy I ask of you by the virtue of your blood." And at the last, she cried out several times: "Blood! Blood!" <note>original: *sangue*. Catherine’s spirituality was deeply centered on the "Blood of Christ" as a purifying force.</note> Ultimately, following the example of our Savior, she said: "Father, into your hands I commend my soul and my spirit" <note>original: *Padre ne le mãe tue comando laia & lo spõ mio*. These are the last words of Jesus on the Cross (Luke 23:46).</note> and so sweetly, with a face looking entirely angelic, bowing her head, she yielded up her spirit <note>original: *emisit spiritum*</note>. 

Her passing occurred on Sunday at about the sixth hour <term>sixth hour: according to the traditional Roman counting of time, this is midday (noon)</term>, and we kept her until the end of Tuesday at the hour of compline <term>compline: the final prayer service of the day, usually held after sunset</term> without any human odor <note>In hagiography, the "odor of sanctity" (the absence of decay or a sweet smell) was a sign of holiness.</note>. And so that holy body remained pure, firm, and fragrant; and her arms, legs, and neck would bend as if she were a living person. With great tumult and devotion, the people visited the body during those three days, and anyone who could touch her held themselves blessed. God has shown many miracles and signs through her, which I pass over saying because of my haste. Her sepulcher is visited with devotion, as are those of the other holy bodies there; and God performs many graces in the name of this, his blessed spouse. I do not doubt that we shall yet hear of great deeds. I have nothing else to say to you. Commend me to the prior and to all the sisters who are now in this time of need; may God preserve you and increase you in the grace of sweet Jesus Christ.

->¶ The Dialogues end.<-

¶ The following verses were composed by the most holy lord, Lord Pius II, Pope <note>Pope Pius II (Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini) canonized Catherine of Siena in 1461.</note>, to the praise of the seraphic spouse of our Lord Jesus Christ, the most blessed Catherine of Siena, of the order of penance of Blessed Dominic <note>The "Order of Penance of St. Dominic" refers to the Dominican Third Order, to which Catherine belonged.</note>.

## In Praise of the Divine Catherine of Siena

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'Q' with floral and foliate motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc>
Who could sing of these sacred deeds? What tongue, however eloquent and powerful, could worthily proclaim the excellence with which this second Catherine <note>original: *catherina secunda*. This refers to Catherine of Siena being seen as the successor in sanctity to Saint Catherine of Alexandria.</note>, spouse of God, shone forth, celebrated throughout the whole world? I am not worthy to extol one so deserving with such high praise; yet, dear traveler, I shall briefly relate to you the nature of her blessed life and her soul's holy character.

She rose from Siena, where she received the habit of Saint Dominic <note>The "habit" refers to the black and white robes of the Dominican Third Order (the *Mantellate*).</note>. Under a threefold vow <term>threefold vow: the traditional monastic vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience</term> and through every virtue, she surpassed the learned men present in the divine law. Powerful in both word and deed, she drew the hearts of all men to herself, just as a magnet draws iron. 

Then Christ betrothed her to himself; he instructed her with his own mouth in sacred teachings. Like an excellent mother and a virgin, she had many disciples, for whom this happy woman completed the arduous Rule of Life and fourteen <note>original: *bis septem* (twice seven)</note> small works of holy piety. She was a sublime consolation to all those suffering, alas, in the failings of this present life.

That soul asked the Lord that her heart be renewed; meditating continually, she happily achieved her high desire. She saw Christ pluck out her old heart and hand her a new one, burning with flames. Having fasted for a long time, she was sometimes snatched up to the stars; she saw the wonders of God, and once even returned to life from death <note>This refers to Catherine's "mystical death" in 1370, a four-hour trance during which she believed she saw heaven and hell before being commanded by God to return to public life.</note>.

Refreshed by the sacred bread of heaven—the bread of salvation—and always carrying the cross in her mindful heart, she suffered the wounds of Christ <note>original: *stigmata*. Catherine is said to have received the stigmata (the wounds of the crucifixion) in 1375, though they were invisible until after her death.</note>, a marvelous thing to tell. She went to the Popes, who considered it their unique glory to stand in conversation with her. She brought to them with her own mouth the favors she wished to be granted; so great was the grace of her eloquent tongue. Indeed, a prophetess full of divine breath, she revealed many secrets of both peace and war. Exhorting everyone, she wrote down things both wonderful and amazing.

# In Praise of God

She, knowing the day had come in which it was necessary to leave this world, cried out: "O best God, into your hands I commend my soul <note>original: *In manibus commendo tuis*. These are the last words of Christ on the cross, signaling Catherine's final imitation of his life.</note>; and I commend your handmaid to you continually." Thus the blessed bride passed to her blessed groom, adorned with three crowns <note>The "three crowns" in hagiography usually symbolize virginity, martyrdom (or spiritual suffering), and doctorate (holy wisdom).</note>. She performed many miracles in this life; and then, after death, she shone brightly with innumerable wonders. If you wish to know these, and how holily she always lived in the world, read through this sacred history with devotion. She lived for thirty-three years—as many as Christ—and fittingly so; for it is right for the bride to be the same age as her groom. In the year one thousand three hundred and eighty, the illustrious virgin Catherine of Siena died in Rome.

¶ A chapter in rhyme composed by Anastagio da Montaltino <note>Anastagio was a poet and member of the "Caterinati," the group of disciples who followed Catherine's teachings.</note> in praise and reverence of Saint Catherine of Siena, the seraphic bride of Christ, written while she was still living this present life.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'I' featuring a portrait of a bearded man with a hood, likely a saint or monk.</image-desc>

In truth, my lazy soul, what are you doing?
O foolish, O slow one, why do you still sleep?
You see that time flies, yet you remain still.
Ensure that your intellect applies itself
to speaking of this bride of Jesus,
who moves the world in such graceful ranks.
What marvel was ever here below,
angelic or human? Or what miracle?
Hardly even that of the Baptist <note>St. John the Baptist.</note> was greater.
This blessed woman is a bold obstacle to vices,
for she drives them all away; and she has filled
every virtue into her holy tabernacle <note>A metaphor for her body or soul as a vessel for the divine.</note>.
Now, Holy Spirit, guide the reins
of the intellect to speak of this saint,
so that the weak heart does not fail.

### Saint Catherine

From the crown of her head down to the soles of her feet,
  she is full of Christ; she is the true handmaid <note>original: *ancilla*</note>
  who sings His glory day and night.
She always keeps her eyes turned toward heaven,
  bathed in pious tears,
  from which every good grace sparkles forth.
Let no one ever imagine that she did anything but place
  her sweet mouth at the holy feet
  of Him who submitted to death for us,
So that He might forgive our wicked, false, and guilty deeds
  to anyone who, with true penance <note>original: *penitencia*</note>,
  confesses and says, "Have mercy on me" <note>original: *miserere mei*</note>.
Her charitable conscience
  would give even her pure blood,
  so courteous is she, and so full of mercy.
She is a palisade, a moat, and a firm wall <note>These military metaphors describe Catherine as a spiritual fortress protecting those who seek her intercession.</note>
  to every sinner who takes refuge in her;
  she promises them certain help.
Such great knowledge flows from her mind—
  sent into her by the divine flame—
  that all human wisdom is consumed before it.
O dear, O sweet, O venerable mother <note>original: *mamma*. Catherine’s disciples and followers affectionately called her "Mamma" regardless of their age or status.</note>,
  as I see you at the foot of the holy altar,
  you who do not possess even a single grain of life left in your body,
Because your spirit rises up to venerate
  that exalted Lord in the pure Host <note>original: *hostia*</note>,
  whom you wait to receive in communion <note>original: *communicare*</note>.
Suspended in that high state by Him who holds you,
  the priest stands ready in his stole,
  appearing transformed in his figure.
To see how that Host flies
  into its sacred vessel <note>original: *uasello*. This refers to a famous mystical event where the consecrated Host reportedly flew from the priest's hand directly into Catherine's mouth.</note>—O what a marvel
  You show, Father, in this Your daughter!

# Saint Catherine

From the crown of her head to the soles of her feet,
she is full of Christ; she is the true handmaid
who sings His glory by day and by night.
She always keeps her eyes turned toward heaven,
bathed in pious tears,
from which every good grace sparkles forth.
Let no one ever think that she rested
her sweet mouth anywhere but at the holy feet
of Him who offered Himself to death for us.
May He forgive our wicked, false, and guilty deeds
to anyone who, with true penitence,
having confessed, says: "Have mercy on me" <note>original: *miserere mei*. This is a reference to Psalm 51, a central prayer of repentance in the liturgy.</note>.
Her charitable conscience
would give even her pure blood in return,
so gracious is she, and full of mercy.
She is a palisade, a moat, and a firm wall
to every sinner who takes refuge in her;
she promises her sure help.
Such great knowledge flows into her mind,
sent into her by the divine flame,
that all human wisdom is here eclipsed <note>literally "destroyed" or "melted away" (*strugie*).</note>.
O dear, O sweet, O venerable mother,
how I see you at the feet of the holy altar,
where you have not even a drachm <note>original: *drāma*. A tiny unit of weight, used here to suggest she has no earthly life or physical strength left during her ecstasy.</note> of life left in you.
For your spirit rises to venerate
that exalted Lord in the pure Host <note>original: *lhoftia pura*. The consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note>,
whom you wait to receive in communion.
By Him who keeps you suspended in that height,
the priest stands ready with his stole,
revealing you to be of an entirely different form.
To see how that Host flies
into its sacred vessel—O wonder
that you show, Father, in this your daughter!

# Sancta Catharina

But while I remain in this desert, <note>The "desert" is a common medieval metaphor for the spiritual trials of earthly life.</note>
minister to my every spiritual need
as you are accustomed to do for your servant, <note>original: *offerto*, referring to one who has "offered" themselves to the service of a saint or God.</note>
so that you save me from eternal evil,
from every deceit and every hidden snare,
always protected beneath your wings.

And I pray this may be done for every one
of yours who confesses you through God, <note>original: *per idio*. The poet asks Catherine to act as an intermediary, presenting her followers' faith to God.</note>
so that they may be free from evil's entanglement.
I do not pray for the world, no;
but rather that you preserve them from all evil,
so that you may later say of each one, "this is mine."

But let the world weep with all its servants,
for it was no longer worthy of such a treasure,
nor did they recognize it, they who are so arrogant. <term>proterui: describes those who are stubbornly haughty or contemptuous of divine truth.</term>
And let Adam weep with a long dwelling,
since he is deprived of such a paradise,
and let him live by the sweat of his labor. <note>A reference to the Fall of Man and the subsequent curse of toil in Genesis.</note>

Let Abel take care that he is not killed,
and look well to see with whom he walks in the field,
and let him always remain divided from Cain.
For if the flood <term>diluuio: the biblical Great Flood, here symbolizing a coming divine judgment.</term> comes, it will be without an ark,
because our name has gone up to heaven,
entirely free from every heavy burden.

And let every man who was bold enough
to make mockery of her joy fear greatly,
for vengeance now rests within her finger. <note>Suggests that Catherine, now in heaven, has the power to point out and punish the unrepentant.</note>
And let no one in Shinar <note>original: *Senaar*. Shinar is the biblical plain where the Tower of Babel was built.</note> believe they can ever reach
the height of the great tower,
without bearing the bitterness of the confusion of tongues.

For whoever hastens along such paths,
following the actions of proud sects,
whatever they might have gained, they will then be forced to lose.

In the sun there is only Leah <note>original: *liya*. In medieval tradition, Leah represents the "active life," which is considered less perfect than the "contemplative life."</note>: whom among the less perfect

those who follow the footsteps of the servants of God,

he who is holy considers within himself,
just as these outward things are often vain.
**L**et us honor this image with all our heart,
for in it, the greatest honor is given to God,
and a mantle of glory is procured for us.
**J**ust as it is the honor of the emperor
to have his image on the crown, <note>A common medieval analogy: just as an emperor’s authority is respected through his image on coins or regalia, God is honored when His image is respected in the human soul.</note>
so it is done in this case for his Creator.
**B**ut what is worse, often the person
does not wish to crown, out of charity,
the image of God, which is so good;
**B**ut detracting with anger and with grief
from that which God placed there with His hands,
they would willingly clothe themselves in the spoils.
**N**ow let us not wish to be worse than dogs,
but let us respond to Him who often calls,
and show our wounds so that we may be healed.
**F**ollow, follow, everyone who loves her; <note>The poet likely refers to following Saint Catherine’s example or teachings.</note>
I, to make him, if possible, white with goodness,
so that his fame does not fail, but grows.
**N**or should any wise man excuse himself from this.

# Concerning Saint Catherine

## In Praise

...who, through the wisdom of this world below,
is called foolishness before the Trinity <note>original: *trino & uno*, meaning "the Three and One."</note>.
Let him who is ignorant of this take heed,
for he who does not learn will be punished
and, as an ignorant man, will be left in great confusion.
Nor should anyone, for being a youth,
ever excuse himself: because he is cursed,
the child who is gray-haired at a hundred years old. <note>A reference to Isaiah 65:20, implying that a long life spent in sin or spiritual ignorance is a curse, regardless of age.</note>
Nor for being powerful, or a great elect,
should anyone excuse themselves; if they have not followed
those who are masters over their every defect,
they will be powerfully tormented.

# Saint Catherine

There our labor is healed
with peace, rest, and perfection;
there she resides, with the heavenly host.
The first is he who was the vessel of choice <note>original: *vas delectione*, referring to Saint Paul, the "vessel of election" (Acts 9:15), whom Catherine frequently cited as a spiritual model.</note>
who moved her mind to speak to us
the doctrine written in his holy discourse.
The second is he who then girded
her limbs with the holy habit <note>original: *sancta uesta*. This refers to Saint Dominic, the founder of the Dominican Order; Catherine was a member of the Mantellate, the Dominican third order.</note>
who gave an example through this to all his own.
The third is that mother so modest
who was given to her; to whom every pain
of the flesh of Christ was made manifest. <note>The Virgin Mary, who in Catherine's visions acted as a spiritual mother and intermediary.</note>
This is the burning, sweet Magdalene
who added fire to this pure virgin
so that she bound her with a chain of love. <note>Mary Magdalene was Catherine’s primary model for contemplative love and apostolic zeal.</note>
She was a unique creature in the world
in her own time; for which I now strongly long
to renew myself in her, through her nature.
So that I still call out her praises,
that we might follow what she wrote,
though we set it aside for human thoughts.
This woman fixed her mind's intellect
with a nail of love into her Spouse <note>Christ, the "Eternal Bridegroom" in Catherine's mystical theology.</note>
and with Him, she fixed herself entirely upon the cross.
"O sweet," she always said, "my rest,
O immense charity, O true peace,
O eloquent Word of every good.
O light, O truth, how much I love
your essence in that human flesh
which showed you as a burning torch of love."
Divine mirror where the soul finds
honey-sweet doctrine <note>original: *doctrina melliflua*. This term suggests her words were as sweet and nourishing as honey, a common medieval metaphor for divinely inspired writing.</note>—the kind
which never finds those who do not wish to taste it.

This woman set feathered wings to her heart,
flying to draw down here below Him
who moved her toward the good from such great evil.

And they were so well-founded [in faith]; let them pray to Him,
that a dart of humble and strong love,
which made her a light for our dark paths, [might guide us].

**Chosen** by divine fate,
she lifted her mind toward Christ,
with her body [left behind] before her natural death. <note>This refers to Catherine’s frequent "ecstatic deaths" or trances, during which her soul was said to leave her body to converse with God.</note>

**High** lifted up to converse with Christ,
she spoke of the incarnation of this Word,
and how He was three persons in one.

**In** a single essence: in a mystery, <note>original: *riserbo*, implying something set aside or hidden from common view; here referring to the nature of the Godhead.</note>
uncreated, not made; and this point of doctrine
this virgin clarified with her own word.

**Fixed** she stood, and firm as a stone, <note>original: *stechita*, likely *stecchita*, referring to the physical rigidity common in her mystical raptures.</note>
transformed into Jesus, entirely joyful,
filled with such height here in this lowly world.

**Set** with her face crimson and cleansed
by that Sun, <note>A common metaphor for God or the "Sun of Justice."</note> and washed with tears,
she returned to her body on this unclean earth.

**And** there she reproached our sins,
showing through her doctrine how bitter
was the price paid so that the soul might be cleansed.

**And** she spoke of the blood, so precious,
given through immense charity and through sorrow,
all of it given for our refuge.

**Augustine**, Gregory the Confessor,
Jerome, and Ambrose <note>The four "Great Doctors" of the Western Church. The poet suggests that Catherine reached through love the same truths they reached through lifelong academic study.</note> obtained with great labor
what she received through burning love.

**This** woman, made chaste by her [Saint] Paul,
whom she accompanied by following his style,
writing to every friend, both man and woman. <note>Catherine was a prolific correspondent, dictated over 300 letters to people of all social classes, often mirroring the apostolic zeal of Saint Paul.</note>

# Saint Catherine

**And** with her spirit she followed Christ,
always looking upon sin—
but not at those sinners she called,

**Saying**, “O my father, o my children,
fix your eyes on the blood that was shed
from the holy breast, hands, and holy feet.”

**So that** in the holy fire in which she burned,
you might walk forever; this she said
so that ungrateful and meager minds would not taste [this]. <note>The "meager minds" refers to those who lack spiritual depth or refuse to accept the grace of Catherine's teachings.</note>

**These** sweet sermons that she gave
are food to those who taste them, just as she
fed herself without any other human food. <note>A reference to Catherine’s famous fasting, or *inedia*, where she reportedly lived for years consuming nothing but the Eucharist.</note>

**In** that shining sun, she became a star
for us here, to turn away our troubles
and to guide us straight with her little ship. <note>original: *nauicella*. In Catherine’s *Dialogue*, the "navicella" or "little boat" represents the Church, which she worked tirelessly to reform and guide.</note>

**Kings**, princes, communes, and great tyrants
were urged by her to rethink
what those thoughts were that most deceived them. <note>Catherine was a prolific letter-writer, corresponding with the Pope, the King of France, and various Italian city-state rulers to promote peace and church reform.</note>

**And** she made many turn the sails
of every ship of theirs laden with malice,
and, repentant and confessed, to make amends.

**Blessed** was he who ran to the ark,
called by her who descended
to the port of salvation in this boat.

**She** always stretched out her merciful palms
toward heaven, toward that <term>Word Incarnate</term> <note>original: *uerbo incarnato*; the theological term for Jesus as the Word of God made flesh.</note>
to make herself a shield against our evil.

**Her** father, the blessed <term>Dominic</term>, <note>Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers (Dominicans). Catherine was a member of the Mantellate, a third-order Dominican group.</note>
was the beginning of this oracle for her,
as the founder of her every state.

**Sweet** was that which came out of the <term>tabernacle</term>, <note>While usually referring to the vessel holding the Eucharist, here it may also metaphorically refer to the "tabernacle" of her heart or the physical church where she prayed.</note>
that prayer so immense that it was fitting
that no cause should pose an obstacle.

# In Praise of God

**To** the Word I invoke: from which He does not hold back
His holy army nor Himself, <note>original: *militia*. In a medieval religious context, this refers to the "Heavenly Host" or the company of angels and saints.</note>
for He comes to give the ring to everyone. <note>This refers to the "Mystical Marriage," a spiritual union where Catherine received a ring from Christ, visible only to her.</note>

**And** He placed the heart of this virgin
so firmly upon charity with the Father
that He drove every human thought from it.

**Her** prayers were always "thieves,"
stealing souls away from the world through her rhythm <note>original: *metro*. This likely refers to the persuasive "measure" or song-like quality of her prayers and speech.</note>
and drawing them toward the Holy Mother Church.

**And** she always desired to drink from the glass <note>original: *bere al uetro*. Likely a metaphor for clear spiritual vision or a specific visionary experience of the divine "crystalline" heavens.</note>
alongside Agatha, Ursula, and Lucy, <note>Saints Agatha, Ursula, and Lucy were popular virgin martyrs often invoked alongside Catherine as models of female sanctity.</note>
to shed more light upon our dark path.

**But** by another path and another way,
as it pleased Him, He took her up,
so that she might also do as those who, with Mary,

**Were** compelled to shed blood in His name;
but having received the martyrdom of the price already paid, <note>Refers to the idea that Catherine suffered a "spiritual martyrdom" of desire, even though she did not die a violent death like the early saints.</note>
she desired this more than any other suffering.

**It** was indeed He, with a sapphire gem,
who made this bride so worthy
that she joined the heavenly circle alongside the others.

**Afterward**, she always longed to raise the banner
toward those who have not known
the death that was so worthy for their sake. <note>A reference to the Crucifixion of Christ.</note>

**And** calling for help from the Word of God
through that Mother who was born of blood <note>original: *madre che di ſangue nacque*. In Catherine’s theology, the Church was "born" from the blood flowing from the side of Christ on the Cross.</note>
and who was aided by grace for her sake,

**This** virgin pleased Christ so greatly
that many times while she stood in contemplation,
washing us with the water of her tears,

**Christ** would leave the hands of the priest
at the incensed altars—as an example to us—
and enter into her as if into His own temple. <note>This describes a famous miracle recorded by Catherine’s biographers, where the consecrated Host was said to fly miraculously from the priest's hands into Catherine's mouth during the Mass.</note>

# Saint Catherine

**These** foods were to her much more dear,
wherefore without other food she remained full
of this; for of others she took but rarely. <note>This refers to Catherine’s "holy anorexia" or *inedia*. Historical accounts claim that for much of her later life, she was unable to eat ordinary food and lived almost entirely on the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note>

**O** virginal city: O sweet Siena,
blessed more by her than by any other glory of yours,
though you have made yourself so distant from her. <note>The poet rebukes the city of Siena for failing to follow Catherine's holy example or for the political strife that ignored her calls for peace.</note>

**Up**, up, let us run with attentive memory
to clear the mists of what sin abhors;
let us have victory over ourselves, just as she did.

**Pray** to her then, that she may help you,
as a true imitator of the Father, <note>original: *padre*. This likely refers to Saint Dominic, the founder of the Dominican Order to which Catherine belonged as a lay member, though it may also refer to God the Father.</note>
and that she may anticipate our every plea.

**O** happy virgin chosen by heaven,
O one full of contemplative virtue
in Him who was the root of our salvation.

**Make** me write, along with your other servants,
O holy virgin, you from whom distills for me
that which does not diminish my speaking of you. <note>The poet asks for a "distillation" of grace or inspiration, a common metaphor for receiving divine wisdom to write sacred poetry.</note>

**You**, blessed among the others, a true handmaid, <note>original: *ancilla*. A Latin term for a female servant or handmaid, famously used by the Virgin Mary (*Ancilla Domini*).</note>
seraphic among the other seraphim,
where your bright ray shines out among the rest. <note>In medieval theology, Seraphim are the highest order of angels, defined by their "burning" love. Catherine is traditionally known as the "Seraphic Virgin" because of her intense mystical love for Christ.</note>

**You** live up there among the cherubim;
now you are filled by your serene Spouse,
for you find yourself there within His essence.

**O** sweet light among us that does not fail,
may you be praised, and also the holy body <note>original: *telo*. Literally "cloth" or "canvas," but here used metaphorically to describe the "fabric" or "vessel" of her recorded teachings and doctrine.</note>
of your doctrine, with which you have filled us—
an example on earth and a joy in heaven.

->Amen<-

# In praise of God

### Praise in honor of the seraphic Saint Catherine of Siena composed by the aforementioned Raynerio.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a leafy, floral design within a square border.</image-desc>**To** heaven has returned
the bride to her groom;
the loving woman to the loving man,
and the beloved to the lover. <note>This imagery reflects the "Mystical Marriage" of Saint Catherine to Jesus, a central theme in her hagiography where she is said to have been spiritually wed to Christ.</note>
**To** the immaculate lamb
went the humble little lamb;
that which she so greatly desired,
she possesses now with great peace.
**And** this star shines more
than a thousand, thousand others,
because more sparks of love
were found by her for her lover.
**Not** sparks but a great flame
was the love of such a furnace;
and therefore she was made a mother
here by the divine peace, <note>Catherine was often called "Mamma" by her circle of followers (the *Caterinaia*), reflecting her role as a spiritual mother and guide.</note>
**Whence** she pleased and pleases so much
the entire blessed kingdom,
that the world was no longer worthy
to have such a lover.
**Because** she wept with those who weep,
therefore she rejoices with those who rejoice.

<column-break/>

**She** did not walk with slow steps
to flee the infernal fraud;
and because she, the humble little one,
fled from human praise,
**Like** a great queen
she is exalted above many.
She was also found keeping watch
during every vigil of the night,
**Wherefore** to the Father <note>original: *padre*. This likely refers to God the Father, though it may also allude to Saint Dominic, the spiritual "father" of her order.</note> it pleases much
to minister to his daughter;
and in short, God makes great,
great indeed, those who resemble Him.
**Because** He spreads the name
of those who gather with Him.
Her lamp was always furnished
with oil and with fire <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matthew 25), who must keep their lamps burning to meet the Bridegroom.</note>
**To** buy the pearl; <note>original: *margarita*. A reference to the "Pearl of Great Price" (Matthew 13:45–46), representing the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>
what she had, she gave, and not a little.
Wherefore she now has a principal place
at the wedding feast, where to go
**She** did not care to make excuses,
but well accepted the invitation.

### The Front Cover and Binding

This page displays the front cover of a leather-bound manuscript, featuring elaborate **gold tooling** <note>Gold tooling is a decorative technique where a bookbinder uses heated metal stamps to press gold leaf into the leather, creating permanent, shimmering designs.</note> on deep brown leather. The binding is decorated with multiple rectangular gilt borders, a hallmark of fine Renaissance craftsmanship.

->**The Central Illustration**<-

At the heart of the cover is a mandorla-shaped <note>A "mandorla" (the Italian word for almond) is an oval or almond-shaped frame used in art to surround sacred figures.</note> **cartouche** <term>cartouche</term> <note>A cartouche is an ornamental frame, often featuring curved lines or scrollwork, used to highlight a central image.</note> formed by ornate foliate scrollwork. Within this central frame is a gold-stamped illustration of the **Crucifixion**:

*   **Jesus Christ** is depicted on the cross.
*   He is flanked by two standing figures, traditionally identified in Christian iconography as the **Virgin Mary** and **Saint John the Evangelist**.

Surrounding the central frame are four stylized **fleur-de-lis** <note>The fleur-de-lis is a stylized lily symbol, often associated with royalty or the Virgin Mary.</note> symbols, one positioned in each corner of the inner decorative field. The spine edge of the cover shows evidence of original binding cords or clasps, which would have held the book tightly shut, and the leather exhibits wear and age-related distressing at the edges, testifying to the book's long history since the late 16th century.
